text: PC Gareth Browning, 33, was on foot in Whitley, Reading on 30 November when he was hit by a black Mazda Aerosport driven by Luke Haywood, 28. Haywood admitted causing death by dangerous driving and seven counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving at Reading Crown Court today (12 January). Gareth died after being rushed to the Royal Berkshire Hospital with severe head injuries. He had been walking near his home in Upper Merton Road when he was struck. A postmortem examination found that Mr Browning suffered multiple fractures as well as other internal organ damage due to the force of collision. Luke Haywood's car Credit: Thames Valley PolicePA Wire The court heard that Haywood had "a long history" of offending but did not have any previous convictions for dangerous driving or drink-driving before this incident. However, police said they were unable to determine whether he was under the influence of alcohol at the time of the crash because there was no breath test available at the hospital. Mr Browning's family described him as "the adored" father of five children aged between 12 weeks and 26 years old who are all now without their dad. Speaking outside Reading Crown Court today, Detective Inspector Kate Collins, from the Serious Collision Investigation Unit based at Reading, thanked witnesses who came forward immediately following Mr Browning's accident about what happened. She also paid tribute to those men whose efforts helped save Mr Browning's life during CPR attempts. Det Insp Collins added: 'Both incidents involved two drivers travelling through residential areas at speed. They should never have been doing so - but sadly lives have been lost as a result."

I thought I was lucky when I ended up first in line to the new Hot Angels nightclub. Now I'm not so sure. I know you're supposed to arrive at a club casually late, but I couldn't help it. I had heard so much about the club since they announced the grand opening last week, and supposedly they were going to be giving out a new drink for free to until supplies ran out. Which could be soon, considering how many people could cram into the large refurbished factory. So I had shoved my friend Kara into a mini skirt and dragged her out into the brisk spring air two hours before the club opened. The odd thing was, the bouncer was a thin old woman. She looked like she could snap in the force of the next stiff breeze, but I had watched enough YouTube to know that you couldn't judge such aged books by their covers. In one video I had seen an old woman half her size and probably ten years older kick the shit out of a shoplifter twice her size. I even dragged one of my videography school buddies over to the computer to verify that it wasn't faked. After ages of avoiding eye contact with the bouncer, and walking in small circles with Kara to keep our bare legs warm while I endured her barrage of whining, the bouncer finally reached for the velvet rope that acted as the gate between the front of the line and the club. As she did so with her left hand, she reached up to my forehead with her right and said, in unison with the hundred people who stood in line behind us, "Before we enter, we pray." I froze, my eyes finding Kara to my left. She looked like she had just shoved a handful of chocolate in her mouth and discovered it was dog crap. I didn't know if I wanted to laugh, or cry. What the hell was this? Had we waited for two hours in front of the wrong club? I didn't want to interrupt as the old woman and the crowd muttered something in a language I couldn't quite make out. When they were done, the bouncer stepped back and said, "Go right in." I started to walk away from the door, a polite smile on my face as I said, "I think we're at the wrong place." The old woman grabbed my arm just above the elbow with an iron grip, returning my polite smile as she said, "Nonsense. You are exactly where you are meant to be, child." I looked to Kara for help, but she just shrugged and tried to back away. I always was the worst at picking friends. But before she could escape, a tall woman grabbed her by the shoulders and propelled her toward the club. Was it a club? Everyone was certainly dressed for the part, but no one was acting it. The old lady half-dragged me into the dark hallway, the sound of music already thumping from some distant speakers. It sounded like normal club music. The hall looked and smelled like a normal dance club hallway. I wanted to doubt what I had just seen, to chalk up the whole praying thing as a hallucination, but the bouncer's painful grip on my arm reminded me that I wasn't in Kansas anymore. The hall opened onto a large dance floor, new, yet thoroughly scuffed, with a large stage to the right, a man with a gaudy gold medallion hanging from his neck already bobbing his head as he played with the soundboard. The medallion looked religious, but it wasn't any symbol I recognized. To the left was a bar, with a cage on the wall behind it, a scantily dressed woman standing inside. At first, I thought she was a dancer. Then I realized she wasn't moving. Chains connected from her wrists to the ceiling of the cage, holding her upright. In the dim light, I couldn't tell if she was conscious or not, but I could make out a thin red cord extending from her thigh down to one of the taps. A row of glasses filled with a red beverage already lined the bar: tonight's limited edition new drink.

Despite prioritizing Mongol and related ethnic groups through a hierarchical system, granting them greater prestige than the dominant Han Chinese population, the position of Han Chinese advisors was ambiguous; they frequently exerted considerable influence despite lacking formal recognition. Kublai Khan discontinued the traditional Chinese civil service examination system, a practice revived only under his successor, Ayurbarwada Buyantu Khan. As Rossabi notes, Kublai understood the need to utilize Chinese counsel while simultaneously maintaining power by navigating the contrast between Mongol culture and Chinese society – “concerned with both the welfare of his Chinese subjects and his own imperial ambitions,” his priorities shifted throughout his reign. Similarly, Van Praag argues in *The Status of Tibet* that Tibet and Mongolia maintained a distinct dual governance structure based on mutual dependence, justifying Mongol khan succession as universal Buddhist authority. He emphasizes Tibet’s autonomy, illustrating this with the continued operation of a permitted trade route between China and Tibet during the Yuan dynasty.

Some say it was Satan's way of tempting us or the gods way of judging us. Some claimed it to be aliens. Plenty more considered it evolution. Me? I'm going with the whole gist of'I don't know how it started, that doesn't matter, it's here now.' 15 Years ago, at the peak of the twenty first century, everyone gained the same ability - to'break' reality, to change themselves to'snap' their minds. You basically break a piece off, in return you unlock some form of power - be it near useless or something out of a comic book. People had varying amounts of control, but one thing remained common..... the larger the power, the greater the hole left behind - and that hole -always- filled itself with bad stuff. Once people learned how to'snap' their minds, there were thousands of vegetables worldwide who ignored the warnings everyone gave them, the powers of gods locked in a empty husk in a mind. So people began to try and find the'edge', where they keep their mind intact but still gained hefty powers. Chaos ensued shortly after. Major city's burnt and rioted as violent powers were soon given to those were now insane psychopaths. People who chose to do good or to heal any disease soon found themselves suicidal and depressed, never able to live long enough to use their powers the way they'd truly wanted. So the art of training ones mind to control exactly how much you snap and what powers you gain became the trend. I joined one of those once - they were very helpful in getting me where I am now. Of course plenty of people abused this and got subtle, weak powers while able to keep their mind more-or-less steady enough to use them correctly. There's the unending war of'super heroes' who took their powers to defend the innocent who refused to risk their minds from the'super-villains' who'd taken more power they can control and had gone mad. My father had been one of these super villains - he'd been away in middle east, fighting the latest conflict we'd decided to get involved with - and he wanted the power to end it without losing anymore lives. Word has it he's still rampaging through the desert, slaughtering indiscriminately. My mother is still a Senior Doctor, she wanted the ability to close flesh and wounds the like with the touch of a finger - able to perform conflicted operations in seconds and save countless lives. Sadly this gave her late-stage Alzheimer's and the next day she gets into work she's forgotten the name of all the patients she has saved, and quite often mine too. I however am the first in attempting a very particular type of snap - the reverse snap. Lose a power, regain a mental ability. I've suffered with both depression and autism my entire life until I tried this. I've lost the'power' to speak and move my legs. But personally, I think I've become the most powerful of them all - finally able to appreciate life for what it truly is.

Despite worries regarding the preparedness of Poland and Ukraine to jointly host the competition due to fears of fan violence and racism, Pohorecki emphasized the overall success of Euro 2012. “We’re proud that many doubted our ability, but we proved them wrong,” he stated. The expanded tournament featured 24 nations – an increase from the 16 participating in 2012 – playing 51 games within a single month. A contentious match between Russia and Poland in Warsaw saw clashes among rival fans on June 12th. While acknowledging improvements were made, Pohorecki minimized concerns about these incidents and isolated instances of racial abuse.  He noted that future tournaments in France would benefit from their experience, stating they would share insights gained.  Pohorecki was taken aback by a BBC Panorama program preceding the tournament, which questioned Uefa’s choice of hosts, citing evidence of violence. He argued that such investigative programs are possible in any country hosting a major event, and that issues inevitably arise with large-scale events.  He pointed out that a hospital admission rate of six individuals during a riot was comparable to a typical Polish wedding, suggesting the focus is on how those issues are presented. Pohorecki supported Uefa President Michel Platini’s proposal to distribute the 2020 European Championship across multiple European locations.

It includes the code as well as videos of the software in action.

Several barriers protect organisms from infection, including mechanical, chemical, and biological barriers. The waxy cuticle of many leaves, the exoskeleton of insects, the shells and membranes of externally deposited eggs, and skin are examples of mechanical barriers that are the first line of defense against infection. However, as organisms cannot be completely sealed from their environments, other systems act to protect body openings such as the lungs, intestines, and the genitourinary tract. In the lungs, coughing and sneezing mechanically eject pathogens and other irritants from the respiratory tract. The flushing action of tears and urine also mechanically expels pathogens, while mucus secreted by the respiratory and gastrointestinal tract serves to trap and entangle microorganisms.

Service composition using choreography often assumes services fulfill their assigned roles faithfully, even when facing malicious actors. Our work introduces a contract model built upon an expanded version of Petri nets, enabling services to defend themselves during choreography execution. This model is connected to Propositional Contract Logic through a translation process that maintains logical agreement and supports compositional validation.

Step 9: Marking Door Strike Location on Shaft If using two deadbolts like we have here, mark where they will be installed for easy reference when installing them. Remember the location where each strike should sit flush against the door frame so that we'll know which direction we need to install our long screws. We're going to use these marks as guides while putting together both lock mechanisms but also make sure there isn't any wood between the bolt headkeyway area and either the first or second holes drilled into our shafts. The easiest way I've found to do this was with masking tape wrapped around the bolts, then tracing out their exact path onto my piece of wood laying across the doorsill just below the top edge of the casing. I marked with pencil, since I'm not too confident about drilling through stainless steel...but if anyone has better advice please let me know!:) Once you've got everything lined up correctly, drill pilot holes into the bottom edges of the cleats near those marks, making certain to keep things even throughout the length of the hole. This may take some manipulation depending upon how close the faceplate sits to the outer edge, etc., but try to stay consistent otherwise the longer screw won't line back up properly after installation. Place the nuts over the ends of the threaded rods before tightening down each setscrew - remember what size nut goes on what sized rod? It's ok if you don't; most hardware stores sell kits specifically designed to solve such problems anyway. Once again, test fit the parts before fully assembling anything else because more often than not something might look right on paper only to require minor tweaks once tightened down completely. In other words, check stuff every step along the way rather than waiting till its almost time to put things away for winter. This Halloween experience, beyond Las Vegas’ offerings, stood out significantly. Seeking spooky fun on a free Sunday evening, we visited the Freakling Brothers Trilogy Of Terror. The exterior resembled a disquieting carnival, hinting at fates unknown. However, discovering the houses were built on trailers truly elevated the experience, rivaling some of the top haunted houses I’ve encountered. Each attraction was exceptionally crafted. To avoid spoilers, I recommend purchasing a VIP fast-pass; it includes a t-shirt and a $10 discount. Our journey began with Circus of Terror, where even the staff were costumed, greeted by a ringmaster setting the tone. Inside, I was struck by the intricate detail, darkness, and unsettling atmosphere. It involved interactive elements – rooms demanding action and others requiring puzzle-solving. The finale left a lasting impression. Next, we explored Castle Vampyre, overseen by Igor and a chilling vampire hostess. Like the previous houses, it was intensely atmospheric and disturbing. Personally, this was my favorite. Several rooms presented challenges, and certain effects genuinely startled me, prompting a reflexive reaction. The conclusion evoked a sense of wonder rather than simply fear. Finally, we tackled the Gates of Hell, necessitating a signed waiver due to its mature content (restricted to those 17+). While initially apprehensive about specific scenes, I found myself thoroughly immersed within it.

Each time you perceive something, a previous version of yourself fades away—a continuous process. Time’s significance lies solely in our subjective experience. Consider the possibility that each fleeting ‘you’ is perpetually trapped within its own instant, while the perception of passing time is simply a construct. The many-worlds interpretation suggests countless alternate futures exist, each experienced by a different iteration of you. Regardless of these questions about reality, recall that you’re fundamentally composed of minuscule vibrations within the universe’s underlying structure – sentient life essentially mirroring the cosmos’ self-awareness. Worrying about eternal nonexistence feels equally daunting as fearing endless existence. Ultimately, the vastness of what *could* occur or *is* occurring surpasses human understanding, limited as it is to a single lifetime. Observing others struggling with unfulfilled aspirations distresses me; their focus on impending mortality overshadows the present. Yet, reflecting on the simple miracle of having lived, as my grandfather urged—"Why fear death? It’s entirely natural"—and living fully as if today were final offers solace.

Cluster-wise linear regression (CLR), a clustering problem intertwined with regression, is to find clusters of entities such that the overall sum of squared errors from regressions performed over these clusters is minimized, where each cluster may have different variances. We generalize the CLR problem by allowing each entity to have more than one observation, and refer to it as generalized CLR. We propose an exact mathematical programming based approach relying on column generation, a column generation based heuristic algorithm that clusters predefined groups of entities, a metaheuristic genetic algorithm with adapted Lloyd's algorithm for K-means clustering, a two-stage approach, and a modified algorithm of Spath for solving generalized CLR. We examine the performance of our algorithms on a stock keeping unit (SKU) clustering problem employed in forecasting halo and cannibalization effects in promotions using real-world retail data from a large supermarket chain. In the SKU clustering problem, the retailer needs to cluster SKUs based on their seasonal effects in response to promotions. The seasonal effects are the results of regressions with predictors being promotion mechanisms and seasonal dummies performed over clusters generated. We compare the performance of all proposed algorithms for the SKU problem with real-world and synthetic data.

The Great Suspender, a popular Chrome extension that automatically suspended open tabs that haven't been used for a while, has been removed from Google's Chrome Web Store. Apparently, some sketchy code was included in the extension that violated Google's terms of service. Google has removed The Great Suspender from its Chrome Web Store, citing suspicious code that violated its terms of service. According to reports, the extension was collecting user information and sending it to a remote server, which could have been used for malicious purposes. In response, Google has disabled the extension and is warning users to uninstall it if they had already installed it. The developers of The Great Suspender deny any malicious intent and claim that the data collected was only being used to improve the extension's features. However, they have agreed to shut down the project and delete all associated data. Google's decision to remove The Great Suspender demonstrates its commitment to protecting user privacy, as well as its willingness to take swift action when necessary. It also serves as a reminder that users should be cautious when installing browser extensions, as some may contain malicious code.

It’s probably challenging, but essentially, parenthood builds on self-care. You brought these kids into the world, creating a responsibility to ensure their survival and well-being. Massive MIMO base stations utilizing Time Division Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (TD-OFDM) and relying on uplink training for both transmissions present a promising solution for 5G due to their potential for excellent spatial and power efficiency alongside low latency. This study explores using non-orthogonal uplink pilot signals to enhance downlink area spectral efficiency in these networks. We propose a set of pilot designs that maintain orthogonality within individual cells while ensuring minimal cross-cell interference. By leveraging channel estimations derived from observing these pilots, each cell independently delivers MU-MIMO transmissions to nearby users, simultaneously minimizing interference to distant, heavily impacted users. Simulation results demonstrate that employing these pilot codes leads to improved user rate cumulative distribution functions compared to standard methods, ultimately boosting overall cell and/or cell throughput.

While significant improvements have been made in recent years in terms of end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) performance, such improvements were obtained through the use of very large neural networks, unfit for embedded use on edge devices. That being said, in this paper, we work on simplifying and compressing Transformer-based encoder-decoder architectures for the end-to-end ASR task. We empirically introduce a more compact Speech-Transformer by investigating the impact of discarding particular modules on the performance of the model. Moreover, we evaluate reducing the numerical precision of our network's weights and activations while maintaining the performance of the full-precision model. Our experiments show that we can reduce the number of parameters of the full-precision model and then further compress the model 4x by fully quantizing to 8-bit fixed point precision.

In his book, The Greatest Show on Earth: The Evidence for Evolution, biologist Richard Dawkins grapples with the question of why pain has to be so very painful. He describes the alternative as a simple, mental raising of a "red flag." To argue why that red flag might be insufficient, Dawkins explains that drives must compete with each other within living beings. The most fit creature would be the one whose pains are well balanced. Those pains which mean certain death when ignored will become the most powerfully felt. The relative intensities of pain, then, may resemble the relative importance of that risk to our ancestors (lack of food, too much cold, or serious injuries are felt as agony, whereas minor damage is felt as mere discomfort). This resemblance will not be perfect, however, because natural selection can be a poor designer. The result is often glitches in animals, including supernormal stimuli. Such glitches help explain pains which are not, or at least no longer directly adaptive (e.g. perhaps some forms of toothache, or injury to fingernails).

These materials are best described as fluorescent, rather than neon, as “fluorescence” accurately reflects their behavior. Fluorescence involves absorbing invisible light – often ultraviolet – and immediately re-emitting it as visible light. These objects absorb UV radiation and convert it into colored light we can perceive. They’re often brighter than white due to this process; a highlighter will intensely glow under blacklight illumination. Fluorescent bulbs operate on the same principle: electricity creates UV light which then stimulates a coating within the bulb, causing it to emit visible light. Similarly, everyday items like safety vests and brightly colored clothing utilize fluorescent dyes. Sunlight or artificial UV sources trigger this glow, though it may be subtle without UV examination. Even laundry detergents contain these dyes, causing white fabrics to subtly fluoresce under UV light, creating a noticeable effect when worn or used in activities like glow-in-the-dark bowling.

The latter are more common then you'd think, and they require someone watching the bomb's location with a cell phone to actually detonate. So if a patrol sees someone eyeing the area who's not got a good reason already to be doing so.... well, see above: it's a pretty good indicator. The idea that unifying all of the small countries in Europe into a single nation like the United States is a misguided one. Small countries often have their own distinct cultural identities and traditions, which would be lost if they were to be unified into one large nation. Furthermore, it would be difficult to adequately represent the needs and interests of all of these disparate cultures in a single government. Additionally, larger nations tend to have more centralized power, which could lead to a loss of local autonomy and increased inequality among citizens. Ultimately, there are better ways to ensure peace and stability in Europe without sacrificing the individual identities of its many small countries.

I think it's important for us as young scholars of literature at UBC to be reminded about what we learn from Fitzgerald. The importance of working on projects outside of our own fields is critical. We are all guilty of this; however, in the case of students like Fitzgerald who were interested in travelling abroad instead of pursuing their dreams, it may have affected his writing more than any potential employment. He probably would not have been able to take his studies abroad for several reasons: firstly (and most importantly), he did not want to leave his family behind, secondly because he knew that studying overseas would require him to sacrifice time away from them, and finally, because he felt pressure from an external perspective to pursue something outside of his field. However, by being exposed to new ideas, different perspectives and cultures he experienced through these experiences which "woke" within him, it opened up avenues for future exploration of himself. Through such experiences, the drive to write became stronger. This drives me towards the next topic: How do writers travel? How can the arts community encourage people to keep exploring themselves? Fitzgerald wrote about his travels in an autobiographical essay titled "Butterfly in the Garden" . In this piece, he discusses going to New York City to read a play during one of his trips, meeting others in New York for the first time who shared similar customs and lifestyles as he did, and trying to fit into their worlds. He also describes the sounds he hears at the theatre while performing; the way patrons whisper each other without knowing anyone else is eerie. He goes onto describe how everyone reacts differently depending upon whether they are wearing shoes or socks in public places. He went on to say that traveling inspired him to become a writer, but also called attention to the ways in which people can change over time: ..."you may begin your journey of self-discovery... then in a few years you must decide that art isn't for you anymore...." His last trip took place in Paris where he stayed with Soraya Jain, an English teacher who helped him realise scriving doesn't make life better in itself. She told him she had spent her days teaching children in Pakistan, only to see herself driven into the arms of a man twenty years older than her. He found out later that she was married to a neurosurgeon. And yet, despite these events, he continued to write, although the two ended up breaking off their relationship due to incompatibilities. What emerges from this experience is his determination to stay true to himself, and his drive to find a love and connection with someone who challenged him. Often rules apply to all goods neutrally, but may have a greater practical effect on imports than domestic products. For such "indirect" discriminatory (or "indistinctly applicable measures the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has developed the so-called "Mezza di Pasta doctrine." The Mezza di Pasta doctrine entails that in case an indirect discriminatory measure leads to an infringement of a fundamental freedom of the EU Treaty (e.g. free movement of goods, freedom of establishment, free movement of workers or capital), the EU-legislator may not apply the discriminatory measure. This has been confirmed by the CJEU in its recent judgement in the case "C-55016." In this case, the question arose whether the Mezza di Pasta doctrine would be applicable in the case of a restrictive measure for the import of products, in so far as the relevant regulation contained a derogation for the protection of public health. The case concerned the import of products, which had been tested in a laboratory outside the EU and, therefore, were not subject to the EU rules on the protection of laboratory animals. The EU-legislator considered that these products should be considered as not in conformity with the Directive on the protection of laboratory animals and prohibited the import thereof. However, the CJEU considered that the Directive on the protection of laboratory animals could not be applied to products imported from third countries, since this would lead to an infringement of the free movement of goods. According to the CJEU, the Directive could only apply to products that were manufactured in the EU, if the rules were applied in a non-discriminatory manner. The CJEU also considered the provision of the Directive, which provided for a derogation from the fundamental freedoms if they had to be limited for the protection of public health. However, the CJEU considered that this provision could not be applied in the present case, since the Directive was intended to protect laboratory animals and not to protect the health of humans. This judgement of the CJEU is important for companies importing products into the EU. The judgement shows that the EU-legislator cannot rely on a derogation for the protection of public health, if the EU-legislation in question does not aim to protect human health. Source: Judgement of 15 November 2018, case C-55016 International Trade, Customs WTO

Local Policy Search is a popular reinforcement learning approach for handling large state spaces. Formally, it searches locally in a parameterized policy space in order to maximize the associated value function averaged over some predefined distribution. It is probably commonly believed that the best one can hope in general from such an approach is to get a local optimum of this criterion. In this article, we show the following surprising result: any (approximate) local optimum enjoys a global performance guarantee . We compare this guarantee with the one that is satisfied by Direct Policy Iteration, an approximate dynamic programming algorithm that does some form of Policy Search: if the approximation error of Local Policy Search may generally be bigger (because local search requires to consider a space of stochastic policies), we argue that the concentrability coefficient that appears in the performance bound is much nicer. Finally, we discuss several practical and theoretical consequences of our analysis.

There are two types of common OTC painkillers in the US: acetaminophen (called paracetamol in most other countries, and best known as the ordinary Tylenol brand) and NSAIDs. Acetaminophen in the right dosage has fewer side effects, but (and it's a big but), it doesn't take a lot to take too much of it, causing serious liver damage. This is a problem because many multi-symptom cold medicines also contain it, and it can be bad if you take both acetaminophen for a headache and a cold medicine that also contains acetaminophen. NSAID stands for non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, which mean these not only reduce pain but also reduce inflammation (which acetaminophen doesn't). One of their side effects is stomach irritation, so you'd probably avoid them if you frequently have heartburn or upset stomach. But for most people, if you're only going to have one painkiller in the house, an NSAID is preferable for two reasons: One, it's better for joint and muscle pain than acetaminophen, and two, so many cold medicines are bundled with acetaminophen, that there's a risk of accidental overdose if you take both a cold medicine and a painkiller that has acetaminophen. After aspirin, the most commonly used OTC NSAID is ibuprofen, which is fine. For more chronic pain (say hand or wrist pain from too much typing), IMHO naproxen would be a better choice. But, they are always learning more about these drugs, so stay informed. They're safe to take as directed, which means for something like a sore joint, several days in a row is ok. But if you're getting headaches as frequently as once a week, it's time to see a doctor. Not because the medications are bad at that level (many people with arthritis will take such things daily), but because frequent headaches might be a symptom of something else that requires medical attention. Likewise for a very severe headache (which could be a migraine but could also be an indication of meningitis). Splits on canned beans appear in the process of preparation and canning. Researchers are studying how they are influenced by cooking environment and genotype. However, there is no existing method to automatically quantify or to characterize the severity of splits. To solve this, we propose two measures: the Bean Split Ratio (BSR) that quantifies the overall severity of splits, and the Bean Split Histogram (BSH) that characterizes the size distribution of splits. We create a pixel-wise segmentation method to automatically estimate these measures from images. We also present a bean dataset of recombinant inbred lines of two genotypes, use the BSR and BSH to assess canning quality, and explore heritability of these properties.

Adaptive Independent Component Analysis (ICA), a method for reducing data dimensions beneficial for machine learning models like Bayesian neural networks, often exhibits slower convergence compared to its non-adaptive versions.  Due to this inherent slowness and the limitations of current low-clock-frequency hardware, significant advancements are needed in both algorithmic and architectural designs. This research introduces an algorithm optimized for efficient hardware execution of ICA.  Our Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) implementation of adaptive ICA achieves a minimum clock frequency increase of one order of magnitude and a minimum throughput improvement of two orders of magnitude over prior approaches. Furthermore, this novel algorithm’s utility extends beyond ICA and applies broadly to machine learning tasks utilizing stochastic gradient descent.

We propose to combine the robustness merit of model-based approaches and the learning power of data-driven approaches for image restoration. Specifically, by integrating graph Laplacian regularization as a trainable module into a deep learning framework, we are less susceptible to overfitting than pure CNN-based approaches, achieving higher robustness to small dataset and cross-domain denoising. First, a sparse neighborhood graph is built from the output of a convolutional neural network (CNN). Then the image is restored by solving an unconstrained quadratic programming problem, using a corresponding graph Laplacian regularizer as a prior term. The proposed restoration pipeline is fully differentiable and hence can be end-to-end trained. Experimental results demonstrate that our work avoids overfitting given small training data. It is also endowed with strong cross-domain generalization power, outperforming the state-of-the-art approaches by remarkable margin.

It was a normal day just like any other day. I had woken up early morning and headed to work while the sun was still rising. I had been feeling off for the last few weeks, but nothing had been out of the ordinary that would make me suspicious. I had been experiencing nausea, fatigue, and lack of appetite but these were symptoms, which were common to me whenever I had flu. But something didn't feel right, and I couldn't put my finger on it. As the days went by, I started to feel even more tired and weak than usual. I was signed off from work for two days, hoping that some rest would help me feel better. As I lay in bed, I couldn't shake off the feeling that something was different. I did a quick online search of my symptoms and was stunned when the search results showed that these could be early signs of pregnancy. I had never been pregnant before, and the thought of it was overwhelming. I didn't know how I would feel about it. I was scared, and my heart was racing faster than usual. I decided to take a test to confirm it. As I waited for the test results, my thoughts went crazy, thinking about all the responsibilities that come with being a mother. A few minutes went by, and I finally got the courage to check the results. I couldn't believe it! The test was positive. Tears rolled down my eyes as I looked at the test results. The thought of bringing another life in the world was overwhelming, but I knew I had to accept the responsibility. The day, which had started out to be normal, turned out to be an extraordinary day, and a new journey began. Although I was scared and didn't know what the future held, I knew I had to embrace it with an open mind and heart. Looking back now, I can't believe that it's been five years since the day I found out I was pregnant. My daughter, who is now five, is the joy of my life, and I wouldn't have it any other way. That was the day that changed my life forever.

Neuroscience questions often lack definitive answers, but various theories exist. Your initial inquiry – “How can our minds perceive things our brains weren’t designed to detect?” – suggests you believe the brain evolved specifically to recognize elements of the natural world, limiting its capacity for newer phenomena. However, this isn’t accurate; the brain possesses remarkable plasticity—the ability to adapt and change at every level, from molecular structures to large cell formations. Early development involves shaping the brain to interpret surroundings; a consequence of this is that lack of exposure to certain stimuli during childhood can hinder perception later in life, exemplified by kittens raised on vertical lines failing to discern horizontal ones due to altered neural wiring. It’s important not to equate this with an inability to perceive a toothbrush if never exposed to it as a child, though early experiences undeniably impact brain development. Essentially, the brain adjusts to its environment through its inherent adaptability. While the precise mechanisms governing these changes remain somewhat mysterious, consider the analogy of a computer: despite possessing roughly two billion transistors, it pales in comparison to the human brain’s approximately 200 billion neurons, each forming numerous connections—potentially hundreds of times more complex.

In paintings, Mary is traditionally portrayed in blue. This tradition can trace its origin to the Byzantine Empire, from c.500 AD, where blue was "the colour of an empress." A more practical explanation for the use of this colour is that in Medieval and Renaissance Europe, the blue pigment was derived from the rock lapis lazuli, a stone imported from Afghanistan of greater value than gold. Beyond a painter's retainer, patrons were expected to purchase any gold or lapis lazuli to be used in the painting. Hence, it was an expression of devotion and glorification to swathe the Virgin in gowns of blue.

Wireless Network-on-Chip (WNoC) offers a potentially better approach than traditional interconnects for small chips. Previous research on WNoC using millimeter wave frequencies has focused on the physical, networking, and architectural aspects but lacked thorough investigation within real chip packaging scenarios. Consequently, the behavior of these wireless channels hasn’t been completely characterized. This study corrects this gap by creating an accurate model of a flip-chip package and simulating signal propagation within it. Parameterized analyses reveal a best layout for a 60 GHz WNoC, demonstrating achievable chip-wide attenuation below 32.6 dB using typical manufacturing techniques.  The method's broader applicability to higher frequency bands and other integrated systems like Software-Defined Metamaterials (SDM) is also considered.

European art music is largely distinguished from many other non-European and popular musical forms by its system of staff notation, in use since about the 16th century. Western staff notation is used by composers to prescribe to the performer the pitches (e.g., melodies, basslines andor chords), tempo, meter and rhythms for a piece of music. This leaves less room for practices such as improvisation and ad libitum ornamentation, which are frequently heard in non-European art music and in popular music styles such as jazz and blues. Another difference is that whereas most popular styles lend themselves to the song form, classical music has been noted for its development of highly sophisticated forms of instrumental music such as the concerto, symphony, sonata, and mixed vocal and instrumental styles such as opera which, since they are written down, can attain a high level of complexity.

Do you mean rugs made in Iran, or the general category of "Oriental" rugs? "Orientals" - which we'll describe generally as hand-tufted wool rugs - are, well, handmade. Since they're wool (or silk), typically on a cotton warp, with good care they'll last forever, and like other antiques, antique "Oriental" rugs appreciate with age (all other things like condition and workmanship being equal). The designs are original, and because they're handmade you get that made-by-hand quirkiness a lot of us like. Wool and silk also absorb dye (and reflect light) like no other fiber. They also "work" with virtually every decor style. We love them with Danish Modern furniture, for example, while my grandparents had them with the classic Jacobean repro furniture of the 1920s-30s. Persian rugs are particularly fine, with the best having more tufts of yarn per square inch than your average Central Asian tribal rug, for example. They're known for their pictorial (rather than geometric) motifs, which can be amazingly elaborate, looking more like fine embroidery than tufting. So basically: artistic quality, fine materials, and an incredible amount of labor.

The miracle involved the healing of a Brazilian man with several brain tumours in 2008, the Vatican said. Mother Teresa died in 1997 and was beatified - the first step towards sainthood - in 2003. She won the Nobel Peace Prize for her work with the poor in the slums of Indian city of Kolkata (Calcutta). "The Holy Father has authorised the Congregation for the Causes of Saints to proclaim the decree concerning the miracle attributed to the intercession of blessed Mother Teresa," the Vatican said on Friday. She is expected to be canonised in Rome in September. Beatification by the Catholic Church requires one miracle, while the process of becoming recognised as a saint requires proof of at least two miracles. Mother Teresa was beatified in 2003 after Pope John Paul II accepted as authentic a miracle attributed to her. He judged that the curing of an Indian woman suffering from an abdominal tumour was the result of the supernatural intervention of the late Mother Teresa - a claim challenged by Indian rationalists. There are few details about the recovery of the Brazilian man, whose life the Vatican says was saved in the second miracle. His identity has not been disclosed to maintain the discretion needed for the investigation, the Catholic New Agency has said. It says he was unexpectedly cured from brain tumours in 2008 after his priest prayed for Mother Teresa's intervention with God. Born Agnes Gonxhe Bojaxhiu in Skopje, Macedonia, in 1910, she founded the Missionaries of Charity in 1949, dedicating her life to caring for impoverished and sick people in Kolkata. Known as the "saint of the gutter," she earned worldwide acclaim for her efforts. Her critics, however, accused her of mixing with dictators and peddling a hardline Catholicism.

MIT announced that it is planning a 1 billion college called the MIT Stephen A. Schwarzman College of Computing, named after Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman who donated 350 million. The 300 million gift is the largest single donation in MIT's history. In the same announcement, MIT said that it will be using some of the gift to fund an ethics and AI study program, as well as a 5 million gift from the Omidyar Foundation for the same. "The MIT Schwarzman College of Computing will constitute both a global center for computing research and education, and an intellectual foundry for powerful new AI tools," MIT President L. Rafael Reif wrote in a letter to the university community. "In a world where machines will increasingly augment and even replace human capabilities, the college will equip students and researchers in any discipline to use computing to advance their fields; to think critically about the human impact of their work; and to hone both their skills and their responsibilities." The gift will help MIT create 50 new faculty positions within the college, as well as 100 new graduate fellowships. The college will also have new dedicated space within the university's main campus. "We are in an era of profound and unprecedented change, and MIT is uniquely situated to address the consequent opportunities and challenges," Reif said. "The MIT Schwarzman College of Computing will constitute both a global center for computing research and education, and an intellectual foundry for powerful new AI tools. In a world where machines will increasingly augment and even replace human capabilities, the college will equip students and researchers in any discipline to use computing to advance their fields; to think critically about the human impact of their work; and to hone both their skills and their responsibilities." The AI Ethics and Policy Initiative will be led by Harvard University's Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society, the MIT Media Lab, and the MIT Institute for Data Systems and Society (IDSS). The initiative will look at both technical and ethical issues surrounding AI. "We have to think about the societal and ethical implications of artificial intelligence," MIT Provost Martin Schmidt said in a statement. "We need to understand how we control these systems, how they are going to behave, how they are going to affect society, how we can get the most out of them, how we can make sure they are safe." The effort will include a "five-day residency for 25 U.S. mayors focused on the policy and governance issues arising from advances in AI and related technologies." It will also support "research that addresses policy and ethics questions in artificial intelligence and related technologies, as well as the development of curricula for students to study these issues." "As the impact of AI and other technologies on society becomes more significant, it is important to ensure that these technologies are designed with ethical considerations in mind," Omidyar Network managing partner Matt Bannick said in a statement. "We are proud to partner with MIT to support the Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence Initiative, which will convene global experts to develop frameworks to guide and govern the development and application of these powerful technologies."

This time, they used a small rocket to carry sterilized vials, packed inside an insulating "biobox" made from polymers including styrene sulfonate. Four chambers held each type of microorganism: Bacillus subtilis (two) and Penicillium chrysogenum (one), both common soil microbes; and Aspergilli spp., also known as moulds or mildews.[34] The box was ejected at around 100 kilometreshour, after which its temperature rose rapidly. On Earth, temperatures reached almost 45 C,[5] causing condensation within minutes, which meant water vapour and carbon dioxide formed ice crystals instead of gas bubbles.[6] Researchers expected to see similar results during this flight but did not expect how quickly it would happen as a result of the insulated biobox and expedited ejection.[7] A press release by NASA stated that "after just 6 minutes... The personal copying exemption in the copyright law of EU member states stems from the EU Copyright Directive of 2001, which is generally devised to allow EU members to enact laws sanctioning making copies without authorization, as long as they are for personal, noncommerical use. The Copyright Directive was not intended to legitimize file-sharing, but rather the common practice of space shifting copyright-protected content from a legally purchased CD (for example) to certain kinds of devices and media, provided rights holders are compensated and no copy protection measures are circumvented. Rights-holder compensation takes various forms, depending on the country, but is generally either a levy on "recording" devices and media, or a tax on the content itself. In some countries, such as Canada, the applicability of such laws to copying onto general-purpose storage devices like computer hard drives, portable media players, and phones, for which no levies are collected, has been the subject of debate and further efforts to reform copyright law.

Dr Henry McLaughlin believes that physical and mental wellbeing can be improved by a daily mountain climb. The idea is that people climb to the top of Slievemartin outside Rostrevor - known locally as the Cairn - take a selfie and then post the picture on the'Cairnuary' Facebook page. The mountain is 485m high, so Dr McLaughlin said if you climb it 31 times in a month, you've climbed higher than Everest. He said he could see how his patients have benefitted. "January's a time when I see a lot of depression and this challenge is pretty good for mental health and physical health," Dr McLaughlin said. "A lot of people buy exercise bikes and then they gather dust. So this is something that's free, they get to climb up the mountain every day for a month. "It's a good hard exercise, it takes them about an hour. "They don't need exercise bikes and they don't need to join gyms and pay money for stuff, it's out there and they can discover the mountains." Those climbing the mountain can chose their own route - which could involve anything up to a 10km hike - or they can use a bike if they want. Dr McLaughlin said between 30 to 50 people were now climbing the mountain daily and all sorts of people are taking part. "There's one lady who's a patient of mine who's been very ill in the past and has had surgeries to her feet and really shouldn't be able to do it, but she's going from the car park half way up the mountain and she's doing it every day," he said. "There's people with depression doing it - I know it's good for them - people who are overweight doing it, there are people who are very healthy doing it as well. "People are all very encouraging of each other." Dr McLaughlin said he climbed the mountain at about 06:00 GMT on Thursday and had eight other people for company. "Normally you'd climb the mountain at six o'clock in the morning and you wouldn't see a soul," he said. The final climb will be a communal one on Sunday, but Dr McLaughlin said he hoped to come up with something else to keep his patients exercising. "I'm hoping to follow it on with some sort of challenge for the rest of the year that will keep them doing stuff," he said. "As far as I'm concerned, it's probably doing my work good in that maybe some people are going to get fit that I won't see. "I'd recommend it to anybody. There could be a cairn near you, it doesn't have to be my cairn, it could be a hill or a mountain near you."

Early diagnosis and accurate segmentation of brain tumors are imperative for successful treatment. Unfortunately, manual segmentation is time consuming, costly and despite extensive human expertise often inaccurate. Here, we present an MRI-based tumor segmentation framework using an autoencoder-regularized 3D-convolutional neural network. We trained the model on manually segmented structural T1, T1ce, T2, and Flair MRI images of 335 patients with tumors of variable severity, size and location. We then tested the model using independent data of 125 patients and successfully segmented brain tumors into three subregions: the tumor core (TC), the enhancing tumor (ET) and the whole tumor (WT). We also explored several data augmentations and preprocessing steps to improve segmentation performance. Importantly, our model was implemented on a single NVIDIA GTX1060 graphics unit and hence optimizes tumor segmentation for widely affordable hardware. In sum, we present a memory-efficient and affordable solution to tumor segmentation to support the accurate diagnostics of oncological brain pathologies.

Fractals possess a unique characteristic: they maintain intricate detail regardless of magnification. The Sierpinski triangle exemplifies this; begin with an equilateral triangle, remove a central triangle, repeating this process recursively across each remaining section creates successively smaller triangles – nine, twenty-seven, and so forth, extending infinitely. Zooming into a fractal reveals an endless repetition of miniature versions of itself, unlike a standard triangle, where zooming simply reveals a smoother, straighter line. Fractals aim to mirror the irregularity found throughout nature, where perfection is absent—consider the British coastline. Its overall length provides an initial estimation, yet closer inspection continuously uncovers more detail, increasing the measured length indefinitely. This demonstrates that a linear representation fundamentally misrepresents the coastline’s true complexity, leading to the term “fractal.” Essentially, fractals are forms that defy traditional geometric expectations when viewed closely, mirroring the inherent complexities of natural phenomena.  Self-similar fractals, such as the Sierpinski gasket, can be generated through repeated iterations of basic rules.

During the pre-Hellenistic era, numerous Greek colonies existed along the coasts of the Crimean and Taman peninsulas. The Bosporan Kingdom emerged as a diverse realm comprised of Greek city-states alongside indigenous groups like the Maeotians, Thracians, Crimean Scythians, and Cimmerians, ruled by the Spartocid dynasty (438-110 BCE). Originating as a Hellenized Thracian family from Panticapaeum, the Bosporans maintained extensive trade relationships with the Scythian tribes inhabiting the Pontic-Caspian steppe; Hellenistic cultural impacts are evident in Scythian settlements in Crimea, exemplified by Neapolis.  The reign of Paerisades V faced Scythian pressure, ultimately leading to the Bosporan kingdom’s submission to Pontic King Mithradates VI for defense around 107 BCE. Subsequently, it transitioned into a Roman client state. Meanwhile, Scythian leaders in Central Asia interacted with Hellenistic culture via connections with the Greeks of Bactria, often acquiring Greek goods and incorporating Greek artistic styles. Some Scythians underwent Hellenization, evidenced by internal disputes among elite families regarding the embrace of Greek customs – these individuals were termed the “young Scythians.” Nearby, the people of Pontic Olvia, the Callipidae, formed a mixed population of Hellenized Greco-Scythians.

Rebecca Minnock and her son Ethan disappeared from Highbridge, Somerset, on 27 May, the day a court ruled he should live with his father. She told newspapers she knew it was wrong but she could not give Ethan up. Det Ch Insp Marie Wright told her: "You don't have to carry on hiding. There's always a solution." In a video posted on Avon and Somerset Police's Facebook page, Det Ch Insp Wright said she had passed on her personal number to staff in 999 and 111 call centres, so Miss Minnock could contact her personally. In a direct message to Ms Minnock, she said: "I want to make sure you and Ethan are safe. "I know that you are going to be under a huge amount of emotional pressure and strain and I want you to come to the right decision about you and Ethan." "I'm more than happy to speak to you on the phone and we can work out what's the best way to get you and Ethan back to some sort of normal life." She went on to tell Ms Minnock to contact the Missing People charity if she felt uncomfortable calling the police. She added: "Please can you get in touch one way or another and let's start talking." The search for Ms Minnock and Ethan has widened to Cheltenham and Birmingham. Media attention has intensified since a judge lifted reporting restrictions on the case. On Thursday Ms Minnock contacted the Daily Mail and accepted her actions were "wrong," adding: "I know I'm going to get caught and he will be taken from me." She said although she had thought about contacting the police, she "could not bear to give her son up." Miss Minnock has been engaged in a two-year legal battle with Ethan's father Roger Williams over contact with their son. In February, a district judge found she had fabricated allegations against Mr Williams in order to "frustrate contact" between him and Ethan A social worker reported that Ethan was not "emotionally safe" with his mother. Ethan had been staying with his father four nights a week since February. Ms Minnock did not attend a court hearing on 27 May where a judge ruled that Ethan should live with his father. She was seen withdrawing cash in Highbridge before getting into a black Ford Focus. Police believe Ms Minnock and her son are being hidden by friends or relatives. Andrew Butt, a family friend who owns a black Ford Focus, has been convicted of contempt of court in connection with the case. He was appearing at Bristol Crown Court on Friday where he could face a jail sentence.

From 2017 to 2019 the Text REtrieval Conference (TREC) held a challenge task on precision medicine using documents from medical publications (PubMed) and clinical trials. Despite lots of performance measurements carried out in these evaluation campaigns, the scientific community is still pretty unsure about the impact individual system features and their weights have on the overall system performance. In order to overcome this explanatory gap, we first determined optimal feature configurations using the Sequential Model-based Algorithm Configuration (SMAC) program and applied its output to a BM25-based search engine. We then ran an ablation study to systematically assess the individual contributions of relevant system features: BM25 parameters, query type and weighting schema, query expansion, stop word filtering, and keyword boosting. For evaluation, we employed the gold standard data from the three installments to evaluate the effectiveness of different features using the commonly shared infNDCG metric.

To answer your question, AMD processors are cheap because they perform worse than a comparable speed Intel processor. However, the price-to-performance ratio is comparable (if not a bit better) than Intel. If you don't have any budget constraints then you would probably choose Intel over AMD, whereas if you had very little money to spend you would probably go with AMD over Intel.

Quantum teleportation has a deceptive name. It doesn’t involve physically moving an object; instead, it relies on a phenomenon called entanglement. Entanglement links two quantum particles together – if you alter one, the other instantaneously changes too, regardless of the distance separating them. A quantum particle, unlike a normal particle, can exist in multiple states simultaneously, such as pointing both up and down at once. Creating quantum teleportation requires using two entangled particles, placing them far apart, and “poking” one. The other immediately responds, seemingly without delay. This instantaneous reaction defies the universal speed limit of light, challenging established physics. Scientists aren’t sure how this occurs, marking it as a significant puzzle in contemporary scientific research. Consider this analogy: you have two cards—a king and a queen—and place each in a separate box. Separating the boxes by any distance, opening one reveals its contents, instantly informing you about the card in the other.

Almost every digital device relies on a pairing of two types of transistors, NMOS and PMOS. To make smaller circuits, the space between these transistors needs to get smaller. Intel has devised a new way to close the gap, stacking the pairs so that one is atop the other. The UK’s Personal Genome Project offers a potentially transformative, free resource for scientific research into disease and human genetics, though participants face significant risks. While individuals receive DNA analysis, their data would become accessible globally, and complete anonymity isn’t assured. Concerns exist about unforeseen repercussions for both participants and their family members. Research into diseases like Alzheimer’s, comparing the DNA of afflicted and unaffected individuals, suggests a shift towards recognizing complex conditions as clusters of rarer diseases – as exemplified by cancer’s evolution into numerous subtypes. Analyzing 100,000 genomes could yield breakthroughs in prevalent illnesses like diabetes, according to Professor George Church, who leads a similar project in the United States. He notes that many common diseases are actually composed of various rare diseases. Potential downsides include immediate risks and future complications arising from advancing genetic technologies. Ethicist Dr. Peter Mills cautions that sharing genetic information involves not only personal exposure but also implicates relatives. Despite this risk, there’s substantial potential benefit, although the long-term impact remains uncertain, particularly concerning individuals, families, and future generations. Cian Murphy, a PhD student considering participation, believes individual samples could play a crucial role in accelerating medical discoveries.

We consider a multi-agent resource allocation setting that models the assignment of papers to reviewers. A recurring issue in allocation problems is the compatibility of welfareefficiency and fairness. Given an oracle to find a welfare-achieving allocation, we embed such an oracle into a flexible algorithm called the Constrained Round Robin (CRR) algorithm, that achieves the required welfare level. Our algorithm also allows the system designer to lower the welfare requirements in order to achieve a higher degree of fairness. If the welfare requirement is lowered enough, a strengthening of envy-freeness up to one item is guaranteed. Hence, our algorithm can be viewed as a computationally efficient way to interpolate between welfare and approximate envy-freeness in allocation problems.

Dwarf Fortress, the iconic ASCII-based computer game, has been in development for over two decades, and is still going strong. In a world where game developers often rush to release their latest titles, Dwarf Fortress stands out as a testament to one man's dedication, vision, and skill. The game, which has a massive following, is built entirely by Tarn Adams, who started working on it in 2002. Dwarf Fortress simulates a complex and intricate world, complete with complex social interactions and elaborate systems. With over 700,000 lines of code, the game is more complex than most modern computer programs. According to Adams, the game's staggering complexity is a result of his desire to create a truly unique experience for players. Dwarf Fortress features a procedurally generated world, with players tasked with building a thriving fortress while also dealing with the dangers and challenges that come with it. The game's development process has been long and arduous, with Adams frequently having to work through issues and bugs that would have simply been patched out in a modern game. Despite this, Adams has continued to push forward and improve his creation, adding new features over the years and building a dedicated community. For many players, Dwarf Fortress has been a beloved part of their gaming lives for years, with some even playing the game for over a decade. The game's dedicated following has even inspired numerous projects, from mods to countless YouTube tutorials. While Dwarf Fortress may not be a household name like mainstream titles such as Fortnite or Call of Duty, its impact on gaming culture cannot be overstated. The game is a reminder of the potential that lies in passion and dedication, and a testament to what one person can create through sheer force of will. As Adams continues to work on Dwarf Fortress, it's clear that his dedication to the game is unwavering. For players, this is surely a source of comfort, knowing that their favorite game will continue to improve and evolve for years to come.

I believe that people convicted and found guilty of violent crimes that were premeditated and life-altering for the victim andor the victim's family should be imprisoned for life without parole. For example: premeditated murder, breaking into someone's house to rape someone, kidnapping and sexual assaultmolestation, armed robbery where victims are tied up and beaten. In my opinion, perpetrators of these crimes have shown themselves to be violent in a planned and premeditated way that cannot be rehabilitated. Basically if you plan to commit a violent crime (as opposed to committing a violent crime of passion), you're done. Off the streets. Once you've shown that kind of behavior, you should be removed from society. Period. We all know that those crimes are wrong, and there's no excuse for letting perpetrators of these crimes back on the streets. Things I would not include in this: heat-of-the-moment murders, manslaughter (or involuntary murder), larceny, date rape without evidence of drugging, to name a few. To address prison over-crowding, I think drug possession charges should be dropped and those convicted released, unless they were dealing at a high level andor committed a violent crime while high. But simple possession and low-level dealing should be dealt with through rehab, not prison. Originally, ASCII was the standard, using 7 bits per character and supporting only 128 symbols – primarily designed for English with numerals and common symbols. When non-English speakers sought to utilize computers, they needed additional characters like European accents and special glyphs. To accommodate these, ISO-8859 was created, expanding ASCII to 8 bits and 256 characters, reserving space for diverse linguistic symbols. However, not all languages fit within this framework, leading to separate character sets like ISO-8859-1 (for Western Europe) and ISO-8859-5 (for Russian). Microsoft also introduced proprietary encodings for features such as varied quotation mark styles. This approach proved problematic due to the need to identify the correct character set and the limitation of using only one at a time. Eventually, Unicode and UTF-8 emerged as the dominant standards, offering universal support for all characters. Despite software’s ability to handle these complex codes, misinterpretations can occur; for instance, examining “Rene” in UTF-8 reveals “Ren.” as ASCII-compatible characters, while “e” is represented as a UTF-8 Unicode sequence that might yield different results depending on the encoding used.

It operates by iteratively refining a policy within a defined parameter space to improve its value function, considering a specific probability distribution. Traditionally, it’s assumed that local optimization methods like this will only yield a local maximum. However, we demonstrate a counterintuitive outcome: any approximate local optimum found through this method also offers a global performance assurance.  We contrast this guarantee with that provided by Direct Policy Iteration, an approximate dynamic programming algorithm utilizing a similar strategy; despite potentially larger approximation errors due to the stochastic nature of local search, we contend that the concentration coefficient within the performance bound is significantly better. A varilet transform involves selecting a suitable varilet basis for a function f; filtering f then modifies these coefficients.

The human body consistently strives to maintain a core temperature between 95 and 100 degrees Fahrenheit. When this range is disrupted, the body initiates mechanisms to adjust, often by creating discomfort – increased pain when excessively cold or hot. Cold sensitivity arises partly due to pre-existing “pain signals” triggered by low temperatures. Numbness in extremities frequently occurs as the body prioritizes blood supply to essential organs like the heart and lungs during extreme cold, diverting circulation away from hands and feet and hindering nerve cell activity. Interestingly, evolutionary adaptations have enabled pain receptors to operate effectively even with reduced blood flow, allowing us to still perceive pain despite the cold.

Natural selection operates solely on adaptation and doesn’t rely on instinct. Initially, early winged creatures likely couldn’t achieve true powered flight; instead, they probably utilized their wings for gliding between trees. Gliding proved significantly more efficient than climbing, allowing these creatures to move quickly and cover greater distances without expending as much energy. These early “flying” animals resembled flying squirrels rather than modern birds of prey.  Even once powered flight evolved, it wasn’t for extended journeys – it mainly served as a means of escaping predators and pursuing prey within trees. A helpful video explaining this concept is available here: URL0. Partially developed wings offered advantages in slowing falls to avoid injury and enhancing gliding capabilities, as discussed by another commenter. Consider an animal that leaps from branches to catch food: offspring with slightly improved arm grace wouldn't truly fly, yet they might fall less severely and capture prey more easily. Through natural selection, this inclination toward enhanced falling would persist over generations. The distinction between falling and gliding is gradual, eventually leading to creatures becoming adept gliders. Similarly, the boundary between sustained gliding and genuine flight becomes indistinct; exceptional gliders may transition into poor flyers, which then evolve into effective fliers. For example, bats possess arms resembling our own, but with exceptionally large, webbed fingers—URL1.

The introduction of LTE over unlicensed bands (LTE-U) will enable LTE base stations (BSs) to boost their capacity and offload their traffic by exploiting the underused unlicensed bands. However, to ensure fair coexistence with other wireless technologies sharing these bands, the LTE-U system needs to implement listen-before-talk (LBT) protocols to avoid interfering with other systems. This is a significant challenge for LTE-U, since the timing and duration of LTE-U transmissions must be carefully coordinated to avoid collisions with other systems sharing the same band. To address this challenge, LTE-U systems use a carrier sensing mechanism to detect the presence of other wireless signals before transmitting. If the channel is occupied, the LTE-U BS waits until the channel becomes available before transmitting. This approach ensures that transmissions over unlicensed bands do not interfere with other systems sharing the same channel. Overall, LTE-U can significantly boost the capacity of wireless networks by exploiting underutilized unlicensed bands. However, it must implement intelligent protocols like LBT to ensure fair coexistence with other wireless systems in the same band.

Traditional deep learning frameworks typically prioritized either ease of use or execution speed, rarely achieving both effectively. PyTorch distinguishes itself by demonstrating compatibility between these objectives – it offers a Python-friendly, imperative coding approach where code acts as the model, facilitating straightforward debugging and integration with existing scientific tools, all while maintaining high performance and leveraging hardware acceleration like GPUs. This paper outlines the design principles behind PyTorch’s creation and illustrates how they shape its structure. It highlights that every element within PyTorch operates as standard Python code, fully controllable by the user, and details how carefully designed runtime components collaborate to deliver strong performance. The paper showcases the efficiency of various parts of the system and demonstrates PyTorch's speed across multiple standard tests.

Eggshells naturally produce a mucous coating that shields them from bacterial contamination, including pathogens like *Salmonella* found in chicken droppings. In the United States, eggs undergo cleaning and scrubbing, which eliminates dirt and manure but also destroys this protective layer, potentially allowing bacteria to enter. Refrigeration is therefore necessary to inhibit growth. However, in countries like those where eggs aren’t routinely washed, such as some parts of Europe, the natural coating remains intact, making *Salmonella* exposure less likely. While *Salmonella* wasn’t a frequent concern before large-scale factory farming began, its prevalence increased due to these practices. Countries with smaller-scale farming operations generally avoid this problem. For example, Sweden successfully reduced *Salmonella* risks through preventative measures focused on chicken and farm health, leading to widespread consumption of raw eggs without issues. Furthermore, many nations, including possibly Japan, vaccinate chickens to minimize *Salmonella* presence in their eggs.

So why is online dating associated with loneliness? One possibility is that the way people present themselves in online profiles and messages can lead to lower levels of self-worth. A second possibility is that people who are lonely are more likely to seek out relationships online. And the third possibility is that the very act of seeking out partners online may increase loneliness. Based on our research, we suspect that all three of these factors are true. The nonprofit landscape is highly varied, although many people have come to associate NPOs with charitable organizations. Although charities do comprise an often high profile or visible aspect of the sector, there are many other types of nonprofits. Overall, they tend to be either member-serving or community-serving. Member-serving organizations include mutual societies, cooperatives, trade unions, credit unions, industry associations, sports clubs, retired serviceman's clubs and peak bodies - organizations that benefit a particular group of people i.e. the members of the organization. Typically, community-serving organizations are focused on providing services to the community in general, either globally or locally: organizations delivering human services programs or projects, aid and development programs, medical research, education and health services, and so on. It could be argued many nonprofits sit across both camps, at least in terms of the impact they make. For example, the grassroots support group that provides a lifeline to those with a particular condition or disease could be deemed to be serving both its members (by directly supporting them) and the broader community (through the provision of a helping service for fellow citizens).
