A Local Area Network (LAN) allows computers and devices connected through shared networking hardware—like your home Wi-Fi—to communicate directly, bypassing the internet. These devices receive private Internal Protocol version 4 (IPv4) addresses, enabling them to send data packets internally without needing an internet connection. Convention dictates that IP addresses beginning with ‘10.’, ‘172.16,’ and ‘192.168’ are designated for LAN use, while others are reserved for the public internet. Typically, a single public IP address is provided by your Internet Service Provider (ISP) and shared amongst all devices on your home LAN; your router then directs incoming data to the appropriate device within the LAN based on its private IP address.

We consider a contextual version of multi-armed bandit problem with global knapsack constraints. In each round, the outcome of pulling an arm is a scalar reward and a resource consumption measure, where the resources are obtained from the other arms. We also introduce a subgame structure to distribute the rewards in such a way that they do not depend on the total number of available arms but rather on their relative scarcity. Our model allows us to show how strategies which allocate an arm equally among all possible outcomes can be used as more efficient than those for equal distribution of cost. Abstract: Machine Learning has become one of the most important fields in computer science since it revolutionized several areas including web search, image recognition and natural language processing (NLP). NLP deals with converting human language into machine readable form so it could later be processed by machines, e.g., natural language understanding systems or speech recognizers. However, unlike many other machine learning techniques, NLP is still missing a general fundamental building block called unsupervised learning which can learn representations of text without explicit preprocessing steps such as word segmentation or sentence correction. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework based on linear algebraic induction followed by deep reinforcement learning to solve the task of unsupervised learning from unlabeled samples. We first define a new function n that represents syntax trees, i.e., linear functions that map words in texts to their symbols; then, we apply our framework to develop a deep neural network architecture, GAN-NLU, that learns a grammar-based representation of sentences from a set of syntactically similar texts using sequential Monte Carlo methods augmented with random forest classifiers. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art models in both accuracy and speed. In addition, its robustness against variations across text corpora makes it well suited to use in practice applications, such as semantic parsing or question answering from large NLP datasets like Wikipedia.

If you run a finger through water and then run your finger through honey, do you feel the difference in how thick the two different liquids are? That thickness is called viscosity. Honey is more viscous than water. The viscosity of liquids is an important part of the world around us. There are three basic types of liquids: solids, liquids, and gases. The difference in the three states is how the particles are arranged. Solids have their particles packed closely together. They are rigid, which means they do not move. Liquids are much like solids, but their particles are loosely packed and move around. Gases are like liquids, but their particles move quickly and can fill any space. Viscosity is the thickness of a liquid. It is how well the particles stick together. The thicker the liquid, the higher the viscosity. Liquids with low viscosity are called thinner liquids, while liquids with high viscosity are called thicker liquids. In addition to viscosity, another property of liquids is called adhesion. Adhesion is the ability for one surface to stick to another. For example, honey sticks to your fingers. It is hard to remove. Water, on the other hand, does not stick to your fingers. They are named for Sir Isaac Newton who first described the property of viscosity. Some liquids are thick, like honey. They are called non-Newtonian fluids. The viscosity of these fluids changes. They get thicker when pressure is applied to them. For example, if you hit a bowl of honey with your hand, it would splatter all over. The thickness of a liquid affects how it moves and flows. If you pour water from a pitcher into a cup, the water quickly flows out of the pitcher and into the cup. If you pour honey from a pitcher into a cup, the honey slowly moves from the pitcher to the cup. Oil is a liquid with a high viscosity. It is very thick and flows slowly. Oil does not mix with water. If you pour water into a container and then pour oil into the container, the oil will float on top of the water. This is because the particles in water and oil are arranged differently. Quantum teleportation is a bit of a misleading name. Normally we think of "teleportation" as taking an object, and making it disappear and then reappear some distance away. Quantum teleportation is nothing like that at all. So why the name? We'll get to that later. First I'll need to explain entanglement, which is the process that you use to get QT. Entanglement is something that happens between two quantum particles. When they are entangled, the two quantum particles are linked together so that whatever you do to one affects the other. Aside: If you are curious, a quantum particle is basically a regular particle that can be multiple things at the same time. For example, a regular particle either points up or down, while a quantum particle can point both up and down at the same time. If that sounds really weird to you.... good. It is reeeeally weird If you want to create quantum teleportation, first you take two entangled particles and then move them far apart from each other. Then you give one of them a poke, and even though there is nothing physical connecting the two, the other one will react. That is quantum teleportation. Doesn't sound that exciting does it? The crucial part of it, and this is why it got the name quantum teleportation, is that the second particle reacts instantly. There is no delay between the poke and the reaction. One of the most important laws in physics is that nothing can move faster than light, not even information. The fact that the two particles are communicating instantly violates one of our fundamental laws of nature. Something very weird is going on there. How can this happen? No one knows! It's one of the great unsolved mysteries of modern science.','First, imagine you have two playing cards. One is a king, and one is a queen. You grab one at random and stick it in a box. The other goes in another box. Now, you can separate the two cards any distance, then open your box and look into it. You instantly know what card is in the other box. That's because there's a link between these two cards. It's one that's easy to understand, since there were two possibilities to begin with and you are just eliminating one. But it's still demonstrating a real, physical link between the two cards. Quantum entanglement does the same thing to a subatomic particle. A subatomic particle can have some property which is like its "queen-ness," which is mutually exclusive of its "king-ness." When two particles are entangled, the two will always be opposite to one another, so if you observe your particle and it is a king, you automatically know the other is a queen. The difference is, a quantum particle's state is constantly changing, unlike your static playing card. But even though it is always changing in what we believe to be a totally random way, it will continue to always be the case that when you observe the particle, if it is a king, the other is a queen. Their randomness is perfectly opposite to one another. How and why does this happen? That's a damned good question. edit: Important point that many miss about this: forcing either particle to enter a given state does not cause the other to enter the opposite state. The moment you try to do that, the entanglement ends and they are two unrelated particles again.

Early "republics" such as the Vajji (or Vriji) confederation centered in the city of Vaishali, existed as early as the 6th century BCE and persisted in some areas until the 4th century CE. The educated speech at that time was Sanskrit, while the languages of the general population of northern India are referred to as Prakrits. Many of the sixteen kingdoms had coalesced to four major ones by 500400 BCE, by the time of Gautama Buddha. These four were Vatsa, Avanti, Kosala, and Magadha. The Life of Gautam Budhha was mainly associated with these four kingdoms.

The key to free trade is comparative advantage. What that means is that each country is (usually) good at makingdoing something based on a combination of factors (such as their natural resources, education levels, amount of capital, etc.) For example - Cuba is well known for their cigars, Germany for their cars, Taiwan for semiconductors, etc. Free trade allows countries to focus on what they're good at makingdoing and not waste moneyresources on things that they're not good at makingdoing (since they can get those other things from other countries through trade). The opposite of free trade is protectionism. Generally with protectionism, a country's government sets up a policy that makes it really expensive to import goods from outside of a country, which encourages domestic production of everything (or only a few things - protectionist policies can cover just one or two industries in some cases or cover the entire economy in others). The main problem with protectionism is that you end up with a country that is the "jack of all trades, master of none." Since domestic businesses don't have to compete with foreign products, they get lazy. A perfect example of this is that during the 1980s Brazil enforced strict controls on the import of foreign computers in an effort to nurture its own domestic computer industry. This industry never matured; the technological gap between Brazil and the rest of the world actually widened, while the protected industries merely copied low-end foreign computers and sold them at inflated prices. The American auto industry had the same problem in the 1970s - since there was no competition, they got by making sub-standard cars with low reliability. Once the Japanese entered the market (Honda, Toyota, etc.) with superior products they were able to grab a ton of market share. Meanwhile the American automakers struggled to remain competitive. For these specific trade agreements (I'll pick on the agreement with South Korea in particular) it seems like the benefit for the American economy will be much cheaper goods coming in from South Korea (which produces a ton of goods from electronics to cars - Samsung, Kia, Hyundai, LG, etc. are all South Korean companies) and we will also be able to export much more of our agricultural products overseas (American produced beef, chicken, pork, etc. is in high demand all over the world, but especially in Asia).

Research today largely relies on collaborative efforts within sizable teams, which typically excel at securing funding, tackling complex projects, and generating impactful results. However, recent studies indicate that both large and small teams play crucial roles in scientific advancement, leading to an examination of how a nation’s research landscape utilizes different team sizes. Analyzing over 26 million publications from Web of Science, our study reveals that China’s research output has historically been driven primarily by large teams, though this dominance decreased significantly after 2000.  As Chinese research teams grew larger, their diversification – vital for novel discoveries – didn’t expand as substantially as it did elsewhere. Comparing China’s National Natural Science Foundation (NSFC) with the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), we observe that NSFC tends to favor large teams over smaller ones for grants, suggesting a preference for bigger collaborations. This highlights concerns about originality and innovation in China and underscores the importance of fostering a balanced approach between large and small research teams.

A new study by musicologists in Europe suggests that the shape of our ear canals, as well as our own perceptions, is to blame for our distaste in such shrill tones. The researchers believe these are due to a combination of visual cues and auditory information provided by competing "tinnitus" genes. The findings have implications not just for tinnitus patients, but also for humans who find loud sounds unpleasant including those with hearing loss or chronic inflammation around their ears. It's unclear exactly why we dislike certain frequencies so much: some people hate how an electric guitar vibrates, while others really like it. But as more scientists learn about human hearing, they've come up with theories for why there are differences between people's reactions. Now, according to this latest study, one theory may be behind all the bitterness: a difference in how your hearing cells process sound. [What Is Your Ear? What It Can't Tell You] Tinnitus affects millions of people worldwide, making them uncomfortable because of its constant ringing or buzzing sound. People often avoid seeing doctors about it out of fear that they'll get another prescription for pills - raising concerns over drug addiction, and potential health risks from too many restrictions on what you hear. To investigate how the frequency of noise affects perception, researchers at several universities in Switzerland set up 40 volunteers to listen to different types of music using headphones. They then compared how each person perceived the songs' pitch, meaning which notes were louder than others. Then, after testing each person's ability to tune out background noises (such as cars approaching) with his or her ear canal, the team gave each musician a control track that played only silence. Their results revealed that we tend to hear actual music louder when listening through the inner ear than through our outerear. So rather than hearing a song from outside your head, most tinnituses try to make sense of the sounds coming directly into theirs. These include high-pitched sounds like horns, traffic sounds and other car alarms; low pitched sounds like bird calls and quiet footsteps that occur naturally within cyberspace; middle range sounds such as laughter and jokes; and finally, voices. While this isn't necessarily bad news, it does mean that if you want to enjoy some great tunes without worrying about disturbing anyone else in the house, turn down the volume a bit. And since you probably don't pay attention to your environment as carefully as you do your music, maybe consider adding in a Bluetooth speaker system early in the morning before you wake up, or perhaps during your commute.

In November 1960, John F. Kennedy was elected president after a campaign that promised American superiority over the Soviet Union in the fields of space exploration and missile defense. Up to the election of 1960, Kennedy had been speaking out against the "missile gap" that he and many other senators felt had formed between the Soviets and themselves due to the inaction of President Eisenhower. Beyond military power, Kennedy used aerospace technology as a symbol of national prestige, pledging to make the US not "first but, first and, first if, but first period." Despite Kennedy's rhetoric, he did not immediately come to a decision on the status of the Apollo program once he became president. He knew little about the technical details of the space program, and was put off by the massive financial commitment required by a manned Moon landing. When Kennedy's newly appointed NASA Administrator James E. Webb requested a 30 percent budget increase for his agency, Kennedy supported an acceleration of NASA's large booster program but deferred a decision on the broader issue.

At one point while at Bacchanal, sometime after eating a plate overflowing with at least a pound of crab legs and before taking on a final slice of cheesecake (one of four dishes I ordered for dessert), I sat back, stuffed and exhausted, and watched as the crowd at the next table, a group of 20-something women celebrating a bachelorette party, dug into a massive platter of food that could have fed an entire fraternity house. The menu at Bacchanal is impressive enough to make your head spin. Some of the offerings include: a full charcuterie board with house made pates, curing meats, pickled vegetables and Vermont cheeses; a grilled squid salad with arugula, roasted corn and lemon vinaigrette; a braised pork belly with white beans, collards and crispy pig ear salad; and a roasted chicken with confit potatoes and fennel. There's also an impressive wine list with more than 300 bottles, including many hard-to-find selections. You can order off the menu or go with the Bacchanal Experience (45person), a prix fixe meal with a main course (a protein like fish, beef, chicken or pork), two salads, three sides and an appetizer. It's quite a bit of food and more than enough for the average person. If you want to try everything, you can always order some off the menu and supplement the Bacchanal Experience with the additional dishes. There are a lot of fantastic restaurants in New Orleans, but Bacchanal has become one of my favorites. Partly because of the way it's set up - if you're looking for a formal sit down dinner experience, this is not the place for you. You can sit inside or outside, but seating is limited, so if you go on a busy night (Friday and Saturday nights are usually packed) you may have to wait. They do have a bar and a small shop where you can pick up a bottle of wine or cheese and crackers to enjoy while you wait, so you can't really complain if you end up waiting a half hour for a table. Another thing that makes Bacchanal so great is that there's a real sense of community here. This was evident the first time I went when I ran into a friend who I hadn't seen in years. We ended up sitting together at the same table and spending the whole night catching up. There's something very cool about the fact that most people who come here are either locals or have been living here long enough to be considered locals. Even the employees seem happy to see you year after year, and they remember who you are and what you eat. The last time I was at Bacchanal, I was sitting outside and a guy walked by and said "Hey, I remember you! You had a bunch of stuff and you were really drunk." I looked up and realized that it was the bartender from seven years ago. He remembered me. And he remembered the food I ate. When I asked him how he remembered all of this, he just shrugged and said, "I remember people." That's pretty much the way I feel about Bacchanal. I remember people and I remember the food.

The concept of “inverse totalitarianism” involves examining influential entities like media conglomerates such as Disney, Time Warner, CBS, and News Corp, along with financial institutions including Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, CITI bank, and Deutsche Bank, alongside technology giants like Google, Apple, AT&T, and Verizon.  Vanguard, BlackRock, State Street, and Fidelity frequently appear within these organizations. These corporations are allegedly attempting to exert greater control over the internet through legislation like CISPA. Critically, these banks engage in lobbying efforts targeting Congress and possess significant influence over the Federal Reserve Bank, issuing the currency we use—federal reserve notes, not U.S. Treasury Notes. Investigating how the Federal Reserve operates reveals that each regional Federal Reserve Bank functions as a privately held corporation controlled by commercial banks in that area; these banks select two-thirds of the nine-member board, while the remaining seats are appointed by the Federal Reserve Board. This board governs operations, appoints officials, and oversees activities like check processing, lending, and securities trading. A parallel can be drawn to biblical accounts of removing corrupt influences from sacred spaces, regardless of personal beliefs about religion.

The activist, who says he was himself a victim of bullying, told BBC Newsnight that the dossier was given by Ben Howlett, now an MP, to Lord Feldman. Lord Feldman insists he was not aware of any complaints before August 2015. Two activists involved in producing the document say it named Mark Clarke. Mr Clarke is the volunteer organiser at the heart of the bullying scandal which has bedevilled the party since September. He has been accused of bullying, sexually harassing and planning to blackmail other activists - allegations he has robustly denied. Patrick Sullivan, who runs a Conservative think tank, said hard copies of the 2010 dossier were handed to Lord Feldman and Tory co-chair Baroness Sayeeda Warsi. His testimony appears to contradict the account of Lord Feldman, a close friend and political ally of the prime minister. The Tory chairman has maintained consistently that he was "wholly unaware" of the allegations against Mr Clarke until August 2015. Mr Sullivan told Newsnight that Mr Howlett, MP for Bath, had decided to tackle widespread bullying within the party's young activists after being elected to a second term as chair of Conservative Future, the party's youth wing, in 2010. Mr Sullivan said: "He had a strong anti-bullying stance in the campaign because there had been a culture of bullying. As soon as he was elected Ben [Howlett] and myself helped compile a dossier and that dossier was given by Ben to Lord Feldman and Sayeeda Warsi." He said that complaints had been made to the party about Mr Clarke's behaviour even before 2010 when Mr Clarke was removed from the party's list of approved candidates. "The dossier is not the only thing," Mr Sullivan said. "There were complaints about Mark Clarke in 2008. So complaints about Mark Clarke had been something that Conservative Central Office have known about for a very long time." Mr Sullivan said his own bullying at the hand of Mr Clarke seriously damaged his health: "I got depressed. I felt I couldn't leave my home. I felt isolated." He said Mr Howlett had also been a victim of Mr Clarke's bullying. They assembled the dossier over the course of a week along with a third activist. It contained first person accounts from activists who had been bullied, alongside newspaper reports of bullying incidents which were already in the public domain. Mr Sullivan says he first challenged the culture of bullying in the party in 2008 after an 18 year-old woman was "spectacularly" bullied in the run up to a Conservative Future election. He said: "Mark Clarke had a preferred candidate and as a result he started bullying and intimidating people who were opposing that candidate. That was when I first realised how bad he was." Mr Sullivan said he made a speech inside CCHQ attacking the bullying culture in front of Mr Clarke and others. "As a punishment for making that speech I was isolated like a pariah," he said. The bullying scandal has gathered pace since a young activist, Elliott Johnson, took his own life in September. Mr Clarke has denied all allegations of inappropriate behaviour. He has told Newsnight he was not aware of any "dossier" mentioning him in 2010. On Tuesday night Elliott's father Ray told Newsnight: "If Lord Feldman and CCHQ were fully aware of allegations of bullying being made as long ago as five years and they didn't act upon it, then it just confirms my view that they really should have taken action against bullies in the first place and failed to do so." Former co-chairman Grant Shapps resigned last month as a development minister after it emerged that he had given Mr Clarke a formal role in CCHQ despite previous concerns about his behaviour. However both Number 10 and the party have been determined to protect Lord Feldman who has been a member of the prime minister's inner circle since they met at Oxford. Increasingly, however, Lord Feldman has come under pressure, both over his account of when he first became aware of allegations of bullying, and over whether he reacted appropriately to a slew of complaints received in August of this year. Last week Newsnight revealed a former CCHQ worker submitted a memo to a senior party official in August claiming that Mr Clarke was "sociopathic" and "dangerous" and warning that there could be "devastating" consequences if he was not kept away from the party's youth wing. Asked whether he believed Lord Feldman should have done more in response to the memo, Mr Sullivan said: "Yes I do, I think it was quite shocking that Mark Clarke was able to continue with his RoadTrip 2020 whilst this investigation was process." The practice of using “tenths” in gasoline pricing has ancient roots, dating back to the early 20th century when a Nevada newspaper described selling gasoline for eight and nine-tenths cents per gallon – a significant increase compared to eight cents alone. During this era, a single cent held substantial worth, and small price adjustments were made in increments of tenths of a penny to remain competitive. This was further reinforced by the introduction of tax rates also measured in tenths of a cent. Despite its seeming redundancy, this convention endured. For example, in February 2007, the U.S. Energy Information Administration recorded sales of 372,833.5 thousand barrels of motor gasoline, generating $141 million in nine-tenth-of-a-cent payments. Although gasoline prices now typically range between $2.00 and $4.00, the 910 system is largely unnecessary, and attempts to eliminate it have sometimes been made, such as during an Iowa experiment in the 1980s which ultimately reverted to the established format.

Robotic systems capable of learning through observing human demonstrations offer significant advancements due to their ability to avoid manual programming. A key obstacle in imitation learning is the "correspondence problem"—determining matching states and actions across differing agent bodies—which varies in morphology, dynamics, and degrees of freedom. Current methods often resolve this issue through techniques like kinesthetic teaching or teleoperation, applied directly to the robot. Here, we tackle the correspondence problem head-on by creating a distance metric comparing disparate body types. This metric serves as a loss function for mimicking static poses and provides feedback within a deep reinforcement learning system for simulating dynamic movements between robotic arms, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing embodiment similarity and facilitating imitation policy learning via distance reduction.

With the widespread use of mobile phones and scanners to photograph and upload documents, the need for extracting the information trapped in unstructured document images such as retail receipts, insurance claim forms and financial invoices is becoming more acute. A major hurdle to this objective is that these images often contain information in the form of tables and extracting data from tabular sub-images presents a unique set of challenges. This includes accurate detection of the tabular region within an image, and subsequently detecting and extracting information from the rows and columns of the detected table. While some progress has been made in table detection, extracting the table contents is still a challenge since this involves more fine grained table structure (rows columns) recognition. Prior approaches have attempted to solve the table detection and structure recognition problems independently using two separate models. In this paper, we propose TableNet: a novel end-to-end deep learning model for both table detection and structure recognition. The model exploits the interdependence between the twin tasks of table detection and table structure recognition to segment out the table and column regions. This is followed by semantic rule-based row extraction from the identified tabular sub-regions. The proposed model and extraction approach was evaluated on the publicly available ICDAR 2013 and Marmot Table datasets obtaining state of the art results. Additionally, we demonstrate that feeding additional semantic features further improves model performance and that the model exhibits transfer learning across datasets. Another contribution of this paper is to provide additional table structure annotations for the Marmot data, which currently only has annotations for table detection.

Following the American Revolution, significant events in the United States impacted British policy in Canada, leading to the arrival of approximately 40,000 to 100,000 Loyalist refugees. A portion of these Loyalists – around 14,000 settling along the St. John and St. Croix rivers in what was then Nova Scotia – found themselves distant from the governing body in Halifax. Consequently, London established the colony of New Brunswick in 1784. The Constitutional Act of 1791 divided both regions into Upper Canada (predominantly English-speaking) and Lower Canada (primarily French-speaking), aiming to ease conflict between the two groups and mirroring British governmental structures. This was done to reinforce imperial control and prevent the kind of direct citizen influence on governance seen as contributing to the American Revolution.

It was Christian's first day of Seventh grade. He was very nervous. His mom made him a special breakfast to calm his nerves. Christian ate his breakfast and got on the bus. But he hugged his mother goodbye when she dropped off his backpack at their house. As soon as he entered the garage, though, he threw himself into his bike - and took it for a spin around the neighborhood. About half way down the block, he stopped to look back once again. He saw a small group of parents standing behind a fence watching over their children as they played on bikes or scooters. They were not there just because they wanted permission to ride their kids' bikes; they also taught them how to safely do so. That morning, the family watched television together while eating breakfast. The older boys were hanging out with their friends. Christian joined them to play soccer after church on Sunday mornings. On Thursday nights, they went bowling or went swimming. And whenever they could find some adult company, the family enjoyed an ice cream party every Saturday night. Karen DeWitt often finds that her husband, Chris, does not enjoy going to church. So much so, he has chosen not to attend any services during the pandemic. It's safe enough for Karen to accompany Chris to worship services at First Baptist Church. When she attends those services alone, however, she feels like everything feels different. Her husband often says, "The Bible says we should be one body," but it takes more than being a member of a large congregation to meet God each week. She realizes now that the challenge is even greater for people who are homeschooling for many months. In addition to the challenges of social distancing, families have been adjusting to having extended family members stay healthy at home by communicating through technology instead of seeing each other face-to-face. For example, if someone wants to visit a relative or friend, they must go online and schedule a virtual meeting. As Christians, Christians need to remember that our lives don't revolve solely around ourselves anymore. We depend on others to provide the right care for us and take good care of themselves along the way. Our health depends upon theirs. If we can't see one another physically or socially, then we rely on the spirit of God to give us support and encouragement both individually and collectively as a community. We also need to realize that most of what we learn today will come directly from scripture. There is no way of knowing what God is teaching us without relying on scriptures. Without reading Scripture daily and asking questions, we may miss important lessons. Even Jesus rarely spoke without knowing beforehand exactly what he would say next. In fact, several times throughout Matthew, Luke and John, Jesus asked his disciples where they understood Him to be saying those things. Many of these conversations weren't recorded until decades later (circa 1st Century AD). Christ didn't want our mouths full of words, he wanted our ears to hear. Therefore, everyone needs to read scripture daily and ask questions, especially those close to you. This means listening to your pastor (who is actually a person), learning your Bible verse and participating in discussions and sermons using the answers in your bible study guide. Your prayer life will grow exponentially too! During these challenging times, we are all busy trying to cope with new circumstances. However, there is nothing better for mental and spiritual strength than spending time in church each week. According to research conducted at Wesleyan University, faith formation continues to improve with regular attendance at religious services. While there might seem to be fewer people attending in person during the current COVID-19 situation, it is still important for people to attend. After all, God created us to worship Him. If we choose not to worship God, we cannot claim to love Him. Remember, it doesn't matter if you're a new believer or an old one, whether you live alone or with others, or whether you attended church regularly previously. Everyone is called to participate in church and to know God better. No matter what season you're in, go to church and make sure to get up onto the platform and sing songs about the Lord. Sing praises to Him and thank Him for all He has done. Spend time praying together. Just talk to Him and tell Him all of the thoughts that you have for yourself and your loved ones. Ask God to change your heart toward others, and start trusting in Him completely - no longer worrying about what other people think about you, what other people think about other people, etc., but fully committing to believing in God, doing what He tells us to do, loving everybody else as well as yourself.

Consider the task of performing a sequence of searches in a binary search tree. After each search, an algorithm is allowed to arbitrarily restructure the tree, at a cost proportional to its current height and in accordance with any pre-specified optimization functions (e.g., minimizing the number of leaves). As soon as all nodes have been visited or their lower successors were found, this procedure terminates; otherwise it repeats itself. This paper presents several search strategies for finding suboptimal solutions in order to save time by decreasing the size of the searched state space. Although we do not exhaustively discuss different possibilities available for the optimization function, several examples are given below: minimum norm between two numbers, maximum degree within reachable branches, maximum depth among childrens' descendants, etc.. Some initial results on efficiency reduction obtained using these methods will be presented followed by descriptions of some advanced techniques based on dynamic programming algorithms.

Activities also include wife carrying, husband dragging, gravy wrestling, Russian egg roulette, backward running, worm charming and ditch racing. The games, in Llanwrtyd Wells, continue every weekend until 29 August. The original wife carrying contest was held in Finland and is based on a 19th century tale of a man called Herkko Rosvo-Ronkainen who used to steal women away from their homes. In the US, the sport is known as pig racing and has been part of the Iowa State Fair since 1930. "We've had husband dragging before," says Mrs Jones, "but not in an organised event." It's a race of husbands dragged along by wives on sledges or toboggans while they carry bags of coal. They have to go up a hill and down again. "One of the first years we held it, one of the men said that he thought it was worthy of a world record," she says. "So he went off and did some research and discovered that there was no such thing. So we made it up." Mrs Jones wants to turn Llanwrtyd Wells into the sporting capital of Britain. And it seems to be working. 'Totally bonkers' In January this year, the town hosted Europe's largest game of conkers with more than 500 people playing at once. Llanwrtyd Wells was also the venue for the world bog snorkelling championships which attracted more than 100 competitors from around the world. But it's not all about weird sports. In May, the town hosted the European Real Ale Wobble - a nine-day cycling festival. During the event, cyclists toured Wales and England visiting breweries and sampling their beers. "I got the idea when I saw people going across America doing wine tours," says Mrs Jones. "I thought: If they can do it over there, why can't you do it over here? "People are fed up with being told what to do and where to go. They're fed up with big city life and so want to get out in the fresh air and see things like the Brecon Beacons. "And we've got the best real ales in the world." The event proved extremely popular with riders from as far away as Australia and New Zealand taking part. "It was just fantastic," says Mrs Jones. "It was so successful that we are looking at holding it again in 2010." As for her unusual jobs, Mrs Jones is not surprised that she has found herself in this situation. "I always wanted to run my own business and saw the hotel coming up for sale," she says. "I came in and met the owner and told him: 'If you sell it to me, I'll make you rich.' Ever since I could remember, that room has been off limits. I mean, it doesn't really look like anything out of the ordinary; it's just a door. It's wooden and painted white. The door handle is one of those old ones and it looks almost black from numerous hands turning it. The keyhole looks rusty and dusty as though no one has been through the door in ages. I don't know why my parents don't want me to go in that room. I have never even seen them enter it themselves. I hear no strange noises or witness strange smells coming from behind it. But needless to say, I am intensely curious what is behind that door. Until today, I have never even attempted to enter that room. But there is nothing on TV, I have no books to read and my parents have both left for the day. I'm bored and curiosity is about to get the better of me. I step closer to the door and take a deep breath. Taking a long shot, I try the door handle and turn it slowly. It turns with a squeak and I have to pull hard on the door as it sticks. The door opens with a groan or rusty hinges and stale musty air assaults my nose. I sneeze, five times in rapid succession. Stupid allergies. When I glance into the room, I am not sure what I am seeing. The single window is covered by a heavy curtain and the room is dim. I can see shapes against the wall covered in sheets caked in dust. I cross to the window and gently pull back to curtain to let a shiver of light stream across the floor. With the room brightened, I notice pictures on the wall. I slowly walk over, staring at it incredulously. I notice one in particular that is old and covered in a thick layer of dust. I gently wipe it off with my sleeve. In it, my mother sits on a chair with my father behind her as they look grimly in the photographer's direction. The picture is without colour and they are dressed in what looks like clothes from the 1800s, if I was to guess. I guess the part that shocks me the most is that I am in the picture, standing beside my father, with the same grim expression on my face.

Prioritized experience replay allows online reinforcement learning agents to recall and utilize past experiences. Previous methods randomly selected experience transitions from a memory buffer, playing them back at a consistent rate irrespective of their importance. This research introduces a system for weighting experiences, enabling more frequent replay of crucial transitions and ultimately accelerating learning. Applying this prioritized experience replay technique to Deep Q-Networks (DQN), a successful algorithm demonstrating impressive results in various Atari games, yields superior performance—outperforming standard DQN on 41 of 49 tested games and establishing a new benchmark.

His head hurt worse than ever all day long. Something caught his attention as he walked past an open door leading into another part of his house. An old man sat alone in a chair staring straight ahead. A bowl full of soup rested on the table next to him. The electric lights were off so Austin could not see what color the soup or spoon looked like. The sound of footsteps startled Austin back outside and to his surprise he saw no one around. Completely bewildered, he didn't know where to go so he began walking around aimlessly until he heard someone call out "Hey! Over here." There stood two young men who just happened upon him by chance. They weren't armed which calmed him down some. One of them approached him closely while the other stayed behind. "What's your name?" asked one of the boys. "How should I know? Who are you supposed to be asking me this question? Why am I being called 'hey' instead of 'hello'? Where do these people get their manners from?" asked Austin sarcastically. Both of the boys laughed heartily. After the real laughter died down both of them said simultaneously "We're from the hospital. We need you to come with us right away." And then they let him go without saying anything else before disappearing into thin air. At first, Austin thought maybe after everything that has happened he would've chosen hanging himself over coming with these strange kids anyway. But something made him follow along with them nonetheless. Now he wasn't quite sure if he wanted to remain silent or scream at them some more at how stupid and rude they seemed, especially when there were plenty of others around just waiting for any excuse to take advantage of someone who might have conveniently wandered off during the middle of nowhere. At last, the boy stopped abruptly and pointed to a building nearby where there appeared to be some kind of emergency scene. People dressed in white coats rushed about doing whatever doctors did and pieces of equipment lay scattered everywhere. Another group of three older guys stood over a cot containing someone wrapped tightly inside a blanket. What scared Austin most though, was seeing several bodies lying flat against the floor. All of them wore clothes similar to what the ones he shared with Dawn and Billy - brown pants and jacket. As soon as they spotted each other standing across the street, they ran towards each other shouting joyfully. A moment later, Austin felt a hand touch his shoulder lightly, almost timidly. It sent chills through him. He turned and found that both of the teenagers still remained quiet and respectfully watching him curiously. Their hands moved nervously up and down their clothing reaching back down to pull the sleeves up to cover parts of their arms. Yet, they kept themselves from touching anyone else including the person beside Austin. For the life of him, Austin couldn't figure out why they acted differently than everyone else he'd met in the world. But he knew it meant trouble whether he liked it or not. After hugging his friends cautiously, Austin managed to give someone a hug too and then motioned for them to continue following him. The earliest known macrofossil confidently identified as an angiosperm, Archaefructus liaoningensis, is dated to about 125 million years BP (the Cretaceous period), whereas pollen considered to be of angiosperm origin takes the fossil record back to about 130 million years BP. However, one study has suggested that the early-middle Jurassic plant Schmeissneria, traditionally considered a type of ginkgo, may be the earliest known angiosperm, or at least a close relative. In addition, circumstantial chemical evidence has been found for the existence of angiosperms as early as 250 million years ago. Oleanane, a secondary metabolite produced by many flowering plants, has been found in Permian deposits of that age together with fossils of gigantopterids. Gigantopterids are a group of extinct seed plants that share many morphological traits with flowering plants, although they are not known to have been flowering plants themselves.

We introduce submodular hypergraphs, a family of hypergraphs that have different submodular weights associated with different cuts of hyperedges. Submodular hypergraphs arise in clustering applications in which higher-order structures carry different weights. We give a minimum-weight hypergraph matching algorithm and a minimum weight hypergraph partitioning algorithm. We also give a set cover algorithm that finds the minimum weight set of sets satisfying all given constraints and a minimum weight hypergraph cut algorithm. We show that the minimum weight matching and partitioning algorithms run in polynomial time, and we provide a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for the minimum weight set cover problem.

The Ottomans absorbed some of the traditions, art and institutions of cultures in the regions they conquered, and added new dimensions to them. Numerous traditions and cultural traits of previous empires (in fields such as architecture, cuisine, music, leisure and government) were adopted by the Ottoman Turks, who elaborated them into new forms, which resulted in a new and distinctively Ottoman cultural identity. Despite newer added amalgamations, the Ottoman dynasty, like their predecessors in the Sultanate of Rum and the Seljuk Empire, were thoroughly Persianised in their culture, language, habits and customs, and therefore, the empire has been described as a Persianate empire. Intercultural marriages also played their part in creating the characteristic Ottoman elite culture. When compared to the Turkish folk culture, the influence of these new cultures in creating the culture of the Ottoman elite was clear.

Following the crushing loss suffered by the Prussian army at the Battle of Jena-Auerstedt in 1806, Napoleon seized control of Berlin and compelled the members of the Prussian General Directory to pledge their loyalty to him. Simultaneously, King Frederick William III and his wife, Louise, escaped through Königsberg and across the Curonian Spit to Memel. French forces swiftly began the chase, though they encountered resistance at the Battle of Eylau on February 9, 1807, thanks to a group of East Prussian soldiers commanded by General Anton Wilhelm von L’Estocq. Despite being stationed at the Finckenstein Palace, Napoleon eventually captured Danzig – fiercely held by General Count Friedrich Adolf von Kalkreuth after a 75-day siege – in May, aided by Marshal François Joseph Lefebvre’s troops.  Finally, on June 14th, Napoleon secured victory at the Battle of Friedland, concluding the War of the Fourth Coalition. Frederick William and Louise subsequently met with Napoleon for peace talks, culminating in the Prussian monarch signing the Treaty of Tilsit on July 9th.

The energy levels of hydrogen can be calculated fairly accurately using the Bohr model of the atom, which conceptualizes the electron as "orbiting" the proton in analogy to the Earth's orbit of the Sun. However, the electromagnetic force attracts electrons and protons to one another, while planets and celestial objects are attracted to each other by gravity. Because of the discretization of angular momentum postulated in early quantum mechanics by Bohr, the electron in the Bohr model can only occupy certain allowed distances from the proton, and therefore only certain allowed energies.

The first emergency number was the British 999, which America initially copied. On a rotary phone, 999 is memorable, but difficult to dial by accident. For technical reasons, 999 was difficult to implement in the US, so 911 was used instead: the first 1 actually signals to a US exchange that the call is not routine. Meanwhile, in Germany, the death of a child after a traffic accident gave the impetus for an improved emergency number system there. They favoured numbers that could be dialled very quickly. The fastest 3-digit number to dial on a rotary dial would have been 111, but this was rejected as it was thought too prone to accidental dialling: 111 could also be dialled simply by pressing the cradle three times in quick succession. They opted for 110 for the police and 112 for the other emergency services. Other European countries then used the faster 112 for all emergency services. With the advent of mobile phones, 999 came back to bite the UK, as it was ridiculously easy to accidentally butt-dial. A special system was set up: if a 999 call was received and nobody spoke, the call would be forwarded to an automatic system. This plays a pre-recorded message saying that the caller is connected to the police, and if they genuinely require assistance, they must press 5. For tourists, 112 has now been introduced in addition to 999, so that even visitors using phones that don't recognize 999 as an emergency number can still call emergency services.," "The emergency number varies widely across different countries. In the UK, for example, the emergency number is '999'. In Australia, the emergency number is '000'. Many countries also have different emergency numbers that you call depending on whether you want police, firerescue, or ambulance service dispatched. In some countries, the emergency number is only 1 or 2 digits long. '112' is the most common'international standard' but it is not universal. Having said that, if you dial '112' on a GSM-compatible mobile phone (i.e. a phone with a SIM card), then it should automatically redirect you to the local emergency number even if you are in North America. So there are still some situations where a call to '112' will get you emergency services in North America.

In this paper, using the stochastic geometry theory, we present a framework for analyzing the performance of device-to-device (D2D) communications underlaid uplink (UL) cellular networks. In our analysis, we consider in detail both the presence and absence of shared channel resources among various users which are deployed on different cell sites with regard to their respective user profiles. We show that there is no significant difference between D2D communication performance over different cell sites or at all with respect to the number of UL channels available to each user type. Given available bandwidths and quality of service requirements, any cell site can successfully be used as an access point (AP). However, in order to obtain optimal throughput and quality of service, it must have sufficient capacity to support both macro cell aggregation and small cells. Indeed, 4G LTE relies heavily upon shared channel resources jointly provided by multiple base stations and several user equipments (UE), e.g., mobile phones, tablets, etc.. The ability of a UE to transmit data, even when only allocated one single base station's radio resource is constrained, is referred to as multipath fading. If this same UE goes through more than two or three adjacent base stations along its path from the network to the base station, then there will be additional interference due to the inter-channel interference produced by these distant base stations. It has been shown that the effective interference strength increases exponentially as the distance between the UE and the base station increases while the maximum achievable interference intensity decreases linearly unless the UE experiences multi-path fading. Therefore, one approach to optimize the throughput of a D2D system is to design an antenna array so as to minimize multipath interference. Ideally, an optimal antenna array would use only selected countries' coverage areas where multipath fading is not expected to occur. To achieve such a goal, most studies focus on designing efficient antennas corresponding to specific scenarios (e.g. the UTRAN scenario cite22), based on such assumptions that multipath effects are assumed to be absent (i.e., single-user transmission over shared channel resources). Full Text Available BACKGROUND: With the advent of the fourth generation (4G wireless technology, the need for a standardized 5G architecture with low complexity and excellent efficiency is increasing day after day. One of the main goals of 5G is to improve the network mobility as well as provide higher reliability and higher speed. A key element required for achieving high signaling rate and seamless operation is the fast communication interface (ICF. The overall ICF may consist of several parts. Among them are timing synchronization circuits, and multipath propagation cancellation circuit. The first part performs time synchronization and provides accurate timing for the second part providing precise multipath cancellation. Meanwhile, the 3rd party streamer generates uniform multicast packets according to the frame format of the upper layer protocol. Even though there are many works about ICFs, existing ICFs are complicated and require large physical area and power consumption. Hence, there exists a great requirement for developing less complex ICFs. Our recent research work focuses the development of a novel ICF called "Multi-Channel Interference Cancellation" for reducing ICF in UEs. The Multi-Channel Interference Cancellation defines an algorithm which examines each received ICF individually to eliminate interference caused by multiple failures and within given error probability tolerance limits. This algorithm minimizes the mutual interference. Based on a unified computational model, the method also considers the instantaneous activity and the corresponding delay information for the user terminals in terms of MIMO and multiuser environment. As a result, the proposed algorithm enables reliable ICF estimation without violating the distance constraint of the network infrastructure. In this article, we propose a new ICF framework capable of supporting low complexity ICF protocols like HSDPA and WiMax and high reliability ICF protocols like Long Term Evolution (LTE) and WCDMA.

Helper T cells express T cell receptors (TCR) that recognize antigen bound to Class II MHC molecules. The MHC:antigen complex is also recognized by the helper cell's CD4 co-receptor, which recruits molecules inside the T cell (e.g., Lck) that are responsible for the T cell's activation. Helper T cells have a weaker association with the MHC:antigen complex than observed for killer T cells, meaning many receptors (around 200-300) on the helper T cell must be bound by an MHC:antigen in order to activate the helper cell, while killer T cells can be activated by engagement of a single MHC:antigen molecule. Helper T cell activation also requires longer duration of engagement with an antigen-presenting cell. The activation of a resting helper T cell causes it to release cytokines that influence the activity of many cell types. Cytokine signals produced by helper T cells enhance the microbicidal function of macrophages and the activity of killer T cells. In addition, helper T cell activation causes an upregulation of molecules expressed on the T cell's surface, such as CD40 ligand (also called CD154), which provide extra stimulatory signals typically required to activate antibody-producing B cells.

The warmer temperatures in the east US this year may be due to various factors, including El Nino, climate change, and natural fluctuations in weather patterns. While you can intentionally move your knee, maintaining balance and walking involves unconscious adjustments. The thigh muscle spindle automatically tightens the muscle when it senses relaxation, preventing falls – a reaction stimulated by a reflex hammer.

Experience replay lets online reinforcement learning agents remember and reuse experiences from the past. In prior work, experience transitions were uniformly sampled from a replay memory. However, this approach simply replays transitions at the same frequency that they were originally experienced, regardless of their significance. In this paper we develop a framework for prioritizing experience, so as to replay important transitions more frequently, and therefore learn more efficiently. We use prioritized experience replay in Deep Q-Networks (DQN), a reinforcement learning algorithm that achieved human-level performance across many Atari games. DQN with prioritized experience replay achieves a new state-of-the-art, outperforming DQN with uniform replay on 41 out of 49 games.

We introduce symmetric arithmetic circuits, i.e. arithmetic circuits with a natural symmetry restriction. In the context of circuits computing polynomials defined on a matrix of variables, such as the determinant or the permanent, the restriction amounts to requiring that the shape of the circuit is invariant under row and column permutations of the matrix. We establish unconditional, nearly exponential, lower bounds on the size of any symmetric circuit for computing the permanent over any field of characteristic other than 2. In contrast, we show that there are polynomial-size symmetric circuits for computing the determinant over fields of characterisitic zero.

Field sobriety tests (SFSTs) aren’t legally required in most places. Their main function is to influence whether an officer pursues further testing, like a breath or blood test. If a field test isn’t feasible, officers can simply proceed with other investigations if they believe impairment exists. One element of SFSTs, horizontal gaze nystagmus, assesses eye coordination – it merely requires basic eyesight and absence of certain medical issues. Alcohol affects smaller muscles disproportionately, leading to numbness and loss of coordination as consumption increases. A slight amount of alcohol impacts these delicate eye movements, causing a “jitter” or involuntary movement of the eyes (nystagmus) due to muscle incoordination. While SFSTs are a piece of the puzzle, courts also consider various other forms of evidence, including how the driver was operating the vehicle, any detectable alcohol smell, breathalyzer results, and other observations. These additional factors contribute to determining guilt in a DUI case.

A database management system (DBMS) is a computer software application that interacts with the user, other applications, and the database itself to capture and analyze data. A general-purpose DBMS is designed to allow the definition, creation, querying, update, and administration of databases. Well-known DBMSs include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle, Sybase, SAP HANA, and IBM DB2. A database is not generally portable across different DBMSs, but different DBMS can interoperate by using standards such as SQL and ODBC or JDBC to allow a single application to work with more than one DBMS. Database management systems are often classified according to the database model that they support; the most popular database systems since the 1980s have all supported the relational model as represented by the SQL language.[disputed - discuss] Sometimes a DBMS is loosely referred to as a 'database'.

I had a day off work and saw this, so why not: A watershed moment in the history of the early colonization of Mars, the ' Martian Crisis'resulted in the complete overhaul of the United Nations'drafted approach to Martian exploration and settlement. Established as the first permanent, civilian Martian colony in 2140 (following decades of specialized scientific and survey missions on the part of America and various European and Asian governments), Discovery was intended to serve as the transit hub for all further activities on the Red Planet. These activities were expected to include both further settlement and the return of Martian natural resources to Earth. Centrally located within Argyre Planitia due to the aquifer located beneath the basin in 2101, the settlement was perfectly placed to allow for localized expansion in a geographical feature largely protected from outside phenomena. Initially populated entirely by (largely American) specialists and existing as a small collection of pressurized modules, massive investment on the part of private interests eager to begin extracting and transporting the enormous quantities of rare elements discovered on Mars to Earth resulted in the colony's rapid growth. By 2170, Discovery itself had over 300,000 inhabitants from all ethnicities and supported another 200,000 colonists in dozens of smaller settlements and resource extraction camps spread throughout the basin and elsewhere. Discovery itself had begun establishing a service industry and constructed numerous large pressurized domes to allow for its population to spend the vast majority of their time outside of pressure suits. The construction of the Martian space elevator in the city in 2168 in order to allow for the easier transport of processed ores to Earth cemented the city's position as the centre of all Martian actives of note. As a result of this position, Discovery (and by extension, Mars) was by this time was the most economically valuable city occupied by humanity by far, with a GDP greater than that of any one country on Earth. The value of Earth-based stock markets were heavily dependent on the quantities and prices of Martian resources and the revenues of many national governments were largely comprised of taxes on national entities operating on Mars. Despite this, however, Discovery itself had no representative government. The city was administered by the Martian Extraction Commission (MEC), an entity operating under the aegis of the United Nations and which was established alongside the original colony. A 17-member body made decisions by majority rule, and the 17 seats were divided proportionally, by financial contributions, among the countries that had sponsored the original expedition. As such, an American-European clique held complete control over the decisions of the MEC and the administration of Discovery and thus, over the entirety of Mars. Given Discovery's immense wealth, neither the clique nor the corporate interests it had gradually fallen under the influence of were willing to part with any controlling power, and the early scattered calls for reform and local representation were suppressed and ignored. However, following the ' Voros Szikla Incident ', in which a small mining settlement comprised almost entirely of ethnically Hungarian workers were massacred by Discovery police forces during a strike action, and following which the forced investigation uncovered staggering amounts of corruption and fraud among the MEC, political pressure forced Earth entities to make token measures at reform. One MEC seat was re-allocated to be filled by a Discovery citizen determined by direct ballot, and it was hoped that this would mollify the increasingly vocal democratic movement within the city. This was not the case. Recognizing the empty gesture for what it was, a small group of angry colonists formed the ' Discovery League for Representation ', or DLR. The DLR's platform revolved around obtaining majority control of the MEC in order to establish a local municipal government for the city. Full independence from Earth and the United Nations was not a founding goal of the organization. Although it began with fewer than 300 members, by 2180 it boasted over 100,000 declared members, a sizeable proportion of the city's population, and experts believed it had many thousands more sympathizers throughout Discovery and the Martian settlements, undeclared only as a result of harassment and intimidation on the part of the MEC and corporate concerns. Making the simple argument that they deserved local self-autonomy and comparing their situation to that of the population of the Thirteen Colonies prior to the American Revolution, they began to gain significant support among Earth citizens, particularly those in America and Western Europe - the controlling members of the MEC clique. Although the plight of the Martian colonists was not initially a major domestic concern on Earth and corporate sponsors lobbied heavily for political parties to oppose or at least remain neutral towards the DLR, by 2187, following a second MEC corruption scandal, it was no longer feasible for leading politicians to oppose the DLR. Consequently, in 2188 it was declared that 15 of the 17 MEC seats would be filled by direct ballots collected from the Martian colonists every two years, with the final two being occupied by observers from the United Nations. Though the old controlling interests sponsored their own candidates and placed enormous financial resources behind them, DLR candidates overwhelmingly won every seat. Earth governments hoped that the issues that had so dominated Martian politics would subside, however following the election, a power struggle erupted in the DLR. The party was split between moderates who wanted to continue business as usual with Earth, only with hugely increased oversight of all activities and public accountability, and radicals incensed over what they saw as the extremely poor and exploitative treatment of the colonists over many years. The radical faction emerged victorious in 2190, with their candidates sweeping out the moderates in the MEC elections. Using their authority as controllers of the MEC, the DLR exercised a previously unused clause in the original articles of colonization allowing for the collection of customs duties on Martian resources in order to support the colony (considered potentially vital in the early days should the colony have proved unprofitable), effectively levying enormous taxes on Earth-based commercial interests, and physically confiscating processed resources should they not be immediately paid. This immediately provoked a diplomatic crisis as despite the vast profits realized by Martian mining concerns, the overhead on interplanetary transport left such concerns with very thin profit margins (especially when Mars was not orbitally aligned with Earth). The news of sudden taxes sent Earth's economy into an immediate depression, as stock markets crashed and conglomerates dependant on the Martian trade were made insolvent. Only acts of legislation from hundreds of national governments prevented the collapse of the banking sector as well. In 2191, the former American-European clique demanded that the United Nations revoke the MEC's charter and assume direct control of Discovery and Mars. In a very close session, the original body that assigned the charter, the United Nations Organization for the Settlement of Mars (UNOSM), voted 78-76 to do so. The vote itself was mired in controversy, with allegations of bribery and corruption commonplace. With the charter removed, the various national governments immediately began asserting that colonists originating from their territory (and their descendants) were once again under their jurisdiction, and that since they had no laws enforcing mandatory customs duties on Martian exports, the actions of the colonists were illegal. They further asserted that since Mars was unincorporated territory (under their laws), the DLR itself was an illegal organization and had no authority to enforce anything or to even exist. Though they knew the DLR had popular support, they by and large believed that the colonists would follow their legal directives in such a serious situation. They were immediately proven incorrect. On Mars, the DLR refused to recognize the result of the vote, stating that the United Nations had no right to reassign the statehood of second-generation Martian colonists. Declaring the formation of the ' Free City of Discovery ', they arrested the two observing MEC members and called for the Discovery police force (the only major armed force on Mars) to support them in establishing control over the city, which they did in overwhelming numbers. The DLR quickly seized the primary communication and transportation centers and, most importantly, both the base and orbital stations of the space elevator, effectively declaring Earth under embargo. The hastily convened ' Discovery Legislature'passed acts nationalizing all corporate assets within the city, and establishing an armed militia for defense. They also began sending armed parties to the various settlements, which, being wholly dependent on Discovery for all imports and exports, they believed would immediately agree to join them in defiance of Earth. Instant messaging is one of the major channels of computer mediated communication. However, humans are known to be very limited in understanding others' emotions via text-based communication. Aiming on introducing a software system that helps users understand and evaluate another's emotion based on their words, we developed an automated emotional chatbot named Raffi (Research Focused Intelligent Agent). The robot consists of three main components: 1) A language model for identifying emotion from voice encoding; 2) An algorithm for extracting emotional content from audiovideo data; 3) An emotion classifier for distinguishing between different types of human emotional states using this extracted information as input. These components were trained by means of supervised machine learning followed by unsupervised learning through speech recognition and natural syntax analysis respectively. Finally they were applied to unseen examples sent to them over SMS. The results show good performance relative to manual evaluation methods such as the Blany test with 86 accuracy compared to 62 average accuracy achieved by several previous studies [5].

Richard Dawkins, in *The Greatest Show on Earth*, explores the reason behind the intense experience of pain. He suggests an alternative response—a basic mental warning signal—but argues this wouldn’t suffice due to internal competition between biological drives. He proposes that survival favors creatures experiencing a balanced level of pain; those signals indicating imminent death elicit the strongest sensation. Pain intensity reflects the significance of potential dangers faced by ancestors – severe threats like starvation or injury evoke extreme distress, while lesser wounds cause only mild discomfort. However, this similarity isn't flawless, as evolution isn’t always efficient, leading to anomalies like “supernormal stimuli.” These imperfections offer insight into pains that have lost their adaptive purpose, such as specific types of toothaches or nail injuries.

In the heart of an ancient kingdom, there was a temple that housed the statue of a mighty god. The people of the kingdom believed that the god looked out through the statue and watched over them, keeping them safe from harm. Year after year, the people continued to worship the god, never taking their eyes off the statue. They believed that the god blessed them with good harvests, fruitful hunts, and successful battles. But one day, a young boy was chasing after his friends in the temple and bumped into the statue, knocking it off its pedestal. The statue fell to the ground with a loud crash, shattering into a million pieces. The people of the kingdom were devastated. They believed that the god had abandoned them, leaving them vulnerable to harm. Panic and fear spread among the people, and they began to pray and make sacrifices to the god, pleading with him to return. But as days turned into weeks and weeks turned into months, there was no sign of the god. The people grew desperate and turned to other deities, but their prayers remained unanswered. It wasn't until a wise old sage appeared in the kingdom that the people learned the truth. The sage explained that the gods were around as long as they had statues and images of themselves to look out through. Without a statue, the god had no way of watching over the people. The sage taught the people that it was not the statue that held the power of the god but rather their belief and faith in him. And so, the people came together and built a new statue, but instead of worshiping it, they honored it as a symbol of their faith. With renewed hope, the people resumed their daily lives, knowing that their god would always be with them as long as they believed in him.

Israel’s judicial system consists of three levels. Magistrate courts operate throughout the nation’s major urban areas, forming the base of the system. District courts, found in five out of six regions, handle both initial trials and appeal cases. Finally, the Supreme Court, based in Jerusalem, functions as Israel’s ultimate appeals body and also as the High Court of Justice, permitting citizens – including residents and foreigners – to challenge governmental actions through legal petitions. Despite aligning with the International Criminal Court’s objectives, Israel hasn’t signed the Rome Statute due to reservations regarding potential political bias within the international tribunal.

Although cults are religious groups typically, they have a lot of differences which are quite big. - Leadership: Whereas a religion may have a religious head and a hierarchical structure with priests or bishops representing the hierarchy, cults tend to be more pluralistic in their composition (although making up for this through the role hierarchy). They also don't usually have clear demarcations between "members" and "leaders" as is typical on religions. Instead they often include people who perceive themselves to be leaders of others such as teachers, clergyman; pastors, ministers etc. The contrast between them can be seen from their choice of names. Religious organizations have their own sacred texts, but cults do not. Cult members believe that these books represent a true story about God. On the other hand, cult members might act like believers by adhering to one set of rules, while performing rituals associated with these beliefs. Cult membership is sometimes thought of as a religious institution where adherents pay fees and attend meetings. But this definition does not describe too many cults. Some cults operate entirely underground; there is no state organization overseeing their activities or even any official website. Most cults control only small areas within an area, rather than being geographically focused. However, it is still relevant to recognize what's considered a cult because cult activity involves a number of different issues e.g., secrecy, coven-style worship practices, the absence of legal protections for victims, financial incentives to recruit new members, manipulation techniques, fear tactics, intimidation in order to convince recruits to join.

Traditional deraining techniques primarily target rain streak removal and struggle with severely rainy images where intense streaks, dense rain obscuration, and blurring dominate. This research introduces a new approach designed to overcome these challenges. Our solution employs a dual-stage network: initially, a physics-informed backbone estimates rain streaks, transmission, and ambient lighting based on physical principles. A guided filtering technique, utilizing a rain-free residual image, separates the image’s frequency components, ensuring background information remains distinct from the rain streaks. Subsequently, a depth-guided Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) refines the image, restoring lost background details and mitigating artifacts generated during the first stage.  Evaluations demonstrate superior performance compared to existing methods when applied to real-world rainy imagery, resulting in visually clear images with preserved detail.
