One of the challenges in large-scale information retrieval (IR) is to develop fine-grained and domain-specific methods to answer natural language questions. Despite the availability of numerous sources and datasets for IR, the majority of existing research has focused on traditional approaches such as text matching or dictionary lookup based on general-purpose terminology databases like WordNet [3]. Thus, there remains a great need for more effective ways of dealing with complex queries that are typical of many real-world applications. Recently, there have been attempts at developing better tools, resources, and models to deal with such tasks [4, 5, 6, 7], but they still suffer from several drawbacks when it comes to practicality. Most importantly, these systems tend to be over-engineered, since their underlying theories rely heavily on fixed mathematical structures or parameterized patterns of search [8, 9]. In contrast our system uses only simple heuristics inspired by common sense rules of inference and focuses directly on how humans reason about concepts to arrive at answers to natural-language questions [10]. Given an input question, we compute a set of candidate concepts to retrieve from a given corpus using distributional similarity measures [11] combined with various linguistic features extracted automatically from raw texts [12, 13]. We then evaluate each concept according its co-occurrence with other key terms appearing within the same sentences as well as learn textual representations of all entities mentioned in the query [14, 15, 16]. Finally, we rank the candidates so that those involving less noise will receive higher ranks [17]. Results We evaluated our approach against two baselines: 1) A baseline where relations between different records were learned by means of supervised learning techniques [12]; 2) A baseline which used n-gram frequency statistics [13] instead of the semantic based scoring function proposed here. The experiments show that both of these baselines perform poorly compared to ours. This shows that employing some form of knowledge-based reasoning could result in significant improvements of performance. In particular, the above results indicate that utilizing human-machine interaction can greatly benefit our classification model [18]: classic machine-learning classifiers seem unable to capture this kind of ambiguity inherent to natural languages [19]. The rest of this paper consists of three sections: Section 3 describes related work, section 4 presents details of our method, experimental setups and evaluation metrics; finally, conclusions and future directions are discussed in section 5. Related Work There exist many studies focusing primarily on designing new algorithms to improve document retrieval [20, 21]. On the contrary we focus on exploring mechanisms that allow us to assign appropriate weights to retrieved documents [22]. Retrieval error reduction is an important problem [23] as errors in information seeking may lead not only to undesirable consequences in searching process itself [24], but also affect user satisfaction [25]. Diverse solutions were employed to overcome this issue including ontology [26], clustering [27], ranking [28], summarization [29], etc. Among them, MeSH hierarchy [30] was widely applied due to its ability to describe biomedical concepts [31]. Our system employs word vectors [32] derived from unigrams together with additional syntactic [33] and lexical [34] features obtained through automatic analysis of context surrounding named entity mentions [35]. Compared to most previous approaches [36], to date no similar attempt took into account specific properties of medical data [37], especially considering potential ambiguities stemming from use of acronyms. Our solution leverages experts' insights regarding likely relationships between an ambiguous termconcept and other medical terminologies. These relationships aim at pruning irrelevant items out of potentially large number of possible matches. For instance, consider the following scenario. Suppose one needs to find drug names corresponding to "hypertension" -the patient might ask "What drugs treat hypertension?"; however, if current evidence does not support any relationship between hypertension and any other diseasedisease-related condition this would mean that most possible diseases should appear among first few returned hits. Therefore, it is desirable to filter relevant candidates before returning the top hit (es). As another example, suppose one wants to know what medical conditions correspond to "liver cirrhosis." If symptoms associated with liver cirrhosis include dry mouth, dark urine, diarrhea, while "the name of a certain medication helps prevent heart attacks" happens to mention blood circulation, then "Liver Cirrhotic Candidate Modification Algorithm" [16] finds a single match blood pressure elevation" -since "dry mouth" implies "a serious health problem," whereas "no evidence suggests such relationship exists between "blood circulation" and "heart attacks." However, if the latter phrase actually refers to "high cholesterol levels" through "circulation vasoconstriction" mechanism cells lining arteries become stiffen causing narrowing resulting in increased blood flow resistance, i.e., being sick -then "heart attacks" becomes unlikely too. Their conclusion was supported by empirical observation showing that overall accuracy of recall improved significantly thanks to multi-seed setup. The satellite also features a variety of sensors and cameras for monitoring the captured object. SJ-21 is the first satellite of its kind to be sent into space and has already proven successful in its mission. In addition to being able to de-orbit discarded satellites, it is also capable of stabilizing their orbits, allowing them to remain in a safe area of space. This technology could potentially be used to help prevent further collisions between satellites and other space debris. Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJTs) consist of three terminals – emitter, base, and collector – representing the three semiconductor layers. These devices excel as amplifiers due to their ability to manage currents with a modest base current input. Within an n-p-n transistor operating actively, the emitter-base junction is forward-biased, allowing electron and hole recombination, and injecting electrons into the base. Due to the base’s thinness, most of these electrons diffuse across the reverse-biased base-collector junction and flow towards the collector, with only a tiny fraction recombining within the base itself—this recombination significantly contributes to the base current.  Adjusting the rate at which electrons exit the base directly controls the number entering the collector. The collector current is roughly equivalent to (the common-emitter current gain) multiplied by the base current; it's often above 100 for low-power amplifiers but may be lower in designs intended for higher power levels.

Back in the day, everyone used ASCII. ASCII uses 7 bits per character, so it supported 128 characters. It was design by English-speaking people, so it had the characters needed for English, plus numbers and a bunch of symbols and other assorted things. Then others, like Europeans with their accents and umlauts and sss Zhs wanted to use computers. These weren't letters used in English, but unlike, say, Chinese, there were still a manageable number of different letters. So they invented ISO-8859, which extended ASCII to 8 bits and thus 256 characters, and they used the extra ones to add all the symbols needed for various different languages. Unfortunately they didn't all fit in 256, so they had to specify a different one for each language or group of languages. ISO-8859-1 for example works for most things in Western Europe. ISO-8859-5 works for Russian. Etc. Just to be douchebags, Microsoft also invented a bunch of their own, because they wanted dumb things like being able to specify different shapes of quotation marks. Or something. It kinda sucked because (1) you had to know which character set a particular document used, and (2) you could really only use one at a time. Anyway, people eventually realized this was dumb, and invented Unicode and UTF-8, which is what everything modern on the Internet uses, and supports everything, which is why I could put the sharp-s and cyrillic letter next to each other up there. But still.... even if your software can support it, it can still get confused. In your case, on a modern unix system, if you do: echo Rene xxd: 5265 6ec3 a90a Those are hex. And it's UTF-8. 52 65 6e are just "Ren." Those are "boring" characters, backwards compatible with ASCII and everything else. But the next bytes, C3 A9 0A, those are a UTF-8Unicode "e." But if you interpret them as something else.... you get something else. For example, in ISO-8859-1, C3 is A. And A9 is . Etc. So what happened to you us, your computer got some text in UTF-8Unicode but thought it was in ISO-8859-1. This research introduces MOdular FActorial Design (MOFA), a novel approach to automated hyperparameter optimization (HPO) designed to overcome limitations common in current methods like model selection, parallelism challenges, and poor sample usage. MOFA’s core strategy employs experimental design principles for enhanced sample efficiency. It operates through four interconnected modules during each iteration: an Orthogonal Latin Hypercube (OLH)-based sampler ensuring uniform univariate projections and orthogonality; a massively parallel evaluation component; a transformer that condenses OLH results into a Fractional Factorial Design-Orthogonal Array (OA); and an analysis module utilizing Factorial Performance and Importance analyses to refine the optimization process. Through theoretical analysis and practical experiments, we demonstrate that MOFA outperforms traditional model-based and model-free HPO techniques.

Gene repaired cars as a hobby. His friend had a car that needed repair work. He sold the car to Gene for cheap. Gene made the repairs in his spare time and paid him back at an agreed upon rate of 1 per day, or 18 a month (about 180 today). A year later, Gene decided it was too hard to keep up with all the diagnostic problems so he added a mechanic's license to his business card. This allowed him to bill auto repair shops directly and he started earning some serious money. His service area was always small but steady and before long he could afford to hire another mechanic. Within three years, Gene became successful enough to start franchising his business. The first location opened in New Jersey and within five years he had 19 franchises across nine states. Business grew rapidly until he built up a chain of almost 40 locations. In 1984, when he sold out to AutoNation Inc., one of the largest automotive retail groups in America, he was still running about 30 branches on his own. Today, as I mentioned earlier, there are over 11,000 CarMax franchise stores around the world - including their newest store opening soon near my house! CarMax Started Small So how did Carlos Eugenio Ponce de Leon become a billionaire from a tiny roadside garage in Florida? Let's take a closer look... First of all, let me say that I have no problem calling Eugene CarMax "a bit of a genius." Not only has he created a huge company selling used cars, which is obviously very profitable, but he also lost billions of dollars doing it all by himself. It shows incredible entrepreneurial ability. You don't get rich without taking risks. That said, what makes you really wealthy isn't necessarily your vision for the future but rather something much more basic: intelligence. THAT ability enabled CarMax to steal market share from its competitors because they didn't make big investments into technology like the ones CarMax planned to develop early and frequently. During those formative years, CarMax would send employees to college to study Computer Science and Electrical Engineering specifically to stay ahead of the curve. And they kept investing heavily in new technologies even after launching their first franchise stores. This included everything from using computerized inventory systems to analyze sales data to developing the first-ever ecommerce platform designed exclusively for the auto industry. Nowadays, every new car dealer uses these same tools. Another key advantage that set CarMax apart during the 1990s, especially before interest rates went crazy high in 2000, was its willingness to offer competitive financing deals. For example, CarMax offers 0 APR for 84 months right now if you finance your purchase through them. This means your monthly payments won't go up any higher than usual even though many other dealers charge 20 points extra (or whatever) just to fund your loan. They do this because they know most customers will pay off their loans quickly anyway since buying a car is such an expensive expense. They can afford to lose money here and there. Finally, do not underestimate the importance of having good pricing. If you think about it, people who buy a lot of stuff need lots of things to choose from. If you sell something cheaply and reliably, then plenty of people will come to you in search of exactly what you offer. How Fast Can CarMax Grow?

While these features appear superior at representing perceptual qualities and offering more efficient image representations than traditional metrics like SSIM and PSNR, the reasons behind this effectiveness haven’t been thoroughly investigated. Consequently, assessing specific feature sets or strategically choosing subsets for optimal perceptual improvement remains challenging. Our research demonstrates that the ability of these features to enhance perceptual quality aligns with their capacity to capture core elements of human vision, particularly contrast sensitivity and orientation selectivity. We present novel methods for quantifying the frequency and orientation selectivity of features extracted from convolutional layers across popular CNN architectures like VGG-16.  We find that features scoring highest according to our metrics correlate strongly with human assessments of image quality. Additionally, we illustrate how our approach can be utilized to create a new loss function, ultimately boosting the quality of reconstructed images in single-image super-resolution tasks.

There's not much of a question in your post, so I'll just go ahead and rave for a bit about how god damn awesome the heart is. Your heart beats when it does because of a spot near the top of the muscle called the sinoatrial node. It beats partially because the nervous system tells it to, but mostly because of what's called a prepotential, where the electrical polarity of the cells of the SA node gradually changes as sodium leaks into those cells. When they've leaked a certain amount, an "action potential" is produced that causes the heart beat, which is propagated systematically to the rest of the heart. So even without a direct connection to your brain, your heart would still beat at about 80 beats per minute because of the leaky nature of the cells in the SA node. That's god damn amazing. Next, that action potential is communicated to the Atrioventricular node, which sits between the top chambers (atria) and larger bottom chambers (ventricles) of the heart. If, for some reason, the signal isn't conducted from the SA node to the AV node, that doesn't matter - the cells of the AV node are also leaky, but to a slightly lesser degree. Even if they don't get told to continue the heart beat by the SA node, they'll still generate a beat of their own. With no electrical connection between the top and centre parts of your heart, it'll still beat at around 60 beats per minute. That's also god damn amazing. The AV node also does something even cooler: it holds the signal for about 100 milliseconds. This is, funnily enough, pretty much the ideal period of time for the atria to fill so that they squeeze the maximum amount of blood into the ventricles. The heart's timing is just amazing. After the AV node, the electrical signal is conducted to the muscular walls of the ventricles, which contract as they're told to. But what if they don't get told to contract because there's no connection between them and the AV node? Doesn't matter, they'll still beat at a slightly slower rate, around 40 beats per minute. Even with some truly serious connection failures throughout your heart, it can still beat and keep you alive, albeit in a fairly ill state of being. And let's look at it the other way: if your SA node is seriously screwed up, or if you're taking drugs that profoundly increase your heart rate, your heart has a built-in maximum rate of about 180 beats per minute because of the speed bump provided by the AV node's delay. This is, coincidentally, about the maximum rate at which the ventricles can efficiently pump blood around the body; any higher, and there's no time for blood to enter them before they contract again. The heart is god damn amazing. e: Don't get me started on red blood cells, either. Those are god damn amazing too. Disinflation is a reduction in the rate of inflation. If prices rose 3 last year, but only 2 this year, then disinflation has occurred. We may say that the economy disinflated by 1, but it still grew at 2. This is not the same thing as deflation, which is a fall in prices. If inflation is low to begin with, or disinflation occurs over a long period of time, then that MAY lead to deflation, but not always. Disinflation often occurs during a recession. Disinflation is a problem when it is sustained and the economy suffers deflation. Deflation is a problem because the purchasing power of money actually increases. Therefore people are encouraged to save, and not spend, since 1 tomorrow will buy more than 1 today. But this lack of consumption can make a recession worse. Deflation, and increased unemployment, was what happened to Japan from 1990 until recently.','Deflation (I presume you mean this, rather than disinflation, which is something else and not so bad) is bad because it sees prices drop. The World Health Organization reports that breast cancer represents the most prevalent type of cancer for women globally, ranking as the second leading cause of mortality worldwide and ultimately the deadliest cancer form. While various imaging methods assist in breast cancer detection, x-ray mammography remains the most widely utilized and effective technique. Therefore, segmenting mammographic images—specifically analyzing the shape and boundaries of mammary lesions—is crucial for image analysis and diagnostic support. However, mammogram segmentation presents considerable challenges due to its dependence on diverse tissue types. The GrowCut algorithm offers a recent approach to general image segmentation using only a limited number of interior and exterior points, demonstrating effectiveness in complex cases with appropriate point selection. This research introduces a novel semi-supervised segmentation algorithm derived from GrowCut, automating mammographic image segmentation after an area of interest has been identified by a specialist. Our method employs fuzzy Gaussian membership functions to refine the algorithm’s core logic, quantifying pixel uncertainty between object and background. A key benefit is reducing the reliance on expert input regarding initial seed points, eliminating the need for background seed selection. Moreover, the proposed method exhibits resilience to inaccurate seed placement and adaptability to other seed-based approaches. These attributes positively influence both human experts and intelligent systems by enabling the development of segmentation methodologies requiring less specialized knowledge, enhanced robustness, and comparable efficiency to current advanced techniques. We additionally developed an automated point selection system.

Okay, let’s break this down simply. Because this is an “Explain Like I’m Five” response, I want to explain things clearly rather than just giving a quick answer. I’m not a nurse or doctor, but I understand how medications work. In the U.S., we usually use two main types of over-the-counter painkillers: acetaminophen, often sold as Tylenol, and NSAIDs. Acetaminophen generally has fewer side effects when taken correctly, however, it's easy to accidentally overdose, which can seriously harm your liver. Many combination cold remedies include it, so combining it with another product containing acetaminophen could be dangerous. NSAIDs, short for non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, relieve pain *and* reduce swelling – something acetaminophen doesn't do. While they can cause stomach problems, especially if you get heartburn, they’re often preferred for general aches and pains because they’re better for joint and muscle issues. Additionally, many cold medicines contain acetaminophen, increasing the chance of taking too much. Ibuprofen is a common NSAID after aspirin. For ongoing pain like repetitive strain injuries, naproxen might be better. Keep in mind research continues, so stay updated on medication information. These are typically safe when used as directed—a few days straight for a sore joint is usually fine—but persistent headaches occurring weekly warrant a visit to the doctor, as they could signal a deeper issue.

The combination of conflicts of interest between investment managers and their institutions, alongside a surplus of available investment money worldwide, resulted in poor investment decisions regarding inflated credit assets. Investment managers typically earn fees based on the amount of assets they oversee, creating a motivation to increase those assets for higher pay. With declining returns on credit investments due to this excess capital, managers often opted to keep client funds invested in overpriced, low-returning assets rather than return them – a strategy fueled by a perceived lack of significant risk stemming from past experiences with earlier subprime loans.

A LAN is a Local Area Network. It just refers to how computersdevices connected to the same network routing equipment (e.g. your home Wi-Fi router) can communicate with each-other directly without passing data communications over the internet (i.e. without using the DSLCableFiber connection you have to your ISP [Internet Service Provider. Devices on your local network will be assigned internal IP addresses which can be used to address and send packets between devices without requiring any internet connectivity. To distinguish internal from external (public internet) IP addresses, it has been universally decided that IPv4 addresses starting with '10.', '172.16' and '192.168' should be reserved for internal LAN use while all other addresses should be allocated for public internet use. Most home internet connections will have one public IP address assigned to be shared among all computersdevices on that customer's LAN. The router installed in the customer's home is in charge of routing incoming data packets (to the customer's public IP address) to the correct internal IP address (corresponding to the computerdevice on the LAN which requested that data).

This article discusses WebAssembly and its possible future applications. WebAssembly is an intermediate layer between various programming languages and many different execution environments. It can be used to run code from many different languages in the same environment, as well as compile code more quickly and efficiently than traditional methods. WebAssembly is currently being used in web browsers, video game engines, and other applications, but its potential for use in the future goes far beyond that. Possible uses include enabling high-performance machine learning, creating distributed applications across multiple environments, and even running entire operating systems within a browser. WebAssembly also has the potential to be used to create virtualized hardware, allowing users to run applications or services on machines they do not own. By making it easier to move code between platforms, WebAssembly could revolutionize the way code is shared and developed, potentially opening up new opportunities for developers and users alike.

Two employees of the Council on American Islamic Relations (CAIR) were initially quarantined in the office. A note reading "die a painful death, Muslims," was in the envelope with the powder. "Threats like this have been on the increase since 9-11," said Ibrahim Hooper, communications director of CAIR. "They've increased in both number and in seriousness." "There have been some indications that the reason it was sent to CAIR was because of our efforts to fight discrimination," Hooper said. "Our offices have been bombed, there have been shootings in the past. And that is a concern for any group that is trying to work for justice in our society." The FBI is investigating the incident, which took place on the eighth anniversary of the 9-11 attacks, according to a statement released by the agency. "The FBI takes these types of threats seriously and will investigate the matter to determine whether federal laws have been violated," said Special Agent Andrew Ames, spokesman for the FBI's Washington field office. Ames said that the FBI will analyze the powder to determine what it is. The Washington office of CAIR, a Muslim civil rights and advocacy group, received the envelope containing the white powder. The office is located a few blocks from the White House. In the note accompanying the powder, the author of the letter, who said he was a former U.S. Marine, said he was sending the powder because CAIR was a terrorist organization, according to Hooper. Hooper said the letter was also laced with anti-Muslim and anti-Obama sentiment. "People have strong feelings about President Obama," Hooper said. "But he is the president of the United States." Hooper said he believes the letter was part of an overall increase in anti-Muslim rhetoric and incidents. In 2006, the FBI recorded more than 1,500 incidents of anti-Muslim vandalism, threats and harassment, the highest number since 9-11. "We've seen the recent case in New York, the so-called 'Ground Zero Mosque' debate," Hooper said. "Whether it is what's going on in New York, or what's going on in the rest of the country, this kind of hate rhetoric, people are spouting it all over the country, and that's why it's not surprising to see a ratcheting up of these kinds of incidents." Hooper said he is thankful that the two employees who were quarantined are fine. "I'm relieved that this incident did not end up in a tragedy for them," he said. "I'm hoping that this is just a one-time thing." Hooper also said that he has received calls from other Muslim organizations, including the Islamic Society of North America, offering support. "We are very appreciative of that," he said. He said that his organization will continue its work, despite the threats. "We will continue to speak out against hate," he said. "And we will continue to call for mutual understanding." The Council on American Islamic Relations is a Muslim civil rights and advocacy group. The organization says it "enhances understanding of Islam, encourage dialogue, protect civil liberties, empower American Muslims, and build coalitions that promote justice and mutual understanding." The group has offices in 35 states, including Washington, D.C.

Our body wants to be near its optimal running temperature at all times, about 95-100 degrees Fahrenheit. As it gets further and further away from that temperature the body will try to influence itself to get warmer or colder. Part of that is to make it painful if it's really cold really hot. So you tend to be in MORE pain when cold because your body is already sending "pain signals" when it's too cold. As for the numbness, it's most likely because the body moves blood into the chest to keep the vital organs like the heart and lungs functioning well when it gets too cold. This loss of blood to the hands and feet make it harder for nerve cells to function properly. That being said evolution made it so that our pain neurons can run with less blood flow, so even if you're really cold you can detect whether you're in pain or not.

Recently, intermediate feature maps of pre-trained convolutional neural networks have shown significant perceptual quality improvements, when they are used in the loss function for training new networks. It is believed that these features are better at encoding the perceptual quality and provide more efficient representations of input images compared to other perceptual metrics such as SSIM and PSNR. However, there have been no systematic studies to determine the underlying reason. Due to the lack of such an analysis, it is not possible to evaluate the performance of a particular set of features or to improve the perceptual quality even more by carefully selecting a subset of features from a pre-trained CNN. This work shows that the capabilities of pre-trained deep CNN features in optimizing the perceptual quality are correlated with their success in capturing basic human visual perception characteristics. In particular, we focus our analysis on fundamental aspects of human perception, such as the contrast sensitivity and orientation selectivity. We introduce two new formulations to measure the frequency and orientation selectivity of the features learned by convolutional layers for evaluating deep features learned by widely-used deep CNNs such as VGG-16. We demonstrate that the pre-trained CNN features which receive higher scores are better at predicting human quality judgment. Furthermore, we show the possibility of using our method to select deep features to form a new loss function, which improves the image reconstruction quality for the well-known single-image super-resolution problem.

BBC’s international iPlayer app, which required a subscription fee for viewing programs in Western Europe, Australia, and Canada, was never launched in the United States.  Pay-TV companies in America reportedly threatened to remove the BBC America channel if the app went live domestically, fearing viewer loss.  Both BBC America and the international iPlayer offered popular series such as *Doctor Who*, *Top Gear*, *Sherlock*, and *David Attenborough* documentaries. BBC Worldwide initially framed the app as a “pilot” for gathering consumer data before announcing plans to discontinue it in October 2013, shifting focus to the BBC.com website. This decision was reiterated in their annual report last summer, though a specific closure date wasn’t specified until recently. A machine learning system can score well on a given test set by relying on heuristics that are effective for frequent example types but break down in more challenging cases. We study this issue within natural language inference (NLI), the task of determining whether one sentence entails another. We hypothesize that statistical NLI models may adopt three fallible syntactic heuristics: the lexical overlap heuristic, the subsequence heuristic, and the constituent heuristic. To determine whether models have adopted these heuristics, we introduce a controlled evaluation set called HANS (Heuristic Analysis for NLI Systems), which contains many examples where the heuristics fail. We find that models trained on MNLI, including BERT, a state-of-the-art model, perform very poorly on HANS, suggesting that they have indeed adopted these heuristics. We conclude that there is substantial room for improvement in NLI systems, and that the HANS dataset can motivate and measure progress in this area.

Metric learning is a key problem for many data mining and machine learning applications, and has long been dominated by Mahalanobis methods. Recent advances in nonlinear metric learning have demonstrated the potential power of non-Mahalanobis distance functions, particularly tree-based functions. We propose a novel nonlinear metric learning method that uses an iterative, hierarchical variant of semi-supervised max-margin clustering to construct a forest of cluster hierarchies, where each individual hierarchy can be interpreted as a weak metric over the data. By introducing randomness during hierarchy training and combining the output of many of the resulting semi-random weak hierarchy metrics, we can obtain a powerful and robust nonlinear metric model. This method has two primary contributions: first, it is semi-supervised, incorporating information from both constrained and unconstrained points. Second, we take a relaxed approach to constraint satisfaction, allowing the method to satisfy different subsets of the constraints at different levels of the hierarchy rather than attempting to simultaneously satisfy all of them. This leads to a more robust learning algorithm. We compare our method to a number of state-of-the-art benchmarks on k -nearest neighbor classification, large-scale image retrieval and semi-supervised clustering problems, and find that our algorithm yields results comparable or superior to the state-of-the-art, and is significantly more robust to noise.

Those who advocate for statism—the idea that the government should wield significant control over both society and the economy, contrasting with anarchism—often find it objectionable, particularly on platforms like Reddit where Libertarian and anarcho-capitalist viewpoints are prevalent. The recent controversies surrounding the NSA have fueled calls for reduced governmental power among many Redditors. Personally, I identify as a statist, believing a robust central government and national bank with effective policies represent the best societal structure. This doesn’t preclude socialist leanings, such as supporting fair taxation and social safety nets, or libertarian views regarding criminal justice reform and individual liberties. Nor does it contradict conservative principles concerning fiscal responsibility and business support. “Statist” is frequently applied dismissively by those adhering to anarchist or libertarian philosophies, though it’s a remarkably general label; I've rarely encountered anyone using it to describe themselves.

The Mongols never re-conquered their old African Empire, which had been conquered by Timur in the early 15th century.[4] In 1365, Genghis Khan died at age 59 near Jalalabad. He left a son, Chinggis Khaan - who would later become known as Kublai Khan - to succeed him but was forced by his own brother-in-law Boke Khan to appoint Arslan Ajaa instead due to divisions between the two brothers' wives, Bayazid Khoja and Manguuny Ulduar. This division has led some historians such as John Zada Wolff[56] and Peter Sarris to label it as a divided empire in its infancy that may have already begun disintegration through internal strife during Ghengis Khan's life time; others like Rene Jardine claim this narrative is more romantic than historical and adds little to our understanding of the rise and fall of Mongol empires after the death of Ghengis Khan. Nevertheless, despite being unable to name his successor until he did so shortly before dying, Genghis Khan left behind a major legacy though he could not rule over China long enough to establish an era of peace with Ming China under any circumstances whatsoever. Perhaps the most remarkable part about Genghis Khan's rule is how relatively short lived it really was while still leaving a lasting impression onto many peoples throughout Eurasia. As historian George C. Edwards writes: Genghis Khan ruled for only twenty four years from AD; yet within those few decades he acquired almost total control over virtually one fifth of mankind, whose population today numbers just over six billion people - roughly one quarter of humankind! His military campaigns extended from modern day Afghanistan and Pakistan eastwards into Central Asian steppes, then southward and westwards over India down towards Indonesia, Java, Peninsular Malaysia and Southern Thailand. By the end of his career, he controlled nearly half the world's land surface area.[7]

Josh shrugs, hugs her, kisses her earlobe and whispers, "Scrambled." "Pour me a cup?" she asks. "Right away," Josh says, pulling down two cups from the cabinet. A momentary tingling runs down his neck then disappears. Hope it isn't Alzheimer's, he thinks, then duly forgets about it. The world continues to revolve.

Diversity plays a vital role in many text generating applications. In recent years, Conditional Variational Auto Encoders (CVAE) have shown promising performances for this task. However, they often encounter the so called KL-Vanishing problem. Previous works mitigated such problem by heuristic methods such as strengthening the encoder or weakening the decoder while optimizing the CVAE objective function. Nevertheless, the optimizing direction of these methods are implicit and it is hard to find an appropriate degree to which these methods should be applied. In this paper, we propose an explicit optimizing objective to complement the CVAE to directly pull away from KL-vanishing. In fact, this objective term guides the encoder towards the "best encoder" of the decoder to enhance the expressiveness. A labeling network is introduced to estimate the "best encoder." It provides a continuous label in the latent space of CVAE to help build a close connection between latent variables and targets. The whole proposed method is named Self Labeling CVAE (SLCVAE). To accelerate the research of diverse text generation, we also propose a large native one-to-many dataset. Extensive experiments are conducted on two tasks, which show that our method largely improves the generating diversity while achieving comparable accuracy compared with state-of-art algorithms.

There are several counter-arguments that can be made to refute the claim that the Earth is alive. One major argument is that the Earth lacks the necessary biological structures that are needed to qualify as a living organism. While the Earth supports a diverse range of life, it does not have a singular, unified system that acts as the brain or central nervous system of the planet. Additionally, the Earth is subject to physical and chemical laws that are not applicable to living organisms. These laws dictate the movement of tectonic plates, the circulation of the ocean currents, and the behavior of the Earth's atmosphere, among other things. These physical processes are not indicative of a living being, but rather reflect the natural processes of a dynamic planet. Therefore, while the Earth is certainly a magnificent and fascinating planet, it cannot be said to be alive in the same sense as a living organism.

Beth carried her items to the checkout aisle. The cashier quickly scanned everything. Beth tried to give him several coupons. However, he didn't accept it. They were yelling at each other about who turned in their receipt last and when they have a chance of going to the movies together again. "I'm sorry," said the cashier as he reached for his calculator from behind the counter. "Please take my manager card." He gave Beth's an envelope with 100 inside it after she left. The next day, I went back into that store and asked them both what happened. Their story was quite different than how they remembered it. Beth claimed that the man at the register refused all of her vouchers because she had too many items on her bill. She told me she thought that might be one of those errors (like not reading your receipt). When pressed, she admitted there probably could had been some sort of problem if she had paid by credit card rather than cash. In any case, she still insisted on receiving the change. What made this even more surprising is that she never mentioned anything about being rejected due to coupon use until now! Erin certainly remembers the encounter differently. She recalled the cashier over-filling her cart just like she did... and then making sure no items were missing when Beth got home. Erin also said that she felt horrible about hurting Beth's feelings. Despite apologizing profusely, she explained why she didn't want to give her change: we're saving up for Christmas presents! However, she also seemed surprised that the cashier would reject coupons or discounts. Both women understand how important using coupons can help consumers save money but are confused on what exactly should happen if these savings aren't accepted. Here's what you need to know. What Happens If You Don't Accept a Coupon? There is nothing wrong with refusing a coupon that doesn't apply or wasn't intended for a specific item. This happens more often than people think. There may be times where coupons don't stack properly which means it looks like someone double used them. Other times, companies will send out coupons referencing certain products but they actually don't work anymore. These situations shouldn't come as much surprise since most coupons don't have expiration dates attached to them. For example, some of our favorite grocery stores offer free shipping promotions that are considered "coupons" since they expire within 24 hours of getting the email. If nonworking coupons are an issue, there are two things you can do. First, contact customer service so they can put a stop to it immediately. Second, don't beat yourself up over it. We've all done plenty of weird things while trying to stock up on household supplies during the pandemic. It usually only takes a few minutes anyway. So, don't stress. And remember, it always pays to ask! Categories: Features

The Kingdom of Prussia became the leading state of the German Empire after its creation in 1871. However, the Treaty of Versailles following World War I granted West Prussia to Poland and made East Prussia an exclave of Weimar Germany (the new Polish Corridor separating East Prussia from the rest of Germany), while the Memel Territory was detached and was annexed by Lithuania in 1923. Following Nazi Germany's defeat in World War II in 1945, war-torn East Prussia was divided at Joseph Stalin's insistence between the Soviet Union (the Kaliningrad Oblast in the Russian SFSR and the constituent counties of the Klaipeda Region in the Lithuanian SSR) and the People's Republic of Poland (the Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship). The capital city Konigsberg was renamed Kaliningrad in 1946. The German population of the province was largely evacuated during the war or expelled shortly thereafter in the expulsion of Germans after World War II. An estimated 300,000 (around one fifth of the population) died either in war time bombings raids or in the battles to defend the province.[citation needed]

European Union law is applied by the courts of member states and the Court of Justice of the European Union. Where the laws of member states provide for lesser rights than those in force under national legislation, EU law must be taken into account when deciding on a case brought before an Irish court.[1516] The Constitution provides that "the State acknowledges its obligations to respect, protect and fulfil human rights" (Article 40).[17]:19 The State has also committed itself not only to complying with relevant international treaties[18], but further "to ensure through appropriate legislative or other measures that individuals are protected against any form of discrimination, abuse or violence.19] It can thus afford greater protection if it chooses - as evidenced by Ireland's ratification of many key United Nations instruments including: Convention Against Torture; International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; Convention on Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women; Protocols I and II to the Refugee Convention; Conventions on Child Labour; Indigenous People; Migrant Workers etc., which apply equally at domestic level despite being less well known amongst general public here. In addition, certain provisions within our own constitution guarantee equality between all persons irrespective of age, gender, race, religion, sexual orientation etc. Ireland ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in December 2014,[20]. Implementation across various aspects such as health care provision would necessarily follow from this convention. For example, Article 3 requires that advance notice should always be given prior to withdrawing life-saving treatment. Under current practice there may be no time limit specified so there could still exist situations where advance notification was provided after a person had already suffered brain death resulting in their organs having been harvested without consent.[21]

We consider the problem of solving CSPs with state-dependent payoffs for a class of continuous dynamic games with a continuous set of states and payoffs. To our knowledge, this is the first time that the problem of solving continuous POMDPs with state-dependent payoffs has been considered. We prove existence and uniqueness of a solution algorithm for CSPs with state-dependent payoffs. Numerical experiments show that our proposed algorithm converges to the solution of the problem with a polynomial time complexity.

There are three ways an existing treaty can be amended. First, formal amendment requires State parties to the treaty to go through the ratification process all over again. The re-negotiation of treaty provisions can be long and protracted, and often some parties to the original treaty will not become parties to the amended treaty. When determining the legal obligations of states, one party to the original treaty and one a party to the amended treaty, the states will only be bound by the terms they both agreed upon. Treaties can also be amended informally by the treaty executive council when the changes are only procedural, technical change in customary international law can also amend a treaty, where state behavior evinces a new interpretation of the legal obligations under the treaty. Minor corrections to a treaty may be adopted by a proces-verbal; but a proces-verbal is generally reserved for changes to rectify obvious errors in the text adopted, i.e. where the text adopted does not correctly reflect the intention of the parties adopting it.

Analyzing complex networks relies heavily on understanding their degree distribution, which often requires converting them into fixed-length feature vectors. Consequently, extracting relevant features from this distribution is crucial. Furthermore, comparing networks based on their degree distributions frequently arises in various tasks like classification, clustering, evaluating sampling techniques, detecting anomalies, and modeling epidemics. However, current approaches struggle to accurately represent the similarity of degree distributions, especially across networks of differing sizes. Drawing upon insights into how degree distributions evolve within networks, we introduce a novel feature extraction technique and a corresponding similarity function. This approach utilizes the average and standard deviation of node degrees to mitigate the impact of network size on the resulting features. Extensive testing with both synthetic and real-world network data demonstrates that our method surpasses existing techniques in terms of distance function precision and feature effectiveness.

Between the 6th and 12th centuries, the Chalukya Empire – also known as the Kannada “taukj” – governed significant areas of southern and central India through several interconnected but distinct dynasties. Initially, the “Badami Chalukyas,” centered around Vatapi (present-day Badami), emerged after the weakening of the Kadamba kingdom, gaining power under King Pulakeshin II. Their dominance significantly shaped South India’s history, representing a prosperous era for Karnataka. This early empire transformed the region's landscape, transitioning it from fragmented states into a unified empire spanning the area between the Kaveri and Narmada rivers.  Under Chalukya rule, advancements occurred in governance, international trade, and architectural innovation—specifically, “Chalukyan architecture.” They controlled territory encompassing parts of southern and central India, first from Badami (550-750 CE) and later from Kalyani (970-1190 CE).

The 11 imams, sheiks and religious teachers from nine countries met a Holocaust survivor and Poles whose families risked execution to save Jews from the Nazis, in the Polish capital's Nozyk Synagogue as part of the tour. They have been around museums, including the recently opened Museum of the History of Polish Jews on the site of the former Jewish Ghetto in Warsaw. And they also visited the Auschwitz and Dachau concentration camps. "The main aim is to get Muslims who are leaders all over the world, particularly in the Middle East, to acknowledge the reality of what happened here and to be able to teach it to the people that they lead," said trip organiser Rabbi Jack Bemporad, who is executive director of the US-based Center for Interreligious Understanding. He was standing underneath the red brick watchtower over the main entrance to Birkenau, the largest of more than 40 camps that made up the Auschwitz complex. This was where the Nazis installed four gas chambers and crematoria to speed up the murder and disposal of people, who were mostly Jews, from across Europe. Auschwitz-Birkenau, set up by the Germans in Nazi-occupied Poland, is largely intact and is now a museum. Historians estimate 1.1 million people were killed there - one million of them were Jews but there were also Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners of war and others. "I think that when someone wants to deny the Holocaust or think that it is exaggerated, which many of them do and certainly many of their followers do, when they come here and see it, their experience is such that they can no longer think that," Rabbi Bemporad said. Beside the ruins of one of the gas chambers - the Germans blew them up as they retreated, in an effort to hide their crimes - the Muslim leaders paused for a moment's silence. "You may read every book about the Holocaust but it's nothing like when you see this place where people were burned," said Mohamed Magid, president of the Islamic Society of North America. "This is the building, the bricks. If they were to speak to you and I, they would tell you how many cries and screams they have heard." Mr Magid, who is originally from Sudan, first visited Auschwitz-Birkenau during a trip organised for American imams in 2010. He said the experience had led him to hold an annual Seder, a Jewish ceremonial meal, at his mosque in Virginia where he invites people to listen to the story of a Holocaust survivor who was saved by a Muslim family. "We go back more committed to human rights and more understanding of conflicts and how to resolve them, but also to be careful of a curriculum that teaches racism and hatred," he said. Earlier, the group had taken photos as they walked around an exhibition in the red brick barrack blocks at Auschwitz, about 2 miles (3kms) from Birkenau. They made comments such as "Can you imagine?" and "It's beyond comprehension" as they saw a great pile of hair shorn from women prisoners that was used to make rudimentary textiles. They shook their heads as they saw faded children's shoes and dolls in glass cases. After they had seen just two of the 14 exhibition blocks, some of the group asked for a break and they knelt in prayer beside the camp's execution wall. Barakat Hasan, a Palestinian imam and director of the Center for Studies and Islamic Media in Jerusalem, said he "didn't know many details about the Holocaust" before the trip. "I felt my heart bleeding when I was looking at all this. I was fighting back tears," he said through an interpreter. "As a Palestinian living under occupation, I feel sympathy for the pain and injustice that was inflicted on the Jews," he added. Mr Hasan said he did not believe there were people in the Muslim world who denied the Holocaust happened, but he said there was discussion in his community about whether the commonly quoted figure of six million Jewish victims was correct. "Maybe now after seeing what I've seen, maybe the numbers are correct also," he said, adding that he would write articles and mention his trip on Facebook. As he walked along the railway line and unloading ramp at Birkenau - where the trains hauling cattle cars crammed with Jews arrived - Ahmet Muharrem Atlig, a Turkish imam and secretary general of the Journalists and Writers Foundation in Istanbul, said he wept when he saw a photograph that showed children looking scared as they got off a train. "Unfortunately the Muslim communities and congregation don't know much about the Holocaust," he said. "Yes, we've heard something. But we have to come and see what happened here. It's not just about Jews, or Christians, this is all about human beings because the human race suffered here."

My early life was intensely public – my baby photos appeared on tabloid covers, and neighborhood children threw stones at my family’s windows. They labeled me “The Tattooed Baby,” “The Inkfant,” “Cain,” among other names. Despite receiving countless labels after my initial one, I never truly knew my mother; doctors described my birth as extraordinarily challenging. My father did everything he could, though the burden of my existence proved too much for him. I quickly learned to ignore the whispers and stares, but he bore their weight heavily. He desperately attempted to shield me from a world that couldn’t comprehend me, striving tirelessly. His resolve shattered when I returned home with burned clothing and blood flowing from my ear. He departed that night, and tragedy struck those who tormented me. I haven’t seen him since. From that moment, I adopted the name Cain, and all memory of anything prior faded away. It felt like an insurmountable challenge to be born with unexplained markings covering sixty percent of my body—medical anomalies that demanded even greater hardship. These ‘tattoos,’ as others called them, weren’t ink or imagery; rather, they were indecipherable script across my entire being – symbols stretching from my head to my feet, representing a lost or future language. They narrate my life’s story, which they call "the Book of Cain." I instinctively understand this truth, as naturally as knowing the wind or recognizing a familiar face—a fixed, immutable knowledge passed down without instruction or vision.

The essence of the information processing approach is to try to understand brain function in terms of information flow and implementation of algorithms. One of the most influential early contributions was a 1959 paper titled What the frog's eye tells the frog's brain: the paper examined the visual responses of neurons in the retina and optic tectum of frogs, and came to the conclusion that some neurons in the tectum of the frog are wired to combine elementary responses in a way that makes them function as "bug perceivers." A few years later David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel discovered cells in the primary visual cortex of monkeys that become active when sharp edges move across specific points in the field of view - a discovery for which they won a Nobel Prize. Follow-up studies in higher-order visual areas found cells that detect binocular disparity, color, movement, and aspects of shape, with areas located at increasing distances from the primary visual cortex showing increasingly complex responses. Other investigations of brain areas unrelated to vision have revealed cells with a wide variety of response correlates, some related to memory, some to abstract types of cognition such as space.

I felt a sudden wave of emotion as I realized that this child was the recipient of the letter I held in my hand. I handed the envelope over, explaining that it was from 1885 and I had been sent to deliver it to him. The child's eyes lit up as he eagerly opened the envelope and read the contents. Over time, it became clear she lacked genuine insight into the struggles faced by the poor and working class, despite her background as a successful shopkeeper’s daughter. The concept of “silent genes” – the belief that many genes remain inactive – is largely outdated. While some genes aren’t constantly active and don’t produce proteins, they still get transcribed and contribute to cellular processes (like LncRNAs, miRNAs, and rRNAs). Transposons and viral DNA present an exception, though even these potentially harmful genes can sometimes be activated unexpectedly. There isn’t a single, hidden “5000” gene waiting to be switched on. However, if dormant genes are reactivated in specific cells, consequences could include altering oxygen absorption (as with globin genes), leading to health problems, or triggering cell transformation or death. Because our bodies operate with incredible precision, activating such silenced elements would disrupt vital chemical balances, possibly causing disease or cancer.

Existing methods often fail to adequately handle varying prediction errors due to inconsistent misprediction costs. Although recent evaluations use business-focused metrics like the Utility score (which assesses advertiser profitability), these considerations aren’t applied during model training. This work addresses this discrepancy by examining how optimizing for the Utility metric connects to log loss, a common advanced technique for conversion modeling.  We propose incorporating the business value of predictions into the log loss through a novel weighting strategy, demonstrating substantial improvements in both offline and live performance.

The assertion that God isn’t cruel faces challenges. First, if God possesses the ability to alleviate suffering yet chooses not to, then He is malicious—therefore, cruel. Second, a being acting solely on its own desires lacks justice, yet Scripture states “God works all things according to the counsel of His will” (Ephesians 1:11), implying a lack of divine justice. Third, God granted Adam and Eve immortality with a warning of death, allowing a serpent to deliberately lead to humanity’s fall. This suggests God derives pleasure from human misery, akin to a child tormenting insects. Thus, God is cruel. However, God has the capacity to prevent all hardship because of His perfect knowledge and vision. His actions stem from judgments beyond human comprehension – intervening in one situation might inadvertently cause a far greater harm. Saving lives on Earth may ultimately result in more souls condemned to hell, a consequence deemed preferable by God’s infinite wisdom. Because goodness is defined by the will, God necessarily wills only what His wisdom deems righteous. This constitutes His inherent justice, mirroring our adherence to laws issued by a superior authority. Unlike humans bound by external rules, God *is* the law, embodying pure goodness, and everything originating outside of God is inherently evil. Consequently, God is not cruel; He is fundamentally just. We were created with free will, enabling us to choose between good and evil, demonstrating that God is not a tyrannical force compelling obedience.

The key consideration often hinges on the location where footage is captured. In the U.S., the common guideline is whether individuals have a justifiable expectation of privacy.  For instance, filming an interview in a public area with passersby present doesn’t typically raise concerns because those individuals aren’t expecting privacy. However, capturing identifiable people in a public space and then making statements about them – such as describing them as “drug addicts” – can lead to potential defamation lawsuits. Shows like *COPS* illustrate this by blurring some faces while leaving others visible; these visible faces usually consent to a release form, while those who refuse are obscured. *Cheaters*, conversely, displayed unblurred subjects, suggesting staged productions and signed releases for the actors involved. Due to increased legal scrutiny, it’s advisable for editors to prioritize caution and blur potentially problematic faces whenever possible. Ultimately, decisions regarding facial blurring depend largely on editorial judgment, rooted in protecting individual personality rights and preventing unfair exploitation of personal identities.

Nonprofit organizations exhibit considerable diversity, though they’re frequently linked to charity. While charitable groups often receive significant attention, numerous other types exist. Generally, these organizations fall into two categories: those that primarily serve their members and those that focus on benefiting the wider community. Member-serving nonprofits encompass groups like mutual societies, cooperatives, trade unions, credit unions, professional associations, recreational clubs, and veterans’ organizations – entities designed to assist specific individuals within the group. Conversely, community-serving nonprofits concentrate on offering services to the public, whether locally or internationally, including initiatives such as social welfare programs, humanitarian aid, scientific research, educational resources, and healthcare. Many nonprofits actually operate in both areas, depending on the extent of their influence. For instance, a local support network assisting individuals with a specific illness can simultaneously help its members and contribute to the well-being of the larger population.

When you make a credit card transaction you tell the merchant "Here's all of the information you need to take money from my account. Please help yourself to only as much as you're entitled for this transaction, then securely delete my information." This involves various forms of giving this information, but for the most part you're either punching in numbers online or you're swiping your card on a card reader. Debit cards often use a keyed in PIN, while credit cards sometimes ask for a zip code. So on a gas pump you're inputting credit card details when you insert the card and when you key in whatever data it asks you for. All it takes is a criminal putting a device next to the legitimate card reader such that it reads your card, too. These can be nearly undetectable, too. Consider [this] (URL0) side-by-side comparison of an ATM with and without a second device to read the card as it's inserted. Then they either install a device to read the number pad or they just put a camera somewhere to watch you key in your information. From there they just have to use the information to make a new card (this is disgustingly cheap) and they can go and use your card anywhere that they accept that same amount of information. I've even seen one scam where a person will stand at a gas pump and explain to you that they need cash but the ATM is broken, then ask to pump your gas in exchange for cash. They use a stolen card and you give them cash (aside: you're not the one getting ripped off here; the gas station will lose the money when the card is reported stolen). Some credit cards, especially in Europe, work differently and are much more secure. They use a "Chip and pin" system where there is a tiny computer chip embedded on the card. Placing a charge with that kind of card requires the card reader to upload the transaction details to the card as well as the PIN you've just input, at which point the chip will provide a unique number that specifically authorizes that one transaction. Stealing card details and your PIN is not sufficient to defraud this kind of card in the same manner that I described above, since you'd need a full copy of the chip (and you don't get enough information to make one when you run a transaction).', "My debit card was skimmed last week, and fraudulent charges started popping up the day after I used a pay at the pump gas station. What through a red flag to my bank was that it was a debit card that was being used at Walmart and whomever was using it was declining to enter a pin and running it as credit instead. Apparently after that continued several times at a string of Walmarts several states away, they automatically canceled my card. It would've been nice for them to have sent me an email or a text informing me of this, instead of trying to call from a blocked number at 8:30 on a Saturday night which, of course I didn't answer. They didn't have my pin so the fraud was easy to detect, and the manner it was being used, combined with the location allowed fraud prevention to do their job. If whomever made the fraudulent card had been smarter and only used it for a medium size transaction at one store, it probably would not have been caught until I reviewed my ledger. Running it as credit instead of debit raises a flag in the system, do it several times and you're going to get the card shut down.

A rotating armature comprises one or more coils wrapped around a non-magnetic, soft ferromagnetic core. Electricity supplied via brushes passes through the commutator and a single armature coil, creating a pulsating electromagnetic field. This armature’s magnetic field opposes and interacts with a fixed magnetic field generated by permanent magnets or a field coil within the motor housing. This opposing force drives rotation of the motor shaft. A commutator continuously changes the current flow to different armature coils during rotation, preventing the rotor's magnetic poles from locking into alignment with the stator field – thus ensuring continuous movement as long as electricity is provided.

Nonlinear metric learning is crucial across various data analysis and machine learning tasks, traditionally relying heavily on Mahalanobis approaches. Recent progress in this area highlights the effectiveness of non-Mahalanobis distances, especially those based on trees.  Our research introduces a new technique utilizing an iterative, layered version of semi-supervised max-margin clustering to build a collection of nested cluster hierarchies—each hierarchy functioning as a localized metric within the dataset.  We incorporate randomness into the hierarchy construction process and aggregate the outputs of these numerous, partially random weak hierarchies to create a strong and reliable nonlinear metric model.  This work’s main benefits include its semi-supervised nature, leveraging both labeled and unlabeled data, and a flexible constraint handling strategy that allows partial constraint fulfillment across hierarchy levels, enhancing robustness. Experimental evaluations against established methods in k-nearest neighbor classification, image retrieval, and semi-supervised clustering show our algorithm achieving competitive or better performance with improved resilience to noisy data.

Orientalist scholars of the 18th century like Sir William Jones marked a wave of enthusiasm for Indian culture and for Sanskrit. According to Thomas Trautmann, after this period of "Indomania," a certain hostility to Sanskrit and to Indian culture in general began to assert itself in early 19th century Britain, manifested by a neglect of Sanskrit in British academia. This was the beginning of a general push in favor of the idea that India should be culturally, religiously and linguistically assimilated to Britain as far as possible. Trautmann considers two separate and logically opposite sources for the growing hostility: one was "British Indophobia," which he calls essentially a developmentalist, progressivist, liberal, and non-racial-essentialist critique of Hindu civilisation as an aid for the improvement of India along European lines; the other was scientific racism, a theory of the English "common-sense view" that Indians constituted a "separate, inferior and unimprovable race."

A reduction in CAR (competition with radioligand) was observed at approximately 70-75% D2 occupancy, accompanied by catalepsy at 80% occupancy. These findings mirrored human research, showing that 65-70% D2 occupancy correlated with an antipsychotic effect, whereas 80% occupancy produced extrapyramidal symptoms. Moisture absorption occurs when the material is exposed to high humidity or water. Both the resin and the reinforcement may absorb water; water may be also soaked by capillary forces through voids in the materials and along the reinforcement. Epoxies of the FR-4 materials aren't too susceptible, with absorption of only 0.15. Teflon has very low absorption of 0.01. Polyimides and cyanate esters, on the other side, suffer from high water absorption. Absorbed water can lead to significant degradation of key parameters; it impairs tracking resistance, breakdown voltage, and dielectric parameters. Relative dielectric constant of water is about 73, compared to about 4 for common circuitboard materials. Absorbed moisture can also vaporize on heating and cause cracking and delamination, the same effect responsible for "popcorning" damage on wet packaging of electronic parts. Careful baking of the substrates may be required.

Trials frequently drag on for extended periods due to court system congestion and significant logistical challenges. Events like the Boston and Oklahoma City bombings stood out as relatively quick compared to typical cases; securing courtroom time is costly and limited, and selecting juries is a demanding and expensive process. Lawyers face heavy workloads with inflexible schedules, and defendants requesting speedy trials often sacrifice crucial investigative opportunities.  The legal system requires absolute certainty – preventing double jeopardy by ensuring all evidence is complete and rigorously vetted through numerous procedural steps.  Defense attorneys can challenge admissibility of evidence or highlight deficiencies at any stage, placing a high burden of proof on the prosecution.  For a defendant, particularly in a case like the Boston Bomber’s, delaying the trial offers substantial advantages. Witnesses become unavailable, memories fade, evidence deteriorates, and the defense gains leverage through strategic postponements aimed at minimizing potential penalties.

Treaty amendments have three primary methods. Formal amendment necessitates renewed ratification by all original signatory states, a potentially lengthy and complex process that might exclude some from the revised agreement. Obligations between states – one originally party and one subsequently amending the treaty – are governed solely by what both groups consented to. Informal amendments can occur via the treaty’s executive council for minor, procedural adjustments, or through evolving customary international law reflecting a shift in how states understand their commitments. Small textual corrections are typically documented in a procès-verbal, usually used to fix clear factual inaccuracies within the original text rather than substantive alterations.

I asked this question to a CS major friend of mine a while back. I hope I remember this correctly: Usually, when a program is unresponsive, it's stuck in some loop. But being stuck in that loop doesn't prevent all the OTHER operations from all the other programs from continuing. Your operating system (Windows, OSX, Linux, whatever) will keep track of what programs are actually updating and continuing to do stuff and all that good stuff, and if it notices that Spotify has just been looping through the same batch of code too long, it'll give you the "This program is unresponsive" error. On top of that, the reason you'll get the "Hey, this program is unresponsive" error when trying to shut it down, is because the program can't go through its normal shutdown procedures, since it's still stuck in that loop. Then you have to authorize your computer to just kill the program.','Well. Unresponsive programs can not be quickly closed because of how computers work. The thing is, a computer can't do many things at once, which is of course not entirely correct nowadays, but close enough. Early computers actually could only do one thing at a time; the operator would start a program and that would run until it finished, and then the operator would put another program (in the form of a deck of cards or a paper strip with holes in them) into the computer. That was kinda tedious, and so after a while clever people thought that it would be much more productiv to have another program that would take one program after the other and feed it to the computer. The computer was relatively unaware of this, the only difference was that every program had, after it ended, a bit of code attached to load the next program. And in many ways your computer is similar. The operating system basically chops all tasks into slices, and then it puts itself between those slices, and the computer switches between running user programs and os code. So in any given second your computer will run a bit of word, then a bit of the operating system, then a bit of Firefox, then a bit of the OS, and so on. So how can a program end? Basically there are two ways, it might just finish whatever it was doing and in its last time running it will tell the operating system that it is finished; this means signalling being finished in a way that the next time the OS gets executed, it will clean up after the program. The other was is that the operating system might end a program prematurely. To do this, the operating system uses a similar process a program uses, it says "you, program 234543, stop and exit," and the next time the program is run it should check for this and react to it. Again, this is only roughly correct, in truth there are interrupts and such, but anyway. But what if the program just ignores the operating system? Maybe it is stuck in a loop? Maybe it's very busy waiting for something to happen and can't be bothered to check for nice requests to close? So after a while the operating system will be fed up with waiting and issue a more drastic command, perhaps "you, exit now"! And if the program is still stuck, the operating system will finally just forcefully clean up: It will take away the programs execution time and empty the memory where the program resides. So that's why closing unresponsive programs takes some time, because either the operating system notices something is wrong, or you as the user notice this and try to close the program, and at first the OS will very politely ask, then demand, then threaten the program to close (or at least do something productive), and only then will the OS just kill the program. Additionally, unresponsive programs can clog up the computer a bit.','In code, you have loops. A loop would look something like this: while (whatever condition is true) { Do this } A program stops responding when the OS can't set aside enough memory for the program, or it sees that is won't be able to and it stops it before it does. A bad loop would look like this: x 1; while (x 1) { x; } What is happening is simple, while the variable "x" is equal to or greater than 1, it will continue adding 1 to "x," creating an infinite loop. Obviously with more complex programs a lot more can go wrong, but this is a simple example of why that may happen. If the program in stuck in a loop, it has to take care of closing the loop before it can end the program. I could go on a long digression about the assembly behind that, but I won't because that is a 500 word CS paper in itself (okay, maybe not, but still). If I am mistaken about any of this, proceed to downvote and correct me.','Also note: the computer usually gives a program some time to become responsive and close "gracefully" - that is, save files, clean up things, release resources, etc. Eventually, the computer offers you the option to just kill the process.

He's written nine books of nonfiction and two novels, most recently, The Radicals: The Creation of a Counter Culture in the 1960s. Six months a year, Raskin says, he lives in a trailer on the Sonoma coast and the rest of the year he lives in Fairfax. When he's in Fairfax, he likes to buy his food at the Fairfax market. But when he's in his coastal home, he often goes to the seashore to gather wild celery. He likes to go to Salt Point State Park and walk along the rocky shore looking for the stalks that grow just below the surface of the water. He picks the plant and brings it home and boils it in a pot. "It's good in salads," he says. "It's a nice springtime green. It has a very mild taste." He says he also likes to take the seeds that the wild celery produces and soak them in water, and then boil them. He adds some lemon juice to the soup, too. "It tastes good," he says. The dish, he says, is "a little bit like a pea soup." But it's very different, too, he says, because the peas are replaced by the wild celery. "It's a very nice thing to do," he says. Although high-throughput computational materials design using first-principles has shown promise, several challenges hinder its widespread use. Key limitations include inconsistent accuracy and difficulty for those without specialized expertise. Here, we demonstrate a new method that standardizes high-fidelity simulations like Density Functional Theory with Hybrid Screened Exchange (HSE) and GW approximation, making them readily available and reproducible online. We applied this method to analyze 71 different materials—including elements, semiconductors, oxides, and alloys—obtaining accurate electronic band gaps and structures. Our results show that HSE and GW have an average relative error of approximately 20%, compared to 55% for traditional Generalized Gradient Approximation. Furthermore, HSE calculations on a publicly accessible cloud server take an average of 48 hours. This offers a practical, affordable, and easily replicable workflow for conducting high-fidelity first-principles electronic material calculations at scale.

When the scientists added B3 to human blood, it boosted the number of neutrophils, and increased their killing activity against Staphylococcus bacteria. The study was published in the journal Science Translational Medicine. The team also found B3 boosts the survival of white blood cells, known as T-cells, against Staphylococcus bacteria. B3 was first discovered in the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, and later found in humans. The scientists are now looking for a pharmaceutical company to help develop B3 as a potential antibiotic.
