The Museum's collections of South and South-East Asian art are the most comprehensive and important in the West comprising nearly 60,000 objects, including about 10,000 textiles and 6000 paintings, the majority of which are from India, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Nepal, Tibet, Cambodia and Indonesia. The collections date from the third century BC to the present, with the majority of objects dating from the 16th to 19th centuries. The collections of Indian art are the largest and most comprehensive outside India. The holdings include more than 2,000 paintings, a significant number of sculptures, and a large collection of objects in stone, metal, ivory, wood, textiles and clay. The collection of Indian paintings includes works from the 16th to the 19th century. The sculpture collection includes works from the 10th century to the present, and is particularly strong in objects made in the Deccan, South India and the Western Ghats. Indian Archaeology The South Asian archaeological collections are the largest outside India and include approximately 12,000 objects. The strength of the collections lies in sculpture, stone and metalwork, and ceramics. The collection of Indian textiles includes approximately 5,000 objects and is one of the most important outside India. The Museum's textiles collection is especially strong in early Mughal weaving, 16th-18th century European-influenced cotton weaving, and 19th-20th century weaving from Kashmir. The South-East Asian collection comprises more than 10,000 objects, many of which are the most important of their type outside South-East Asia. The strength of the collection lies in sculpture, painting, textiles and ceramics. Nepalese and Himalayan Art The collection of Nepalese and Himalayan art includes approximately 1,000 objects. The strength of the collection lies in sculpture and painting. Indonesian and Southeast Asian Art The collection of Indonesian and Southeast Asian art includes approximately 600 objects, many of which are the most important of their type outside Indonesia. The strength of the collection lies in sculpture, metalwork, textiles, ceramics and paintings. The museum has a small but important collection of Tibetan art and has sponsored research on the history and archaeology of Tibet. The collection includes paintings, sculpture, textiles and manuscripts, as well as objects from the palace of the Dalai Lama, including a throne, many items of jewellery and a number of ceremonial objects. Tibetan Manuscripts The British Library has one of the largest collections of Tibetan manuscripts outside Tibet. The collection contains a wide range of texts, including the major scriptural, philosophical and historical texts of the three main schools of Tibetan Buddhism, as well as important literature from all the other major traditions in Tibet. There are more than 40,000 Tibetan manuscripts in the British Library collection. They are written in a number of different scripts, the most common of which is the Tibetan script, although there are a number of variants of this script, including those used for writing Sanskrit and a number of languages from the Himalayas. There are also some manuscripts written in Mongolian, Chinese, Newari, Chinese and Ladakhi script. The majority of manuscripts are on paper, although there are also several scrolls, and some on palm leaf and bark. Some of the manuscripts are in manuscript books, while others are loose. Peer review is an important part of the scientific process. It helps ensure that papers are of high quality and that they adhere to the standards of the field. The peer review process involves several stages. First, a paper is submitted to a journal or conference for publication. The paper is then sent out to experts in the field who assess it for accuracy and relevance. These experts provide written critiques and suggestions for improvement. Based on these critiques, the editor either rejects the paper, requests revisions, or accepts it for publication. The peer reviewers are typically not compensated for their work, though some journals may offer small honorariums. However, there are other benefits to participating in the peer review process. Peer reviewers can stay up-to-date on the latest research in their field, they can gain name recognition within their field, and they can contribute to the advancement of science. In addition, reviewing someone else's work can help researchers hone their own skills and better understand the reviewing process when their own work is being reviewed.

This causes an increase in power and torque, making your car accelerate rapidly, which can result in you losing control or being caught by a tractor trailer. It seems like an obvious reason why a driver would want to maintain their speed limit until they reach it! But no one does! Now, let me ask this question... Why don't people who go too fast to travel at 70mph use cruise control instead of speeding up? Here comes my point! I believe that many drivers think they have better control with cruise control and do not realize how much damage it could cause them if they were to lose control suddenly. Cruise control uses a computer to constantly monitor what speed you're traveling at and adjusts it to keep it within specified limits. If you allow the computer to adjust itself rather than using the hand controls on the steering wheel, then you risk compromising your own reaction time and possibly losing control of the vehicle altogether! (Although, accidents due to this type of condition are rare, nonetheless). So now back to my original question about why we don't speed on highways above the speed limit. A database management system (DBMS) is software used to handle interactions between users, programs, and databases for data storage and processing. These versatile systems enable defining, building, searching, modifying, and managing databases. Common examples include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle, Sybase, SAP HANA, and IBM DB2. While databases aren’t typically easily moved between different DBMS platforms, compatibility can be achieved through standard protocols like SQL and ODBC/JDBC, permitting a single application to connect to multiple systems. DBMSs are frequently categorized based on the database model they employ; since the 1980s, the relational model—and its associated SQL language—has been the dominant approach in widely used systems, though this has occasionally been questioned.

My phone buzzed for the fourth time that day, and I scrambled to check it, desperately hoping it was a call back from that job I'd applied for. My current job wasn't cutting it, and money was running thin. This editing job wasn't the dream, but if I got the position I'd be able to at least live comfortably. No, it wasn't. It was just an e-mail notification, another of those damned spams asking me to "JOIN THE ILLUMANITI TODAY! WE NEED YOU." Jesus fuck, that had to be the thousandth I'd received in the past month alone, and it had been going on for a long time. No matter what I did to block them, the e-mails returned. Add them to the spam filter? They started coming from other e-mail addresses for the next day, and then the day after that they were back from the first. Block them with another app or adblock? They still showed up. I'd even deleted my e-mail app, but lo and behold, e-mail notifications started coming through other places. Facebook, YouTube, and I even started getting inbox messages on Reddit. I didn't think much of it beyond some asshole pulling an over-the-top prank. There was a fiction writing website that I liked to participate on regularly, and I spent most of my time in the science-fiction section, writing collaborative dystopia stories with a friend. I was always the one to structure those dystopian societies and everything they did. We had a lot of fun, and readers gave us some pretty good reviews. I didn't foresee any negative consequences. The e-mails started when we wrote about a world in which the Illuminati ruled everything. So obviously, I ignored them, figuring that it was my friend pranking me. But as the e-mails kept coming, I asked him, and it was clear he had no idea what I was talking about. So it wasn't him, but it could have easily been someone else from that site. This notification had come through Facebook, so I decided to go ahead and delete that from my phone. It was getting annoying as hell. I'd scarcely finished dragging the app over to the little trash can when the phone began vibrating and buzzing excitedly while the phone call notification bar appeared at the top. Finally, what I'd been waiting for all along! My struggles could be forgotten at last with this job. Forgetting my annoyance, I rushed to press the answer button and held it up to my face, eagerly saying, " Hello? " " Hello, Tom. " A gravelly voice responded from the other end, causing me to frown. This wasn't the voice of the woman who had interviewed me. " Uh, hi? May I ask who I'm speaking with? " I asked my question quickly, desperate to get the call over with as soon as possible. I didn't want to miss that call. It wouldn't look good on me. " Tom, you've been ignoring us for quite a long time. I don't think you understand how serious our offer is. We have waited for long enough. The Illumaniti is your future. We are your only path forward in life. " I sighed in annoyance. " Jesus Christ, dude, knock it the fuck off! I am sick of this stupid joke of yours. Don't you know when something's gone on long enough? Now if you'll excuse me, I'm going to hang up. I'm waiting for a call back. " I was taking the phone away to end the call, but the sound of his laughter stopped me. It was slow and halting, and I honestly could not tell if it was fake or sincere. " Tom, you won't be getting a call from Melissa. Not anytime soon, and not ever. We have told her not to give you the job. And, don't worry about hanging up. I will do it for you. We are waiting outside your apartment. " The call ended abruptly, and there was a harsh rapping at the door. A knot twisted and tied itself in my stomach, and I felt sweat trickling down my face. The last thing I wanted to do was answer it, but what could I do but open that door? Slowly, I crossed my apartment. The knocking did not stop. It was slow and persistent. Knock..... 1..... 2..... Knock..... 1..... 2..... Knock. Finally, I reached the door. I placed my hand on the knob, and hesitated. The knocking continued, and I suddenly panicked and swung it open, certain that the longer I waited, the greater the horror beyond would become. I was greeted with the sight of a slim, balding man, hardly over five and a half feet tall. He wore a suit, far fancier than anything I'd ever even seen in my lifetime, with a neat black tie that pointed to his shining black shoes. In his hands, he carried a briefcase. A bright and cheery smile spread across his face. " Hello, Tom. " It was that same voice I'd heard on the phone. He extended his hand. In the presence of this man who simply oozed luxury and confidence, I felt very awkward standing there in a stained white t-shirt and jeans with holes that weren't meant for fashion. But it would be rude to not shake his hand, so I shrugged my shoulders and accepted. Without waiting for me to invite him, he walked into my apartment, brushing me aside without even having to touch me. He sat at my tiny, pathetic excuse for a dining room table and I dumbly followed him, giving up on making sense of the situation. I sat across from him and then stared at him, trying to discern what his intentions might be. He met my gaze steadily, his cold gray eyes meeting mine without flinching. " So, uh, are you really with the Illuminati? If, uh, it actually exists and all that? " I asked. " You know the answer to that, Tom. That is not why I am here. I am here for you. It is time for you to join us. Your vision is far grander than even you know, Tom. We want you, and you need us. " His eyes did not move, and his happy smile never left his face, but his voice remained slow and deep. It was a voice that was immediately accepted as telling the truth. " Wait, my vision? Is this, uh, about my writing? Cuz that's all fiction, you know. I'm just a writer, just a nobody. I just wan na live a normal life, writing, editing, whatever. Literature is my passion, dude. None of this secret-society or whatever you guys are. " I shook my head, confused, not able to believe what I was hearing. " There is no future for you outside of us. We have made sure of it. Do not worry, Tom. You won't have to stop writing. You will be able to write as much as you want. Is there nothing grander for a writer than to see his vision come to life? Not in a cheap movie that misses the point, but in the whole of society? You will live well, Tom. Above the rich, above the politicians. Above even me. " His smile broadened at that, and he flashed his pure white teeth at me. Then, he opened the briefcase. I looked inside and saw the money. My breath left me all at once. " You know what? You've got yourself a deal. "

The government intends to boost the maximum “right to buy” discount – presently £16,000 to £38,000 – potentially exceeding the proposed £50,000. This aims to encourage greater participation from both renters and mortgage providers, reviving a scheme initiated in the 1980s. However, housing charity Shelter warns that this expansion risks reducing the availability of truly affordable social housing and could burden low-income families with unaffordable mortgages. Launched by Margaret Thatcher’s administration, the “right to buy” initiative has declined in recent years, prompting a recent government consultation suggesting a possible increase to £50,000. Current discount variations range significantly, now reportedly targeting up to £75,000. Despite assurances that existing social homes will be replaced with equivalent affordable properties, Shelter contends that the program will negatively impact social housing. According to Roger Harding, Shelter’s head of policy, the “affordable rent” system allows landlords to set rents up to 80% of market rates, often surpassing standard council rents, ultimately decreasing genuinely affordable options. He further expressed concern about potential increases in the housing benefits bill due to fewer council houses and higher rental costs, highlighting the possibility of tenants struggling with mortgage repayments.

The British failures in North America, combined with other failures in the European theater, led to the fall from power of Newcastle and his principal military advisor, the Duke of Marlborough. Although he continued to lead the British army in France, Marlborough's personal popularity plummeted and he was replaced as Prime Minister by Lord Shelburne. The naval failure in the West Indies in the war's opening months was the last straw. Newcastle was recalled to England and the government, which had been a minority Whig administration, became a Whig-dominated coalition under Shelburne. Shelburne's coalition proved unable to address the many problems facing Britain in the American War of Independence. Despite British success in the early stages of the war, the coalition government began to back away from fighting a long war. It sought to make peace with the colonists in 1775, but the American war continued for several years longer. The American war was not just about military victory, but also about the nation's future. The American War of Independence was the first time that the vast majority of British subjects who lived outside the British Empire engaged in a national struggle against the mother country. The American colonists saw the war as a rebellion against the British Empire. The colonies sought to make their own decisions about their future and to be free of British control. Although many colonists felt that the colonies had been abused by the British government, the war was not fought to punish the colonists. The war was fought to defend British values and to restore the authority of the monarchy. After Britain's defeat in the American War of Independence, it began to reorganize itself. In 1783, it created the British North America Act, which separated the British colonies from the British mainland and established the province of Quebec. Although it lost the colonies in North America, Britain maintained its dominance in the British Isles. The British Navy dominated the seas, while the British Army was the largest in Europe. However, the British Empire, although the most powerful empire in the world, was not an empire of one nation. It was a multinational empire, which included millions of subjects who spoke many different languages. It was also an empire that was divided by religious and cultural differences. The Empire was a patchwork of different groups and peoples. Many of the empire's subjects lived in the colonies, while others lived in the British Isles. It was an empire of aristocrats, clergy, commoners, and immigrants. Many of the empire's subjects were illiterate and the empire was governed by a hierarchical, authoritarian system. The empire's population included millions of Catholics, Protestants, and Jews. The empire's subjects also included thousands of people of African descent, who were the descendants of slaves. Although the British Empire was an empire of many peoples, the British government sought to create a new type of empire. It attempted to transform the empire into a "Commonwealth of Nations," which would be a new type of government, which would be open to all of the empire's subjects. It would be an empire that was free from any racial or religious restrictions. It would be an empire in which all of the empire's subjects could have a voice in government. Although it did not succeed in its aim of creating a new type of empire, the British government did seek to reduce the empire's religious and racial divisions. It abolished the slave trade and outlawed the practice of slavery. The British government also began to allow immigrants to immigrate to the empire and to participate in the British government. The British government also sought to modernize the empire and to improve its institutions. It built new roads, railways, and bridges. It also began to build new schools, hospitals, and orphanages. However, despite these efforts, the empire remained divided by religion, race, and language. The empire was also plagued by rebellions, uprisings, and revolts. The revolt of the American colonies against the British Empire was the first major rebellion in the British Empire. The revolt of the Sepoys against the British in India in 1857 was the first major uprising in the British Empire. It was followed by the Indian Rebellion of 1858 and the Gordon Riots in England in 1801. The 1857 revolt in India led to the partition of Bengal and the creation of two new provinces in India, Bengal and Bombay. The British government also established a new administrative system for the empire, which it called the Imperial Legislative Council.

Machine learning systems often achieve good performance on benchmark datasets through reliance on simple rules—heuristics—that work well with common instances but falter when confronted with difficult ones. This phenomenon is investigated in the context of Natural Language Inference (NLI), specifically, assessing whether one sentence logically implies another. Our research suggests that statistical NLI models might be using flawed syntactic heuristics: looking for word overlap, identifying sequential phrases, and analyzing sentence structure. To investigate this, we created a specialized evaluation set named HANS (Heuristic Analysis for NLI Systems) designed to expose weaknesses in these heuristics. Results show that models like BERT, currently considered leading performers on MNLI, struggle significantly on HANS, indicating their dependence on these unreliable strategies.  Therefore, there’s significant potential for enhancing NLI systems, and the HANS dataset offers a valuable tool for driving future advancements in the field.

This work focuses on finding tightly linked clusters of variables in models incorporating multiple Gaussian distributions, using a graphical model approach. We introduce two new estimation techniques utilizing the Ordered Weighted 1 (OWL) norm: first, Graphical OWL (GOWL), which employs a penalized likelihood with the OWL norm applied to the lower triangular part of the precision matrix; and second, column-by-column Graphical OWL (ccGOWL), which estimates the precision matrix through OWL-regularized linear regression. These approaches simultaneously detect strongly related variable sets and maintain sparsity within the precision matrix.  We frame GOWL as a combined optimization problem and demonstrate its unique global solution. Furthermore, we provide guarantees about the grouping reliability of each column’s estimate in ccGOWL. Proximal descent algorithms are used to solve these estimators. On synthetic datasets exhibiting group structures, ccGOWL performs substantially faster and yields comparable or better results than existing methods. Computational speedup analyses confirm ccGOWL's efficiency, and we show its effectiveness on cancer gene expression and stock market data examples.

Automated hyperparameter optimization (HPO) has shown great power in many machine learning applications. While existing methods suffer from model selection, parallelism, or sample efficiency, this paper presents a new HPO method, MOdular FActorial Design (MOFA), to address these issues simultaneously. The major idea is to use techniques from Experimental Designs to improve sample efficiency of model-free methods. Particularly, MOFA runs with four modules in each iteration: (1) an Orthogonal Latin Hypercube (OLH) -based sampler preserving both univariate projection uniformity and orthogonality; (2) a highly parallelized evaluator; (3) a transformer to collapse the OLH performance table into a specified Fractional Factorial Design-Orthogonal Array (OA); (4) an analyzer including Factorial Performance Analysis and Factorial Importance Analysis to narrow down the search space. We theoretically and empirically show that MOFA has great advantages over existing model-based and model-free methods.

Maximilien de Robespierre was a man of great convictions and great intentions. I still remember the whispered praises of French men and women on their death beds. With but a few remaining mortal breaths they reveled in the hope that'The Incorruptible' had given their lives. No man was more of a hero of the people than he. During this time I admit shame, for I yearned to visit France and discover what new battles he waged. The equality of vote brought him deserved renown. His opposition to slavery displayed chivalry. When he turned to abolish the death penalty I could only feel admiration. That may seem odd to you, but it was originally death by natural cause that gave my birth my predecessors and I. Death by man is an abomination, and I cheered for his cause from the shadows. At some point, a gray haired, ill-groomed man called me as he clutched at his heart amidst a crowd gathered for Robespierre. The Incorruptible's eloquent speech energized my soul in a way no mortal had done before. And so it was through others' misfortune, through eavesdropping in on the final conversations of French lives that I gradually witnessed Robespierre's corruption of spirit. Some say power perverted his integrity. Others believe he simply sacrificed for a greater good. But the dying have no need to lie, and so I can say with certainty that neither party was wrong. So dedicated to his cause, he fully relinquished his moral compass. He rescinded his opposition to the death penalty and executed former friends and allies as readily as Louis XVI. Tens of thousands died by his direction. He demanded citizens be given democracy, but could not abide those who would not embrace their despot's views. From time to time, I can still hear the guillotine working tirelessly to still the surviving opposition in Vendee. Heads filled baskets meant for flowers and fruit. But it was a final pair of brown eyes I would remember best. Robespierre's lifeless stare showed regret, but I know not if for his failures to realize his dream or for the cruelty he enacted to achieve it. After, as has been done many times before and will be done many times after, death took a new face. My retired colleagues thought me brave to handle such massacre. My retired colleagues thought me resolute to see the Reign of Terror to its end. My retired colleagues thought me foolish when I predicted these deaths would be a blip on the radar of human persecution. I admit it was a horrific time, but I am only glad my calling came when it did and not a century and a half later. Nightmares still haunt Tomas in a manner that no angel deserves. And the worst is still yet to come.

It's mostly a matter of training. Yes, some people are born with perfect pitch. A lot of the time, though, you can be trained to play something by ear. The first part of playing by ear is pitch identification. This is normally a crapshoot, but if you're sitting at a keyboard you can identify it by approximating the pitch in your head, then double-checking by playing along with the actual song. However, some people are born with intrinsic pitch identification abilities. The second part is interval identification.'Interval' means the space between two notes. This is easier than pitch because you can identify the intervals and play, even if it's in the wrong key. As I said, a lot of this comes down to training even though some people can just naturally do it.

The '4' and 'a' you see on your screen right now (unless you're using an odd font) are the technically correct glyphs, which is why they appear that way in most typefaces unless it's specifically mimicking handwriting. The "open 4" is use in handwriting because it's easier to distinguish from a 9. When writing quickly, those two digits can often look similar. The other way of writing 'a' is more because it's easier and faster.','There are multiple ways to write any character. Just look at different fonts. It just so happens that in the case of a and 4, there are two popular main styles used in print which are very obviously different. Other equally obvious examples include 1, 7, g, w, l and z. If you look at handwriting, the differences are way bigger.','The "closed 4" comes from the arabian formation of numerals where each numeral has the [number of angles as the number] (URL0), the "open 4," as far as I can tell, comes from the [lcd display] (URL1). Kyra looked down at the metal box she held in her hands, and couldn't help but feel disappointed. "Thanks Uncle Rufus," she said, finally looking up. Kyra schooled her features into polite happiness and grinned at Uncle Rufus, who sat in the rocking chair by the window. Mother didn't like him much, because he refused to remove his muddy boots when he came into their house, and the tartan shirt he wore stunk of pipe-smoke and peat. He still had dirt beneath his fingernails and his red hair was tousled by the wind, beard straggly as a bird's nest. "I really like the present." She placed her hand inside the box and nudged at the small, scaled creature that was coiled inside. It was smaller than a mouse, tiny combs like a cockerel's lining the back of its neck and down to the tiny tail, no wider than a needle at its base. At her touch, the dragon stirred itself and turned towards her hand. Its eyes were blue as sapphires, flashing against the deep royal green of the scales on its face. Two stubs on its back were all that promised the advent of wings. "They grow," Uncle Rufus promised. "That's a Scotch dragon. One of the last. I found the mother myself, after she'd birthed six of'em in a little bothy on my land. Almost burnt myself getting it away from her! Tha' was the smallest, thought it'd be perfect for little Kyra here." The last bit was addressed to Kyra's mother, who frowned. "I'm not sure it's entirely appropriate for a child," she said. Her mouth had become a hard, flat line. Meanwhile, the dragon had nestled against the palm of Kyra's hand, closing its eyes and snuffling quietly. She had wanted a Pets Hospital, but as the dragon's warmth began to blaze against her palm, she realised she didn't mind too much. "I like it, Mum," she said. "It's alright, can I keep it?" A moment of hesitation. "Pleaseeee," she whined. "She can come up to Jura with me if she wants," Uncle Rufus said. He was her dad's brother, not her mum's, and her dad was long gone. Kyra lifted the little green dragon from the box and looked at her Uncle. He stared intently as the dragon scurried up Kyra's arm like a mouse, the claws like small pinpricks on her skin. This is the news title today: Up to 70 of people in developed countries 'have seen incomes stagnate' But at the same time, the following this are observed: "Incomes are rising fastest for the richest" "People in developed countries are becoming richer at a faster pace than in developing countries" "Incomes in the US have grown at almost twice the global average since 2008" "The richest 1 of US households have seen their incomes soar by nearly 150 since 1999" So how do we reconcile these two contradicting points? We are told that the income of the richest in the US has soared by nearly 150 and yet up to 70 of the people in the US and the developed countries have seen their incomes stagnate. If we average out the income growth rate of the 70 of the people that have seen their incomes stagnate, it works out to about 0.5 per year. But the income growth rate of the richest 1 is nearly 3 times that. So the rich are getting richer at a faster pace than the poor are getting poorer. If income inequality is a problem, then we should be measuring how much the richest are getting richer relative to the poorest getting poorer. It is only when the poor get poorer faster than the rich get richer that we can see that there is a problem. But when the rich get richer faster than the poor get poorer, it means that the problem is not income inequality but rather income stagnation. The article is conflating two different issues. The following is taken from the 2017 Federal Budget released last week. The chart on page 14 shows the income and taxation revenue. The top 1 of income earners contribute nearly 30 of the tax revenue. The bottom 50 of the income earners contribute less than 10 of the tax revenue. Now you might be thinking that it is unfair that the top 1 have to pay nearly 30 of the tax revenue while the bottom 50 have to pay less than 10 of the tax revenue. But we are told that the top 1 are getting richer and the bottom 50 are getting poorer. So how can the bottom 50 have to pay less than 10 of the tax revenue when they earn less than 20 of the total income? If the top 1 have to pay 30 of the tax revenue while earning less than 20 of the total income, then the bottom 50 must be paying more than 10 of the tax revenue. In other words, it is a mis-statement to say that the bottom 50 have to pay less than 10 of the tax revenue. They must be paying more than 10 of the tax revenue.

Evaluating competitiveness often involves assessing the value offered relative to cost and profitability. While some companies might generate massive profits, simply looking at those figures isn’t always insightful; considering costs and profit margins provides a clearer picture. Exxon, with a 7.43% profit margin, and Apple, boasting a 21.28% margin, demonstrate this point.  The idea of “non-competitive” is rarely raised within industries like technology. Competition hinges largely on a firm’s ability to influence the price of its product. For example, Exxon cannot arbitrarily raise the price of gasoline significantly without losing sales due to competitors. Increasing the price by a dollar would indicate a lack of competition—a dominance of market share forcing consumers to purchase from them regardless of price. A 50% market share could lead to localized areas where consumers have limited alternatives. It’s crucial to distinguish between total profit and profit margin – the former is revenue minus costs, while the latter is (revenue minus costs) divided by costs.  For instance, a company with $150 billion in revenue and $100 billion in costs earns $50 billion in profit and maintains a 50% profit margin. Exxon, earning $101 billion in 2013 with $100 billion in costs, achieved a 1% profit, resulting in a comparatively low profit margin. Generally, higher profit margins signal reduced competition.

Given a positive integer k, a k -dominating set in a graph G is a set of vertices such that every vertex not in the set has at least k neighbors in the set. A total k -dominating set, also known as a k -tuple total dominating set, is a set of vertices such that every vertex of the graph has at least k neighbors in the set. The problems of finding the minimum size of a k -dominating, respectively total k -dominating set, in a given graph, are referred to as k -domination, respectively total k -domination. These generalizations of the classical domination and total domination problems are known to be NP-hard in the class of chordal graphs, and, more specifically, even in the classes of split graphs (both problems) and undirected path graphs (in the case of total k -domination). On the other hand, it follows from recent work of Kang et al. (2017) that these two families of problems are solvable in time O (V (G) 6 k 4) in the class of interval graphs. We develop faster algorithms for k -domination and total k -domination in the class of proper interval graphs, by means of reduction to a single shortest path computation in a derived directed acyclic graph with O (V (G) 2 k) nodes and O (V (G) 4 k) arcs. We show that a suitable implementation, which avoids constructing all arcs of the digraph, leads to a running time of O (V (G) 3 k). The algorithms are also applicable to the weighted case.

However, many individuals falsely claimed noble lineage, often originating as commoners who relocated and fabricated their social standing.  Hieronim Nekanda Trepka exposed numerous such impostors in his *Liber generationis plebeanorium* during the early 16th century, offering rewards for reporting them. While the exact proportion remains uncertain, scholars generally believe that a considerable portion of the Polish nobility descended from less privileged backgrounds.

I close my eyes. The nurse had marked the time of death as 15:07, but the patient on the table was not yet gone, as far as both the patient and I were concerned. A sudden aortic dissection. She is 27. Her hair is brown and her skin is still warm. My number was on her necklace next to the letters ICE: in case of emergency. I arrived at 14:30 and completed my work at 3:00 the next morning. By the time I had finished, there was no blood left. Only ice. I had met her once when she came to sign her contract for preservation. She liked to mountain bike. She told me about how she used to hit the trails her father when she was a teenager every weekend. He had died from lung cancer. She had gotten used to biking alone. An antifreeze cocktail flowed in as her blood flowed out. I always asked new members why they chose to be preserved. She told me more about her father. He'd arrived in this country from the former Second World. He had read about the far future and computers and robots in Asimov and Heinlein as a child in translation. When his polytechnic bought an old Russian computer, he applied to use it, and kept the first card he punched for it in his wallet until he died. He moved to his new home and worked on a computer every day. She said that he came home each day with a smile on his face. It was the look of a man who was living in a future that had once seemed centuries away. She wanted to travel through time too. I adjusted the packs of ice next to her head. The nurse began removing her jewelry. She removed a necklace from the patient, and flipped open the pendant. It was a photo of father and daughter at Cape Canaveral. Engraved on the back were a few lines in a language I could not read. I imagine that it is a promise they have made to each other. The nurse places it in a bag that will go to the mother. I hope the patient gets it back. With the nurse's help, I placed her on a gurney and move her to the van. Her core temperature was then just above freezing. She is pale. I noticed a tattoo that had been hidden beneath her watch. It is of a spiral galaxy, as though its rotation was how she truly wanted to measure time. She was placed in a precooling chamber. She was slowly brought down to temperature before being placed in one of the larger tanks. She will be upside down so that if there is a systems failure, the head will thaw last when the liquid nitrogen boils away. Is she already with her father? As a spirit or soul? Has she joined him in the universe's entropy? She might soon have a million stories she would want to share with him. I said a quiet goodbye and closed my eyes as I shut the chamber. I open my eyes. She is standing over me. She is eight. She kisses me on the forehead and I pull her towards me. I rub the sleep from my eyes. I feel sharp pains emanating from within my chest. I cough for a moment, and then pull her back towards me. "What will we do today, Daddy? " , she asks, smile gleaming. I stifle another cough. "Plan for the future."

According to the World Health Organization, breast cancer is the most common form of cancer in women. It is the second leading cause of death among women round the world, becoming the most fatal form of cancer. Despite the existence of several imaging techniques useful to aid at the diagnosis of breast cancer, x-ray mammography is still the most used and effective imaging technology. Consequently, mammographic image segmentation is a fundamental task to support image analysis and diagnosis, taking into account shape analysis of mammary lesions and their borders. However, mammogram segmentation is a very hard process, once it is highly dependent on the types of mammary tissues. The GrowCut algorithm is a relatively new method to perform general image segmentation based on the selection of just a few points inside and outside the region of interest, reaching good results at difficult segmentation cases when these points are correctly selected. In this work we present a new semi-supervised segmentation algorithm based on the modification of the GrowCut algorithm to perform automatic mammographic image segmentation once a region of interest is selected by a specialist. In our proposal, we used fuzzy Gaussian membership functions to modify the evolution rule of the original GrowCut algorithm, in order to estimate the uncertainty of a pixel being object or background. The main impact of the proposed method is the significant reduction of expert effort in the initialization of seed points of GrowCut to perform accurate segmentation, once it removes the need of selection of background seeds. Furthermore, the proposed method is robust to wrong seed positioning and can be extended to other seed based techniques. These characteristics have impact on expert and intelligent systems, once it helps to develop a segmentation method with lower required specialist knowledge, being robust and as efficient as state of the art techniques. We also constructed an automatic point selection process based on the simulated annealing optimization method, avoiding the need of human intervention. The proposed approach was qualitatively compared with other state-of-the-art segmentation techniques, considering the shape of segmented regions. In order to validate our proposal, we built an image classifier using a classical multilayer perceptron. We used Zernike moments to extract segmented image features. This analysis employed 685 mammograms from IRMA breast cancer database, using fat and fibroid tissues. Results show that the proposed technique could achieve a classification rate of 91.28 for fat tissues, evidencing the feasibility of our approach.

Human nature often drives desires for wealth, influence, and recognition. The ideal of a system where everyone relinquishes control is unrealistic, yet theoretically, a perfectly equitable governance model could exist. Considering communism – the concept of distributing resources based on individual capabilities and needs – faces significant challenges. Precisely defining “ability” and “need” proves exceptionally difficult; intrinsic motivation plays a crucial role in productivity, and monetary incentives alone aren’t consistently effective. Determining individual requirements also presents issues – providing basic necessities like food and shelter is straightforward, but allocating luxury items becomes arbitrary. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels popularized socialist and communist ideas, outlining societal critiques but lacking concrete solutions. Despite abundant theoretical discussions, practical implementation has repeatedly faltered, revealing a disconnect between idealistic principles and real-world outcomes. Communism, fundamentally an economic framework rather than a governmental one, encompasses diverse approaches—all ultimately unsuccessful due to failing to achieve their stated goals.

We show how to extend traditional intrinsic image decompositions to incorporate further layers above albedo and shading. It is hard to obtain data to learn a multi-layer decomposition. Instead, we can learn to decompose an image into layers that are "like this" by authoring generative models for each layer using proxy examples that capture the P latonic ideal (Mondrian images for albedo; rendered 3D primitives for shading; material swatches for shading detail). Our method then generates image layers, one from each model, that explain the image. Our approach rests on innovation in generative models for images. We introduce a Convolutional Variational Auto Encoder (conv-VAE), a novel VAE architecture that can reconstruct high fidelity images. The approach is general, and does not require that layers admit a physical interpretation.

Bacteria often attach to surfaces and form dense aggregations called biofilms or bacterial mats. These films can range from a few micrometers in thickness to up to half a meter in depth, and may contain multiple species of bacteria, protists and archaea. Bacteria living in biofilms display a complex arrangement of cells and extracellular components, forming secondary structures, such as microcolonies, through which there are networks of channels to enable better diffusion of nutrients. In natural environments, such as soil or the surfaces of plants, the majority of bacteria are bound to surfaces in biofilms. Biofilms are also important in medicine, as these structures are often present during chronic bacterial infections or in infections of implanted medical devices, and bacteria protected within biofilms are much harder to kill than individual isolated bacteria.

One of the most challenging problems in computational advertising is the prediction of click-through and conversion rates for bidding in online advertising auctions. An unaddressed problem in previous approaches is the existence of highly non-uniform misprediction costs. While for model evaluation these costs have been taken into account through recently proposed business-aware offline metrics - such as the Utility metric which measures the impact on advertiser profit - this is not the case when training the models themselves. In this paper, to bridge the gap, we formally analyze the relationship between optimizing the Utility metric and the log loss, which is considered as one of the state-of-the-art approaches in conversion modeling. Our analysis motivates the idea of weighting the log loss with the business value of the predicted outcome. We present and analyze a new cost weighting scheme and show that significant gains in offline and online performance can be achieved.

We consider convolutional networks from a reproducing kernel Hilbert space viewpoint. We establish harmonic decompositions of convolutional networks, that is expansions into sums of elementary functions of increasing order. The decompositions can be viewed as generalizations of the Fourier series for periodic functions or the Taylor series for smooth functions. In this case, the elementary functions are called "convolutional harmonics," which are a family of functions representing the different frequencies of the convolution operation. The use of convolutional harmonics allows us to better understand and interpret the behavior of convolutional networks, and also provides a framework for designing more efficient and effective network architectures. Additionally, the theory of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for studying convolutional networks and their properties.

One significant challenge when tackling continuous Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) lies in estimating the multifaceted distribution of hidden true states and incorporating this uncertainty into the planning process. We frame POMDP filtering and planning as interconnected Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) procedures, one for the actual states and another for potential optimal paths, integrating their strengths within a novel architecture called DualSMC. Specifically, we utilize an adversarial particle filter that exploits the inherent competition among its elements. Subsequently, we develop a planning algorithm built upon existing SMC methods, adapting them for continuous POMDPs with policies sensitive to uncertainty levels. Notably, DualSMC effectively manages intricate observations like visual data while maintaining transparency. Its performance has been validated across three continuous POMDP environments – floor positioning, 3D light-dark navigation, and a variant of the Reacher task – and the code is publicly available.

Primary resistance occurs when a person becomes infected with a resistant strain of TB. A person with fully susceptible MTB may develop secondary (acquired) resistance during therapy because of inadequate treatment, not taking the prescribed regimen appropriately (lack of compliance), or using low-quality medication. Drug-resistant TB is a serious public health issue in many developing countries, as its treatment is longer and requires more expensive drugs. MDR-TB is defined as resistance to the two most effective first-line TB drugs: rifampicin and isoniazid. Extensively drug-resistant TB is also resistant to three or more of the six classes of second-line drugs. Totally drug-resistant TB is resistant to all currently used drugs. It was first observed in 2003 in Italy, but not widely reported until 2012, and has also been found in Iran and India. Bedaquiline is tentatively supported for use in multiple drug-resistant TB.

Social influence begins when someone causes another person to react. Social media researchers often assess these responses using complex behavioral models or relying on signals like retweets, hashtags, links, or mentions. However, much social network content is hard to analyze due to the varied ways people express themselves and our limited understanding of their motivations. We propose “content transfer,” a method based on information theory that estimates how strongly one user’s posts affect another’s without needing elaborate models. This is achieved through new techniques for estimating entropy and improved methods for representing content. Using Twitter data from numerous users, we show that content transfer can identify meaningful connections between users who aren't connected via followers or mentions.  This approach opens up vast amounts of previously ignored social media data for robust statistical investigation of cause and effect.

An Analysis of Count William Reary's Argument Against Sir Tantey's Conclusions About Interdimensional Beings In his essay, An Argument Against Sir Tantey's Conclusions About Interdimensional Beings, famed author, columnist, and essayist Count William Reary argues that Tantey's conclusions lack supporting scientific evidence, writing that " unless one can simply will imaginary sentient lifeforms into existence, Sir Tantey's ideas have no basis whatsoever in science, logic, or even common sense. " Reary scatters effective rhetorical strategies throughout his paper, weaving clever analogies, metaphors, and even emotional appeals within it, providing more than sufficient support to his persuasive argument that Tantey's conclusions are, as he puts it, " bunk to anyone with half a brain and at least the primitive ability to use tools. " The most central aspect of Reary's means of persuasion are his rather surprising and exaggerated appeals to the emotion of his readers, making use of the pride they have in their identity as human beings, as well as members of the technologically advanced first world nations spangling the planet. He uniquely uses this emotion to support science-based thinking, as in the start of his second paragraph, where he writes that " we as a species have advanced far, far beyond other animal orgasms (sic) on the planet by making use of our incredible ability to identify what is true and what is not through a long-developed thinking called ' the scientific method ', and we should not allow ignorant halfwits like Tantey to taint our vast collection of knowledge with his cult-like beliefs in yellow-coloured, tentacle-infused aliens passing through invisible doors to mess with our banking systems. " Reary knows that the readers of his newspaper, The Weekly Reary, have pride in logic and despise extraordinary claims made without extraordinary evidence, and he uses these attributes to his advantage by using ad hominem attacks against Tantey, calling him an " ignorant halfwit. " Reary's less critical, less emotional support includes his analogies, such as one where he compares making conclusions about other realities to " believing that the bats in a cave are white, without even first confirming the existence of the cave. " His simple and easy-to-understand comparisons are very effective, especially considering the ironically low level of education his readers actually have. More complex analogies wouldn't achieve the effect Reary was going for - indeed, that is not what analogies are for. Analogies are supposed to be a simple, understandable comparison, and Reary knows exactly what he is doing. Reary also uses colorful and creative metaphors in order to captivate his readers, painting pictures in their minds with clever imagery and building in their brains an indestructible structure labeled " we are great. " His arguably most effective metaphor is when he says that " the human power of logic and science is a firm foundation upon which we build our cities, our efforts, and our pride. " He then compares this foundation to Tantey's " shakey, weak bridge upon which he transports the animalistic natives he calls his ' undeniable conclusions. These metaphors paint Reary and the rest of humanity as the inhabitants of incredible cities, and Tantey as the lone builder of an insufficient bridge used by tribal people. In conclusion, it is certain that Reary makes a compelling argument against Tantey's strange, almost schizophrenic ramblings. It is an argument that is most definitely effective at convincing his simple, easily-persuaded readers that Tantey does indeed make " shitty conclusions ," and that maybe he should be locked up in a " goddamn mental asylum " so he does not hurt other people.

Quantum annealing (QA) is a quantum computing algorithm that works on the principle of Adiabatic Quantum Computation (AQC), and it has shown significant computational advantages in solving combinatorial optimization problems , which are very common for applications such as problem-solving with biological compounds. However, current QA algorithms suffer from poor robustness to noise in their input signals. One way around this limitation would be through the use of novel noise sources: entangled pairs of photons or superpositions of photons can amplify QA's output signal by orders of magnitude without affecting its robustness. To date, experiments using entangled photons have yielded limited gains due to thermal noise arising during transmission between parties involved in these experiments. In addition, there exists no efficient way to interactively control the temperature at each end of the experiment so as to obtain more useful results over time.

We address the task of identifying densely connected subsets of multivariate Gaussian random variables within a graphical model framework. We propose two novel estimators based on the Ordered Weighted 1 (OWL) norm: 1) The Graphical OWL (GOWL) is a penalized likelihood method that applies the OWL norm to the lower triangle components of the precision matrix. 2) The column-by-column Graphical OWL (ccGOWL) estimates the precision matrix by performing OWL regularized linear regressions. Both methods can simultaneously identify highly correlated groups of variables and control the sparsity in the resulting precision matrix. We formulate GOWL such that it solves a composite optimization problem and establish that the estimator has a unique global solution. In addition, we prove sufficient grouping conditions for each column of the ccGOWL precision matrix estimate. We propose proximal descent algorithms to find the optimum for both estimators. For synthetic data where group structure is present, the ccGOWL estimator requires significantly reduced computation and achieves similar or greater accuracy than state-of-the-art estimators. Timing comparisons are presented and demonstrates the superior computational efficiency of the ccGOWL. We illustrate the grouping performance of the ccGOWL method on a cancer gene expression data set and an equities data set.

The majority of works in distributed storage networks assume a simple network model with a collection of identical storage nodes with the same communication cost between the nodes. In this paper, we consider a realistic multi-rack distributed data storage network and present a code design framework for this model. Considering the cheaper data transmission within the racks, our code construction method is able to locally repair the nodes failure within the same rack by using only the survived nodes in the same rack. However, in the case of severe failure patterns when the information content of the survived nodes is not sufficient to repair the failures, other racks will participate in the repair process. By employing the criteria of our multi-rack storage code, we establish a linear programming bound on the size of the code in order to maximize the code rate.

This paper considers a network of stochastic evidence accumulators, each represented by a drift-diffusion model accruing evidence towards a decision in continuous time by observing a noisy signal and by receiving a time-varying external input. In a mean-field scenario, the influence of one agent on the other is effectively captured by the mean field associated with the distribution of the decision variables. We present an approximate mean-field model to describe the population dynamics of the network. We derive approximate mean-field equations of the decision variables in terms of the distribution of the decision variables, and obtain a closed-form expression of the expected time to reach a decision in the asymptotic limit. Moreover, we show that when the decision problem can be linearly decomposed into subproblems, the mean-field model can be reduced to a set of independent subproblems. These results provide a rigorous mean-field approximation of the population dynamics of stochastic evidence accumulators in continuous time. We discuss extensions of the mean-field model and provide a numerical comparison of the mean-field model with the original system for a specific example.

Extracting road networks from satellite images presents a difficult problem in computer vision. Existing techniques generally divide into two types: those that classify individual pixels as road or non-road, and those that build road graphs step-by-step. These methods each have distinct benefits and drawbacks. Our research introduces Sat2Graph, a new technique that merges the best aspects of both previous approaches within a single system. At its core lies a unique encoding strategy called graph-tensor encoding (GTE), which represents the road graph as a tensor. This allows us to train a straightforward, non-recursive model to predict relevant characteristics about the graph's structure directly from the image data. We tested Sat2Graph on extensive datasets and demonstrated superior performance compared to earlier methods based on TOPO and APLS scores. Notably, unlike previous methods limited to flat roads, Sat2Graph can accurately identify complex structures like elevated roadways, exhibiting strong reliability.

Extracting appropriate features to represent a corpus is an important task for textual mining. Previous attention based work usually enhance feature at the lexical level, which lacks the exploration of feature augmentation at the sentence level. In this paper, we exploit a Dynamic Feature Generation Network (DFGN) to solve this problem. Specifically, DFGN generates features based on a variety of attention mechanisms and attaches features to sentence representation. Then a thresholder is designed to filter the mined features automatically. DFGN extracts the most significant characteristics from datasets to keep its practicability and robustness. Experimental results on multiple well-known answer selection datasets show that our proposed approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Yes, the impact of computer-aided detection (CAD) prompts can influence the sensitivity and specificity of screening mammography. CAD systems have been developed to assist the identification of potentially suspicious areas on mammograms. These systems are designed to serve as a "second pair of eyes" when a radiologist interprets mammograms for signs of breast cancer. Sensitivity refers to the ability of a test to correctly identify individuals with a disease, while specificity refers to the ability of a test to correctly identify individuals without the disease. Studies have shown that the use of CAD can increase the sensitivity of screening mammography. This means that with CAD assistance, radiologists are more likely to detect true positives (actual cases of breast cancer). However, the impact of CAD on specificity has been mixed, with some studies showing a decrease in specificity, which may lead to an increase in false-positive results (identifying someone as having breast cancer when they do not). The overall effect of CAD on sensitivity and specificity may vary based on factors such as the quality of the CAD system, the clinical setting, and the experience of the radiologist using the system. Some studies also suggest that the benefit of CAD may be more pronounced for less experienced radiologists, while more experienced radiologists may not see as much improvement in sensitivity or specificity.

In recent years I have become a big fan of Major League Baseball, watching dozens of games of my team (the Rockies) and following the playoffs. That said, the regular season is too long in terms of the number of games played. Every team plays 162 games per season plus 29 spring training games immediately prior to the season's opening. That's roughly double the amount of games in the NBA regular season, and roughly ten times the number of games in the NFL regular season. This means that every team will play 5-6 games per week, except during the relatively short all-star break, for close to seven months (excluding the postseason). This has a number of negative effects. First, it leads to position players being injured through the wear-and-tear of playing so often. How often is a starting position player put out of commission for a couple weeks because of a tweaked hamstring or shoulder soreness or knee pain? Starting position players often have to be rested even when teams are in still in the hunt for a playoff berth just to avoid these wear-and-tear injuries. Second, the sheer number of games hinders baseball's ability to be a more national sport like basketball or football. There are so many games that just trying to follow your local team will provide more than enough baseball for a year. I don't often feel motivated to watch a Yankees vs. Red Sox game on national TV when I have already seen 5 Rockies' games during the week. Compare with other major sports, especially football, where you can follow your team and still have plenty of time to follow the rest of the action. This is partially what allows football and basketball to be national sports and thus be more relevant in the national culture. The fatigue due to the number of games played dramatically reduces ratings for games on national TV. Third, the number of games also decreases local television ratings and fan attendance at the stadiums. When there are 162 games, there's no sense of missing out if you miss a game or five during the season, because no individual game is of much importance in itself (save for the last 20-30 games of the season played by a handful of the 30 teams chasing a playoff berth in September). This is especially true in the mid-season slog during June, July, and early August. Fourth, it makes it harder for casual fans to become more devoted fans because it is just hard to follow a team with so many games to be played. It requires a great deal of motivation and time investment to become a more devoted fan, especially if your team isn't contending. Fifth, and finally, the number of games means that the season must be very long in terms of time. Spring training starts at the beginning of March, while the World Series is played at the end of October. This causes two major problems. First, because baseball cannot be played in rough weather, and most teams play in open stadiums, this leads to a risk of games being cancelled due to snow in the early part of the season and the late part of the season and, crucially, during the playoffs. Second, this means that baseball must overlap with football at the end of the season which, given the utter dominance of football in the ratings and in sports coverage in the news, can only siphon fan attention and interest away from baseball right when it should be heating up. I believe the regular season should be shortened by at least 20 games, and perhaps as many as 50-60, to deal with the above five issues. So, Reddit, change my view! Hello, users of CMV! QoS-based Web service recommendation has recently gained much attention for providing a promising way to help users find high-quality services. To facilitate such recommendations, existing studies suggest the use of collaborative filtering techniques for personalized QoS prediction. These approaches, by leveraging partially observed QoS values from users, can achieve high accuracy of QoS predictions on the unobserved ones. However, the requirement to collect users' QoS data likely puts user privacy at risk, thus making them unwilling to contribute their usage data to a Web service recommender system. As a result, privacy becomes a critical challenge in developing practical Web service recommender systems. In this paper, we make the first attempt to cope with the privacy concerns for Web service recommendation. Specifically, we propose a simple yet effective privacy-preserving framework by applying data obfuscation techniques, and further develop two representative privacy-preserving QoS prediction approaches under this framework. Evaluation results from a publicly-available QoS dataset of real-world Web services demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of our privacy-preserving QoS prediction approaches. We believe our work can serve as a good starting point to inspire more research efforts on privacy-preserving Web service recommendation.

Because there’s no friction in space, spacecraft movement is highly predictable. Small corrections—taking hours or days—aren't problematic as long as extensive calculations are performed beforehand. Consider driving across a vast country highway with no other vehicles; if you meticulously plan for months, like with space missions, you could precisely predict steering adjustments and pre-program movements, maintaining direction even during brief changes. Space travel operates similarly. The probe possesses sufficient hardware and software to autonomously perform maneuvers, requiring only commands and parameter instructions from Earth. Equipped with diverse sensors – including cameras to identify stars and utilize a built-in star chart for orientation – it may observe the Sun or planets to estimate its position within the solar system and optimize signal reception. It also adjusts its orientation based on incoming signals from Earth. Data transmitted by the probe (telemetry) allows us to determine its location through signal angles, response times, and the Doppler effect to calculate speed. Combining these measurements yields an accurate orbital path. To alter the probe's trajectory, we issue a command specifying the desired pointing, engine activation/deactivation times, and instrument responses under both ideal and error conditions. The probe then executes these commands independently and reports completion back to Earth.

We present an approach to develop folds for nested data types using dependent types. We call such folds dependently typed folds , they have the following properties. (1) Dependently typed folds are defined by well-founded recursion and they can be defined in a total dependently typed language. (2) Dependently typed folds do not depend on maps, map functions and many terminating functions can be defined using dependently typed folds. (3) The induction principles for nested data types follow from the definitions of dependently typed folds and the programs defined by dependently typed folds can be formally verified. (4) Dependently typed folds exist for any nested data types and they can be specialized to the traditional higher-order folds . Using various of examples, we show how to program and reason about dependently typed folds. We also show how to obtain dependently typed folds in general and how to specialize them to the corresponding higher-order folds.

As mobile devices and scanning increase the volume of unstructured document images – like receipts, claims, and invoices – there’s growing demand for automated methods to extract data from them. However, identifying tables within these images and accurately pulling information from their rows and columns remains difficult due to the complex nature of tabular layouts. Existing solutions often tackle table detection and structure recognition separately, but our research introduces TableNet, a new deep learning model designed to handle both simultaneously. TableNet leverages the connection between these tasks to identify table and column areas, then uses rules to extract data from those regions. Evaluation on ICDAR 2013 and Marmot Table datasets shows TableNet achieves top performance, and incorporating extra semantic details enhances accuracy, alongside demonstrating effective transfer learning. Furthermore, we've added detailed structural annotations to the Marmot dataset, addressing its previous limitation of only having detection annotations.

Virtually every tech company relies on open-source projects where developers often work for free. Developers contribute to code to sharpen their skills, gain perspectives from the community, or just to help the industry. When open-source software is maintained on a voluntary basis, sometimes projects are abandoned or mistakes aren't corrected in a timely manner. Some open-source developers end up being hired by companies to maintain support for the code. However, as the code is free for anyone to use, companies may be reluctant to pay for the work, which will often benefit competitors. The open-source community is divided on whether they should be paid for work, with some believing that monetization defeats the purpose of software being free. However, developers who spend time creating software used by millions of people around the world still need to provide for themselves, so monetization eventually becomes a necessity.

High-performance implementations of graph algorithms are challenging toimplement on new parallel hardware such as GPUs because of three challenges: (1) the difficulty of coming up with graph building blocks, (2) their vast dimensionality and (3) the need for large amounts of memory. Given that many graphs contain both directed and undirected edges between nodes, our goal is to design a runtime system in which we can use both memory and GPU resources in an intelligent manner. To support this goal, we designed and implemented a novel algorithm called DIMINI, which has been shown to scale well even if it uses only parts ofthe entire GPU's memory. We will present the precise definition of DIMINI and its architecture; how we achieved fast execution times using both low-level and high-level programming languages; and why, compared to other existing techniques, DIMINI achievesstate-of-the-art results while requiring relatively minimal storage space. Finally, we show that some simulations performed on thousands of real datasets have revealed interesting properties about the algorithm's performance at different levels of complexity.

We present a local routing algorithm which guarantees delivery in all connected graphs embedded on a known surface of genus g. The algorithm transports O (g log n) memory and is SLIPk-optimal in the sense of routing by shortest paths. It is also optimal in the number of hops on any genus g surface. The algorithm is based on a novel parameterization of the space of all possible routes through a connected graph embedded on a surface. This parameterization allows us to construct a constant number of such routes per edge, each of which is guaranteed to deliver messages in the given graph. We also show that this parameterization can be used to construct an efficient distributed data structure for efficient local routing in any graph embedded on a surface.

Chloroplasts' main role is to conduct photosynthesis, where the photosynthetic pigment chlorophyll captures the energy from sunlight and converts it and stores it in the energy-storage molecules ATP and NADPH . When a plant or animal needs food, these stored chemical messages can be released into the body for use as fuel. Presumably, this process of harvesting light through photosynthesis has powered all life on Earth since its formation 4 billion years ago. However, there are exceptions: algae don't have chloroplasts but rather rely upon photoassimilation - they take up carbon dioxide directly instead using an enzyme called RuBisCO that uses electrons captured during normal respiration to draw down CO2. This means that even though plants do not need them, some freshwater species such as cyanobacteria (commonly known as blue green algae) still possess two sets of organelles because their ancestors relied solely on photosynthesis before switching over to ion transport. Blue green algae consume nutrients like glucose which would otherwise be too large for other organisms with more efficient mechanisms - something we humans benefit greatly from today when eating spirulina!

We came to Bratalian for Restaurant Week 2014 and were very excited, given the excellent reviews. Although some aspects of our experience were good, overall it was weak enough that I don't think we'll be back. Service: We called at about 5:15 to make a reservation, but the line did that fax machine screechy sound. Okay, then! We'll take our chances! On the ride there (it's about 25 minutes away from us), we worried that the place would be packed because of Restaurant Week so we called. The hostess was very accommodating and cordial, promising us a table. When we arrived, however, our luck with service changed. We didn't have a single server. Our order was briskly taken by one waiter, the food was dropped by another, and our dessert order was taken and delivered by the manager. The place was pretty busy, but other tables seemed to have good service. We felt overlooked and kind of like nuisances! The biggest issue is that they added an 18 gratuity and then taxed it. This is not typical procedure for Restaurant Week and I resented not necessarily having the gratuity added (I guess), but being taxed on it - I think - is in bad form. Food: From the Restaurant Week menu, we had the meatballs and fried calimari and zuchinni to start. Then, for our entrees, we had the linguine clams and the salmon with a lemon-butter sauce. For dessert, we had the profiteroles and the ricotta cheesecake. I thought the food was fine. The fried calamari didn't have much seasoning and was overly greasy; the dipping sauce on the side was a simple, plain marinara. If the calimari is going to be so plain, at least offer something a bit zestier for dipping. The meatballs were below average. They are VERY large, but, again, there wasn't much flavor. They were also a bit dense and dry; we were hoping for plump, juicy meatballs. The entrees were much better. The clams in the linguine were big and so flavorful. My salmon was probably the best part. The skin was crispy, the fish was cooked perfectly, the lemon-butter was succulent, and the sauteed spinach was a lovely compliment. If I come back, I would get the same entree. I was really looking forward to dessert because of other reviews, but I gotta say, the ricotta cheesecake didn't live up to the hype. I thought it was too dense and bread-y. The flavor was fine, but I didn't finish it because of the density. It was like a having a mouthful of wet sand! The profiteroles that my boyfriend ordered were good. The pastry was flaky and what can go wrong with vanilla ice cream and chocolate sauce?We had a half carafe of red wine along with our food, which gave us about 3 glasses total. Atmosphere: It's a small restaurant, but it's very cute. It's decorated perfectly and arranged so that it's size is not a problem. It's lively - lots of groups. There were a few slip-ups that night: a tray of dishes crashed, the smoke alarm went off in the kitchen. No major issues, really. Just added to the fun. The biggest atmosphere problem for me is the broken lock on the women's room door. I struggled to get out of that bathroom for like five minutes, which doesn't seem like a long time until that's the amount of minutes you spend involuntarily in a bathroom. I had almost resigned myself to my new life as a bathroom-dweller, about to start fashioning a bed out of toilet paper, when I finally escaped. Bratalian, you've got to fix the door. Overall, it was just okay. The service was unexceptional and simply got the job done. The food was fine. Unfortunately, that's not really enough to have me come back.

In his book, Humanism (1997), Tony Davies calls these critics "humanist anti-humanists." Critics of antihumanism, most notably Jurgen Habermas, counter that while antihumanists may highlight humanism's failure to fulfil its emancipatory ideal, they do not offer an alternative emancipatory project of their own. Others, like the German philosopher Heidegger considered themselves humanists on the model of the ancient Greeks, but thought humanism applied only to the German "race" and specifically to the Nazis and thus, in Davies' words, were anti-humanist humanists. Such a reading of Heidegger's thought is itself deeply controversial; Heidegger includes his own views and critique of Humanism in Letter On Humanism. Davies acknowledges that after the horrific experiences of the wars of the 20th century "it should no longer be possible to formulate phrases like 'the destiny of man' or the 'triumph of human reason' without an instant consciousness of the folly and brutality they drag behind them." For "it is almost impossible to think of a crime that has not been committed in the name of human reason." Yet, he continues, "it would be unwise to simply abandon the ground occupied by the historical humanisms. For one thing humanism remains on many occasions the only available alternative to bigotry and persecution. The freedom to speak and write, to organise and campaign in defence of individual or collective interests, to protest and disobey: all these can only be articulated in humanist terms."

K-Medoids (KM) is a standard clustering method, used extensively on semi-metric data. Error analyses of KM have traditionally used an in-sample notion of error, which can be far from the out-of-sample errors that are relevant to real applications. We propose here two forms of out-of-sample analysis: one based only on comparisons with other methods and another using hierarchical clusterings. Using simulated and experimental datasets we compare these various approaches both for their accuracy as well as for computational time and efficiency.
