I was a wonder; my baby pictures graced the covers of tabloids, my childhood contemporaries camped out on my parents' lawn to throw rocks at our windows. The Tattooed Baby, the Inkfant, the marked child, Cain.... I'd been given many names after my parents gave me my first. I never knew my mother for a moment; the doctors said it was the most difficult birth they'd ever seen. But my father had done what he could; he just wasn't cut out for the life I forced upon him by existing. I fast became able to brush aside the comments and the stares, but my father took them hard enough for us both. He tried in vain to shelter me from the cruelties of the world that didn't understand me, he tried his best. When I came home with my clothes burned and blood coming from my ear, it was his breaking point. My father left that night, and something terrible happened to the boys who'd bullied me, and then I never saw him again. That's when I began to refer to myself as Cain; and now I can't remember what it was before that. As if it wasn't enough to be born with medically inexplicable tattoos covering 60 of your body, the forces that be had to make things more exhausting for me. My marks were called tattoos because no one had another word for them, but they weren't ink and they weren't pictures. Furthermore, contrary to the thousands of tattooed folks who'd tried to make me part of some type of pilgrimage, my marks hold no meaning for me. Covering my face, my arms, my torso and legs is script I can not read; script no man can read. Scrawled on me from head to toe are words in a language either long gone or not yet written, and the only thing I know about them is that they tell the story of my life; the book of Cain. I know that's what they say. I know it the way you know the feeling of the wind or the face of a loved one; I was born knowing only one thing: The marks are your story. I was never told this by a person, never visited in a dream; I just know it as a constant, unchanging truth. I spent much of my youth attempting to decipher the code, I have notebooks piled upon themselves filled with transcriptions of the text, rearranged and mirrored and substituted and analyzed; but not one sheet yields a clue. My purpose, my path - they're as cloudy as the day I was born. The search for meaning consumed me, and without any support I allowed it to. I've spent the better part of a decade buried within the reams of paper I'd transcribed but they gave me no quarter and here I sit. This room is dark; a sliver of natural light cascades between the barnboards I hammered to the windows, dust floating carelessly on the imperceptible breeze from the radiator. A small flashlight on my desk casts it's beam onto my chest, and in the small mirror seated next to it, just for an instant, I could swear I read the words "Get off Reddit and go outside."

Let’s begin by clarifying “supernatural” – those concepts where verifiable proof, either confirming or disproving, is inherently impossible. Many arguments on this forum, often centered around religious beliefs, conclude with the claim that we simply can’t rule out the possibility of a particular faith being true. I find this debate repetitive and unproductive. Though all supernatural claims share this characteristic, it doesn’t allow us to prioritize one over another. It’s equally valid to suggest countless fabricated supernatural notions exist, each potentially true—though the probability of any single one being genuinely true is vanishingly small.  Even widespread belief changes nothing; any such idea remains statistically insignificant compared to the overwhelming likelihood of falsehood. Furthermore, any created supernatural concept can easily be contradicted by others, creating an endless array of incompatible possibilities. Therefore, asserting the greater probability of any single supernatural idea being true, over its denial, or even over other competing supernatural ideas, is illogical. Facebook's Deepfake Detection Challenge is an open competition to find algorithms that can spot AI-manipulated videos. This year's winning algorithm could spot real-world examples of deep fakes with an average accuracy of over 98. Deepfakes are videos in which AI has been used to manipulate faces, often with frighteningly realistic results. They have been used to create fake celebrity sex tapes, political propaganda, and even fake news stories. The Deepfake Detection Challenge is a yearly competition organized by Facebook and the University of California, Berkeley. It challenges participants to develop algorithms that can automatically detect deepfakes. This year's challenge was won by a team from the University of Maryland, College Park. Their algorithm was able to detect deepfakes with an average accuracy of over 98. The team plans to open-source their algorithm so that it can be used by anyone who wants to detect deepfakes.

Penny auctions work by having bids increase incrementally, typically by a penny each time. Bidders must purchase these bids upfront, often in sets of ten cents each, which reduces the remaining time in the auction. An item’s price rises steadily with each bid placed. If a bidder raises the price to the winning amount, they acquire the item, but they’ve already spent money on the bids used to achieve that price. The auction operator collects all the individual bid amounts, plus any additional fees, resulting in a profit. Often, unsuccessful bidders receive a discount to simply purchase the item directly, though the operator still generates revenue through bid sales. Related to this is the “dollar auction,” where an item can be sold for more than its face value.

Solid State Drives (SSDs) are better than regular hard drives because they offer faster read and write speeds, increased durability, and lower power consumption. SSDs use flash memory to store data instead of spinning disks like hard drives, which makes them more reliable since there are no moving parts. The absence of these moving parts also means that SSDs can start up much faster than hard drives. SSDs are limited in the number of cycles because each cell in the storage can only be written to a certain amount of times before it fails. This is not necessarily bad, but it does mean that you should take extra care when choosing an SSD for your device. Data should be backed up regularly so that any issues caused by this limitation can be minimized.

Human face analysis is an important task in computer vision. According to cognitive-psychological studies, facial dynamics could provide crucial cues for face analysis. The motion of a facial local region in facial expression is related to the motion of other facial local regions. In this paper, a novel deep learning approach, named facial dynamics interpreter network, has been proposed to interpret the important relations between local dynamics for estimating facial traits from expression sequence. The facial dynamics interpreter network is designed to be able to encode a relational importance, which is used for interpreting the relation between facial local dynamics and estimating facial traits. By comparative experiments, the effectiveness of the proposed method has been verified. Our bodies consist of countless microscopic components – cells – which naturally age and eventually expire, necessitating continuous creation of replacements. Each cell specializes in a specific task, and newly formed cells should ideally continue that role. However, occasionally errors occur, leading new cells to prioritize self-replication over fulfilling their intended function. These replicating cells then generate further copies that lack productive capabilities, demanding significant energy expenditure. Consequently, the body’s resources are diverted towards these unproductive cells, hindering the energy supply for those performing essential tasks. Substances termed “carcinogens” increase the probability of this detrimental process, impeding the body’s ability to eliminate aberrant cells and prevent further proliferation. Similar instances of cancer arise across numerous animal species, including cats, dogs, horses, fish, birds, and hamsters. This prevalence is likely attributable to two primary factors: humans’ extended lifespans, resulting in extensive cellular division with increased risk of errors, and exposure to environmental hazards—such as microwave radiation, poor nutrition, tobacco smoke, certain medications, or cleaning agents—that many wild animals avoid. Cancer has likely existed for an extended period.

Your feet are incredibly vital for movement and survival – often overlooked but essential for getting you where you need to go. Because your body prioritizes warmth for critical functions, it directs heat from its core (like your armpits and groin) to your extremities like your hands, fingers, feet, and toes when they’re feeling cold.  The body can’t generate additional heat, so it redistributes existing warmth to these colder areas. Wearing socks can actually raise your overall body temperature, as your extremities significantly influence the temperature of your entire body. Specifically, your head, hands, and feet have the greatest impact on maintaining your body’s thermal balance—likely due to the larger mass of your torso, hips, and legs, which draws coldness inward toward this central mass.

Same end result, chemicals hang out for a bit longer. -Both have a handful of other receptors that they bind to and have somewhat limited activity, but the above is the major mechanism of action. How your body breaks it down: -Both have peak blood concentrations at right about 3 hours after taking the dose -Ritalin has a half life of about 2-3 hours -Adderall has a half life of about 7-8 hours This results in Adderall more commonly being taken once a day vs twice a day for Ritalin. As to why one medication might work for one patient who tried and failed the other? Patient response does very, similar to how some patients respond to Zoloft but not Prozac (anti-depressants), both work on the exact same receptors in the body, but doesn't always result in the patient getting the same response.

Synthesizing physiologically-accurate human movement in a variety of conditions can help practitioners plan surgeries, design experiments, or prototype assistive devices in simulated environments, reducing time and costs and improving treatment outcomes. The field is developing new techniques for motion capture that are faster than traditional video recording but still retain high quality (thousands to millions of variables) as well as the ability to simulate complex motions with ease." The findings were published November 1st in Science Advances by researchers from Washington University School of Medicine and Argonne National Laboratory. How does it work? A team at Argonne first trained an artificial neural network using images taken before and after people perform a series of exercises such as walking on leg extensions followed by knee extensions. Then they used this information to identify how different muscles contract during those movements - identifying their differences based off muscle activity patterns found in real humans' physical activities. They then fused these data points into computer models to create "graphics" depicting what muscles could move each way given specific instructions provided through software applications called "simulators." This allowed them to train synthetic models to imitate human biological actions like limb extension, bending forward, flexing hips back, raising arms overhead all while maintaining physical realism. In addition to reproducing realistic movements without needing special equipment, the method also helps scientists develop more accurate simulations because they know exactly where every individual parametric point has been located throughout the simulation process. In other words, if someone were to try out the potential application program again under similar circumstances, there would be less uncertainty about whether an action will occur and so results may actually get better. It's essentially another step towards creating prosthetics that feel and function just like natural limbs.

The moment my roommates left for vacation, our house took on a different, darker persona. Something felt..... off. I believed at first that I was imagining things, but it quickly became apparent that this was not the case. I couldn't sleep for the footsteps outside my door. I couldn't turn off the lights for the breathing down my neck. I couldn't hide for the feeling of being endlessly watched. Something was coming, and I was nervous with excitement. I had been ready for this day for so long. My alarm goes off promptly at 6:04 AM. This is just enough time for me to leave my home by 7:19 and arrive at work at exactly 7:30, assuming normal traffic. The Wednesday after my roommates left I awoke as normal. I walked in a tired, unsteady, painful daze to the bathroom and flipped the light switch. From the corner of my tired, sleep-filled eyes, I could see what appeared to be the dark silhouette of a person in the reflection, peering into the bathroom from just outside the window. Without thinking I immediately shut my eyes, let out a horrible screech to cover any sudden sounds, and opened the middle right drawer on the cabinet below the mirror. I had rehearsed this drill enough to know that the hammer was in the back of the drawer laying horizontally. I shattered the mirror, closed the bathroom door, and opened my eyes. "Thank God!" I sighed. "That was close. I nearly saw him!" I performed my morning routine normally and left for work without further incident. Upon returning home that evening, I was filled with a sense of dread. It was already dark on this cold Winter evening and everything, though normal, appeared out of place inside my home. The warm light of my incandescent bulbs (fluorescent bulbs are too hospital-esque for my comfort) seemed awfully cool tonight. Realizing that this deafening silence could at any moment give way to the sudden sound of a frightening orchestral piece, I quickly produced the phone from my pocket and commanded my house-wide speaker system to play Mika's "Grace Kelly" on repeat at full volume. "That should cover up any unexpected violin slides and screeches," I said with a smirk. I turned for no reason in particular toward the black television screen which faces opposite to the front windows of my abode. Though the matte-black screen of this relatively old plasma television blurred any reflections cast upon it, I could see a faint outline and the subtle facial features of somebody peering into my home from the darkened front yard. "Egad!" Without thinking I immediately grabbed the television remote from the coffee table in front of me and hurled it toward the TV screen with a quick cast of the arm. Immediately after removing the reflection I synchronously stomped my feet and clapped my hands twice, producing a sound just loud enough for my decades-old hand-me-down clapper system to recognize over Grace Kelly, triggering the descent of every set of blinds in the house. "You may break in and murder me tonight," I said coyly, "but you won't startle me first!" My sleep was interrupted early in the morning hours by a cold sweat. Whenever this occurs, I flail my limbs and body blindly and wildly before opening my eyes, lest I open them to see someone hovering just above me. Feeling assured that nobody is within my personal space, I slowly opened my eyes, just in time to witness a shadow slip out of my cracked bedroom door and down the hallway. I followed in hot pursuit, making sure to swing both my arms in full circles like the blades of a windmill to knock out anybody who may be near me but not visible. My assailant screamed in fear from somewhere ahead of me. I had him. The stomping of my feet caused the blinds to rise and fall over and over. The phone, always in my pocket just in case, signaled the resumption of my Grace Kelly-only playlist at maximum volume. The situation had suddenly turned spooky. I was losing control. In my efforts to tame the unsettling circumstances I had found myself in, I had only succeeded in scaring myself. Fright filled the whole of my soul and I collapsed. I activated my only remaining defense system. I tightly shut my eyes and flailed as crazily and violently as I could. My arms and legs became maces of war, deadly to anybody within a 3 foot radius of me. Suddenly the music stopped. I sat myself up to a motionless and silent position as the shadow from before - no, two shadows - slid closer to me, inch by terrifying inch. The lights turned on and before me stood none other than my roommates! "Jesus! When did you get back?" I shouted at the top of my exhausted lungs. Both of my shoulders and hips were dislocated. "Daddy, you're scaring me!" said the smaller of my two female roommates. She clutched the leg of the other, who stared angrily and with fiery eyes into my own. I was beckoned to follow. We walked into the kitchen, where the older roommate, Alice, spread her arms out in a grand gesture toward a kitchen counter littered with empty whiskey bottles. "What the fuck, David," she screamed. "What the hell have you done!? The TV is ruined and the bathroom mirror is shattered! Why wouldn't you let us in?" "When did you get back from London?" I stammered, dumbfounded. "London? We went to my mothers for one night and you wouldn't let us back in! How many time are you going to do this to us? We had to go all the way back to mother's and call a locksmith to let us in! And you know what I figured out? She's right. She's always been right. You're a pathetic shell of a man and I regret the day I recited those vows. You either need to get help for the drinking problem that - guess what - you can't even hide anymore, or you need to get out of our life." The child clung to her mother as if for life and shook with nervousness. At that moment I saw myself in her, and not just in her ears which everybody says look identical to mine, but in her soul. She was spooked. How long have I been spooked, I wondered? How long have I been living in a personal prison of spookiness and easy spookification? I stood up and looked down. "I've pissed myself," I slurred drunkenly as I swayed side to side with a breeze that didn't exist. "I've pissed myself and I need to..." I vomited and passed out. When I woke, I was alone. "Oh my..... It was just a dream..." I whispered to nobody. There was a note next to me, folded gently. "David, We need to talk. Sara is at mother's. We'll be back later. -Alice" I stood and walked into the kitchen. I opened a mostly empty bottle of bourbon and quickly downed what was left of it. "Just a dram..." I chuckled. My roommates had just left on vacation, and immediately the house took on a different, darker persona.

As far as the ships in orbit and planetary defenses were concerned, the dropships had left the base for some training flights and to test the repairs. Oh, how they were wrong. They never suspected what might actually be going on inside those small craft, or how large their impact would be. They would soon find out. Everyone would hear the news. Every possible variable had been planned out. Hundreds of people were involved, even if they didn't know it. Arguably most important was the work of a graduate student from the Inner Colonies who wrote a thesis on the geological instability of Radom's moon. The Paladins now planned to make the most of this information, and hope the kid was as good a cartographer as he was a student. The Cleansing Flame the Paladins spoke so highly of would come in the form of a shower of shrapnel from the shattered moon burning up on reentry and destroying all below. All of the crime, corruption, and general vileness of Radom would be turned to ash, a monument showing the consequences of evil. A gleaming warning to others who would stray from their path. The surface of the moon suddenly went from being an uninhabited waste to a waste with a population of about 80. The plan went into motion. The dropships were not the only things that had gone missing from Radom lately. There was also an almost noticeable lack of mining equipment, spaceworthy food containers, O2 tanks, cutting and welding equipment, firearms, and computers capable of accessing the guidance systems of the planetary defenses. Galen wondered if someday someone would appreciate the irony of " making the villainous fall upon their own swords " as the more devout liked to describe it. One by one the teams called in that their " passengers " had arrived safely. Everyone piled back into the ships and sped off toward their next objective. Gaining control of a military ship with which to fan the flames in other systems was a secondary objective, but it was all they could do with their lives once the Spark was struck. In the next thousand years, there wouldn't be a single soul who didn't know who they were or what they had done. Most would not understand that it was necessary for the betterment of Humanity as a whole, much like how Galen doubted it now. Setting tens of millions of people aflame did not seem like a righteous act, even if they were evil, but he didn't make the rules. Concerns over the morality of the plan or doubts that it were possible were always met with the same response, " Our cause is righteous and just, we will not falter. " The plan for taking a ship was simple...if you were completely insane. Galen thought it relied a bit too much on the enemy's skepticism, but that wasn't his problem either. He was just there to shoot people who tried to resist their taking the ship. Galen had never shot anyone before, but some of the " reformed " who had joined the Paladins told him it was easy after you got over the nervousness the first time. He had mixed feelings about that advice. He tried to reassure himself that these people were just as bad as those on the surface and they would kill him just as easily as look at him. He was determined to shoot them first. They landed in the bay of the cruiser just as the orbital guns began to light up... Galen couldn't help but stare in awe, involuntarily mimicking the sound he imagined the guns making even though there was no sound in the vacuum. The streaks from the guns tore across the void and into the pale ball around the planet, setting in motion a set of events that could never be undone and would go down in history as either the best or worst thing they had ever done. The moon shattered into several large shards surrounded by dust. In a few hours, days maybe, that dust would circle the planet like water in a drain until finally crashing into the planet itself. The days of " Sodom Colony " would be done. The shock tactics must have worked because it took several minutes for the soldiers aboard the ship to notice that a large group of armed and uniformed individuals had been running through the ship tying people up, locking doors, and disarming people while their eyes remained glued to the displays showing live reports of the events. When they finally did notice it was too late to put up any meaningful resistance. Those few who did were quickly put down. The entire crew and garrison were soon thrown into escape pods and jettisoned for the other ships to deal with. They would surely notice them when their ships systems came back online. Letting the crew go had been Galen's idea. The original plan was to either kill them all or use them as hostages. Galen convinced enough people that mindless killing of the families aboard would be needless bloodshed and there weren't enough supplies aboard to support everyone for a long period of time, so they let them go. He felt slightly better knowing that he had saved a few lives, in spite of all that he had been involved in. " Our cause is righteous and just, we will not falter. " Galen had grown tired of that excuse. He had never felt less righteous or just in his life. He would have to find a way to live with what he had done, the Paladins wouldn't let him live any other way.

The city is a thing of endless smells. There's the smell of freshly made pretzels coming from the sales-carts on the streets, the smell of the perfume of the woman walking past you, the foul odor of a piece of dog shit it's owner didn't pick up. And then there is that smell you can't quite place your finger on, that smell that is all of the smells of the city sort of coalescing together into a smell that can only be described as the city. For years, I could smell it. Always. Almost every day. From birth to today. I could smell the leaves changing in fall and the new blooms of spring, the hot dogs during a summer baseball game and salted roads of winter. The only times I haven't smelled it have been when I was going to Disney World when I was 11 and when I could smell the beer and weed of my dorm. Other than that, though, it's been the smell of the city. Until today. Today, I can smell fields, and flowers, and miles upon miles of fresh grass, beautiful trees, blue skies, and clear water. I don't know why. I'm just a money man, after all. Not the outdoorsy type. But then I look into the restaurant and see her waiting there. Her name's Clara, some friend of my sister's. From Kansas or Montana or some place like that. And then I realize what I've been smelling. I've been smelling me and her.

Research indicates that intoxicated drivers experience higher injury or fatality rates in accidents compared to those who are sober. A common misconception persists that they perform better, leading to fabricated explanations like claiming increased relaxation. This phenomenon likely stems from confirmation bias – individuals selectively notice and remember instances where drunk drivers survive, reinforcing the false belief. Furthermore, reporting biases contribute to this perception; news outlets tend to highlight incidents involving fatalities of innocent parties, while personal accounts focusing on the survival of drunk drivers are less frequently shared, perpetuating the illusion.

It is possible to use a mechanism based on a pistonless rotary engine such as the Wankel engine in place of the cylinders and valve gear of a conventional reciprocating engine. The vehicle using this type of power generating device (an electric generator) may be driven by an internal combustion engine or a motor, but generally, it can run only under the operation conditions provided for vehicles running with no engine at all. For example, when running down hill, the driving force required from the vehicle becomes large and therefore, if the output shaft of the generator were coupled directly to the drive wheel through a planetary transmission system including a sun gear, a ring gear, first and second drive gears and third and fourth drive wheels, the vehicle would need other devices like brakes etc., making the whole configuration complicated. In addition, the efficiency tends to decrease because of friction loss due to engagement between the engaging members and components during turning of the driving wheel.

We've been together for several years. She is my best friend as well as my lover, and we do almost everything together. I don't want to marry her because I don't like the marriage and divorce laws regarding assets and debts. I see minimal benefit to a legal marriage, but a big risk if we don't work out as life partners. She is happy with how things are, but I think she would like it a bit if we were "official." I'm a little older than her, I have a good paying professional job, own the house we live in, and have some money invested in stocks. I invest a large chunk of my pay. I know what is mine before marriage would stay mine, but I am planning to continue to pay off my mortgage and invest a lot of my income. She is still in school, working on becoming a high-paid professional too. She will likely take out more student loans in the years to come. I am pretty certain she will continue to spend a lot more money than me on things like lattes and clothes. I am totally fine with this, but if we shared finances I would feel like she was buying stuff I don't care about with "our" money, and the money I was saving would also become "ours." I don't want to get married and pretend our finances are separate, knowing that if we get divorced the courts will split everything 5050 (I live in a community property state, meaning assets and debts acquired during marriage are joint). I also don't want to do a pre-nup. To make it legit, both of us would need attorneys during the process, which is expensive. We already live like we are married, it seems silly to get the marriage certificate, and do more paper work to undo a big chunk of what the marriage certificate does. I'm also concerned that she would not like the pre-nup process, and it might make getting married not as fun. I am pretty certain I will accumulate wealth much faster than she. I want to share this wealth with her while we are together, but if for some reason we don't work out I want to keep what I have worked hard to earn, and not be responsible for any debts she may still have. Many times the lower earning person helps the higher earner to make more money. This is not the case with us, we split all the housework and stuff evenly. I'd be wealthier if I were single (mainly because I'd get roommates and charge them rent), but I have no complaints because I love living with my girl and spending some money so we can have a blast. On the flip side, I am pretty sure she will be wealthier with me than if single or with someone else. I know a lot about personal finance, I give her as much advice as she will tolerate (haha), and will encourage her to practice good financial habits and establish financial security of her own. We don't have kids, but if we do we will figure out a fair way to divide labor, because we are both intelligent and can work out a good deal for both of us. If we think it is best for her to take some time off to be a SAHM, I am confident we will figure out a fair deal, including some compensation for missed career building. Or, maybe she'll SAH the first few years, and I'll SAH the next few years. I think the reason we have these divorce laws is because most people don't plan ahead for things. Divorce law is a crappy one-size-fits-all way to handle the problem, better than nothing but it still sucks. I have no problem publicly committing my love to the woman I want to spend my life with, but will not go along with the government dictating how we handle our finances. I don't want to get married, ever. Edit: I have talked to her about all this. I also want to hear other opinions. Thanks! Edit 2: Her view on marriage changes a lot. This can make the math of computing distances simpler for humans and computers. For example, if you had a map of the continental US, you might set the false origin to a point about 500 miles west of Cabo San Lucas in order to ensure all the longitude values were positive.

His name and face flickered up on the screen only after it had started buzzing. I looked over from my computer screen and dully, mild shock registered in my brain. It was 4:00 pm and I was still working. I had not looked at the time all day. The sun had long left the office and darkness was starting to settle in. I had been trying to get through my workload for the day. I was struggling to keep up with it, not just because of my family obligations but also because of my own perfectionist tendencies. I needed to do this and I needed to do it right. I was wondering what the message was about. I had not seen him in over two years. It was odd to get a call from him. I pressed the receive button. "Hey, are you there?" I heard his voice, somewhat jarring, but familiar. I was not sure how to respond. I said, "Yes, I am here." "Hey, how are you? How's life? What's up? What's new?" he began. "I am good. I am fine. Same old, same old. I work. I take care of my kids," I began. He responded, "I am doing well. I just got a new job. I am working for...." And then he went on to tell me his life's story. I listened. His life sounded good. He sounded good. He was not angry with me. In fact, he was congratulating me on my new job. He was offering me help. "So, I saw your blog. I read it. I see you are back at work," he began. "Yes. Yes, I am," I responded. "So, what exactly are you doing?" he asked. I told him. And then I told him the story of how I ended up at that job. And then I told him why I needed to get back to work. "You know, I will help you if you need me. If you need any help, you can call me," he said. I was happy that he offered his help. I was surprised. I was wondering if he would be happy to help me or if he would be upset. He told me, "I hope you are doing well. We are good. I am happy. We are doing great. I am taking care of the kids. I am taking care of my family. I am doing everything I need to do. I am taking care of them. They are with me. They are happy. They are doing well. I am going to take care of them." I was thinking of his life as he was saying all this. Then he asked, "What about you? Are you happy?" I said, "I am good. I am happy." He said, "I just hope you are not missing your children, you know? I hope you are not missing your children." I said, "No, I am not missing them." I thought I had missed them so much and I was so depressed and sad at the beginning. But, now that I have been back at work for a couple of months, I realized that I am not missing them. I miss them, but I do not miss them as much as I thought I would. I thought it was great that he was taking care of the kids. I did not want to be the primary caretaker of the kids. I never wanted to be the primary caretaker of the kids. I wanted to be the working parent. I wanted to be the one with the career. I wanted to be the one who was out in the world. I wanted to be the one who went out every day, who was independent, who earned money, who felt useful. But, I was not expecting him to actually do it. I thought he would be resentful. I thought he would be angry with me. I thought he would try to get back at me. I thought he would try to hurt me. I thought he would try to punish me. I thought he would do anything and everything in his power to punish me for taking the kids away from him. I thought he would do anything and everything in his power to make sure that I was miserable. But, that was not what was happening. And that was why I was surprised by his call. I was not expecting it. I was not expecting anything from him. I was not expecting him to be nice. I was not expecting him to be friendly. I was not expecting him to be kind. This research explores automated poetry generation using deep learning techniques. By training a system—specifically, a refined version of GPT-2—on a collection of poems, it learns to mimic poetic styles. Our method builds upon existing approaches by incorporating emotional expression and “dream poetry,” which aims to evoke feelings and utilize surreal imagery. The resulting poems successfully triggered sadness and joy in readers approximately 87.5% and 85% of the time, respectively. Furthermore, the model’s dream-inspired verses achieved scores of at least 3.2 on a Likert scale, as assessed through human evaluation and supported by Coh-Metrix quality measurements.

The degree distribution is an important characteristic of complex networks. In many data analysis applications, the networks should be represented as fixed-length feature vectors and therefore the feature extraction from the degree distribution is a necessary step. Moreover, many applications need a similarity function for comparison of complex networks based on their degree distributions. Such a similarity measure has many applications including classification and clustering of network instances, evaluation of network sampling methods, anomaly detection, and study of epidemic dynamics. The existing methods are unable to effectively capture the similarity of degree distributions, particularly when the corresponding networks have different sizes. Based on our observations about the structure of the degree distributions in networks over time, we propose a feature extraction and a similarity function for the degree distributions in complex networks. We propose to calculate the feature values based on the mean and standard deviation of the node degrees in order to decrease the effect of the network size on the extracted features. The proposed method is evaluated using different artificial and real network datasets, and it outperforms the state of the art methods with respect to the accuracy of the distance function and the effectiveness of the extracted features.

It was the middle of the night, and I was sound asleep. The only noise in the house was the soft snores coming from my dog asleep on the end of my bed. Suddenly, my iPhone started to ring, and I bolted upright. I looked at the caller ID, and my heart skipped a beat when I saw the name: my grandmother, who had passed away just three days ago. I hesitated for a moment, not sure if I wanted to answer or if I even could answer. I took a deep breath and swiped to answer the call. My grandmother's face appeared on the screen, and for a moment, I forgot that she was gone. "Hello?" I said, trying to keep the fear out of my voice. "Hello, dear," my grandmother said, her voice soft and comforting as ever. "I'm sorry to bother you in the middle of the night, but I need to talk to you." I was frozen, unsure of what to do or say. Was this some kind of cruel joke, or was I really seeing and hearing my grandmother despite her passing? But as we continued to talk, my doubts faded, and the conversation flowed as naturally as it had when she was alive. We talked about everything from the weather to family news to our favorite memories together. It was like no time had passed at all, and I felt like I was talking to her in person. Eventually, my grandmother said she had to go, and I realized that the sun was starting to come up. I hung up the call, still in disbelief over what had just happened. The next morning, I called my mother and told her what had happened. She was skeptical at first, but when I told her the details of our conversation, she became teary-eyed and told me that she believed my grandmother's spirit had reached out to me. I knew that I may never be able to fully explain what had happened, but in that moment, I felt grateful to have had one more conversation with my beloved grandmother.

Prime Minister David Cameron expressed condolences to the families, and Labour leader Ed Miliband highlighted the brave sacrifices of the armed forces. The crash site, near the Pakistani border, has also fueled speculation about possible external factors.

In 1881, Tesla moved to Budapest to work under Ferenc Puskas at a telegraph company, the Budapest Telephone Exchange. Upon arrival, Tesla realized that the company, then under construction, was using inefficient direct current (DC) dynamos. He proposed an alternating current (AC) system that would be more efficient and cost-effective, but was rejected by Puskas who favored the existing DC system. Tesla then resigned from the company, but continued to consult for them for a short time. In 1882, he moved to Paris, where he worked for two years as an electrical engineer at the Continental Edison Company. In 1884, Tesla moved to New York City, where he worked until his death in 1943. During this period, Tesla designed and built a number of revolutionary AC motors and generators, conducted experiments with new forms of energy production, and developed several patents related to radio and wireless communication. He also founded the Tesla Electric Light Manufacturing Company in 1886, which later became the Tesla Coil Company. His inventions revolutionized the way electricity was used and distributed around the world.

Netflix has bought Scanline, a major player in the special effects industry. Scanline has worked on several large productions, such as Game of Thrones, Godzilla vs. King Kong, and Justice League Dark. It's an excellent acquisition for Netflix to make given its heavy investment into its own visual effects efforts, both indie projects like The Witcher, as well as blockbuster films that pump out tens of millions of dollars' worth of VFX shots each year (see: Thor 4). What does this mean? Well, it means Netflix is building up capabilities to do their own CG production work at scale - something they've already been doing with smaller acquisitions of companies like Storyboard Films or Pixomondo - but in the critical realm where other studios flounder (e.g., Avengers: Endgame), Scanline should bolster them.

To be 80-5 and give away a 200-run lead is a problem in any Test, let alone one where you know the pitch is going to get more difficult to bat on later in the match. However, for as tricky as the surface became - and some deliveries did do a lot - there were too many dismissals in England's second innings in particular that were not down to the pitch. The tourists were shown the way initially by Ben Stokes and Jonny Bairstow in the first innings, then by opening pair Alastair Cook and Haseeb Hameed in the second. Yet, English collapses - Michael Vaughan has referred to a "little disease" when panic appears to set in - were common. Four wickets for 29 runs and then four wickets for 30 runs in the first innings, eight wickets for 68 runs on the final day. It ultimately comes down to a batsman's state of mind. When you get a difficult delivery or the ball misbehaves, it can be very hard to put that out of your thoughts, but that is what the very best are able to do. The ability to clear your mind and focus on the next delivery is a skill my Test Match Special colleague Geoffrey Boycott speaks of so often. Can they keep their chins up if they lose the toss? Can they be positive without being reckless? Can they remember that they have played some good cricket? Do they believe that they can beat India? The answers to those questions are not straightforward because India is such a difficult place to tour. We knew from the start that playing five matches here straight after two in Bangladesh was going to be difficult in terms of managing morale and keeping spirits high. England do not have to look too far into the past for inspiration. They came from behind to win here four years ago. Going further into the past, the 1984-85 tour led by David Gower that I was part of was a real success because the togetherness of the team helped us overcame everything that was thrown at us. Indira Gandhi, the prime minister, was assassinated hours after the touring party arrived. The UK's deputy high commissioner Percy Norris later suffered the same fate, a day after hosting a reception for the England team. England stayed out there despite fears the tour would be cancelled, then lost the first Test because of some questionable umpiring. Yet, England came back to win that series 2-1 and that is the mindset that the class of 2016 have to adopt. If they can, India can be beaten because we have already seen that these are two evenly matched sides. The hosts' only advantage is they have greater experience playing in these conditions. Off-spinner Ravichandran Ashwin, the world's leading Test wicket-taker this year, does not look too frightening when conditions are not in his favour. The same can be said for his partner in crime Ravindra Jadeja. These are bowlers that can be handled. India also have plenty of batsmen yet to register runs. Openers KL Rahul and Murali Vijay both need a score, as do Ajinkya Rahane and wicketkeeper Wriddhiman Saha. Yes, Cheteshwar Pujara is in good form and captain Virat Kohli was in stellar touch in Visakhapatnam - he scored 248 runs and the winning margin was 246, so imagine the boon it would be for England if they can remove him cheaply. Not that the tourists do not have personnel issues of their own. Ben Duckett, who has made only 18 runs in three innings, looks very unlikely to play in the third Test in Mohali. England got into a muddle by not opening the batting with Hameed in Bangladesh and now both Gary Ballance and Duckett have failed at number four. The next available option appears to be Jos Buttler, one of the most exciting limited-overs players in the world. Is he the answer in the top order of a Test line-up against the spinning ball? We just do not know. Add to that the fact Buttler has played only one first-class match in the past year and there will be a lot of pressure on him if he is chosen to play in the next Test. Anyone saying with certainty that Buttler is the cavalry to solve England's problems is making a very big statement. Spinner Zafar Ansari is another who looks set to miss out on playing in the third Test. He may well have been left out anyway in order for England to play a fourth pace bowler, but he had a poor time with both ball and bat in Visakhapatnam. Those two aside, the other players that England have used in this series will all feel good. Cook, Hameed, Joe Root, Moeen Ali, Stokes and Bairstow have all made runs. Adil Rashid is really looking the part as a Test spin bowler, James Anderson has made an excellent return from injury and Chris Woakes will be raring to go after being rested for the second Test. The only question England will have is over the fitness of Stuart Broad, who returned his best bowling figures in India with a strained tendon in his foot. At 6 AM, a mighty thud shook my house, cutting short the nice dream I was having in which some higher-order being was the one responsible for the temperature. I had dropped to the floor and scrambled fully beneath my bed before realizing it wasn't an earthquake: it was even worse. Damnit, how had they found me again? From outside, the speakers began to blast their usual script. "Every thirty seconds, a polar bear dies from heatstroke." For what little it was worth, the climate change activists were the least obnoxious of all the groups that regularly came to pester me. I peered out my front window: sure enough, they had erected their projector screen and begun to play the dying baby polar bear slide show I had seen at least a hundred times already. They could've at least made a new one: I had seen Perry and Popo and Patrick die so many times that it was beginning to lose its emotional impact. "Hey, missy!" A man in a suit had noticed me looking through my curtains and stormed up to my window. "You better lower the temperature this instant, or you'll be sorry when your heating breaks!" The radiator sales industry was on the opposite end of the annoyance spectrum; they tended to resort to scare tactics to try and sway my mood. Recently, they had threatened to impose a nationwide boycott on selling to me if I didn't lower the temperature in time for winter. In my mind, it was a dubious strategy: first of all, I didn't even need a radiator if I maintained the warmth outside, and second of all, their ham-fisted attempts to cow me made me angrier than afraid, thus keeping the temperature high. Their plans were miraculously not the worst of the bunch: North Face had threatened to somehow render all my clothing choices fashionably obsolete if I didn't comply with their demands for cooler temperatures. "Go blow hot air somewhere else," I shouted back at him. "Yeah, if you need someone to vent to, we're here for you." Another man approached him from across my front yard. Judging from his uniform, he was a member of the nationwide union of air conditioning repairmen. "Don't listen to these people, girl. Just keep trucking; we got your back." A woman with an ice cream cone hat joined. I was naturally predisposed to supporting the groups who strove to make me happy - the farmers, the convertible manufacturers, the beachwear industry - even though I knew most of them didn't give two shits about my actual feelings; they just wanted to profit off the warm weather. In the past, some assholes even had the bright idea of trying to make me angry in order to keep the temperature high, under the impression that it was easier than making me happy or something. Even after three years, I can still remember that annoying sun screen commercial that played 247 on the lawn of my third house. They hadn't stopped until I had gotten so angry that their equipment melted. "She's killing our jobs!" A spokesman from the hot cocoa industry threw himself onto the grass in what I can only assume was an attempt to elicit my sympathy. "The ice caps are melting day by day," the loudspeaker droned. Perhaps it was time to move again. It had only been a week, so most of my belongings were still packed in my boxes. At this point, was it worth bothering with even a semi-permanent residence? They would find me again, and they would set up their speakers and projectors and one-act-plays to try and sway my emotions. Settling down would never be a realistic option. As I slumped against the wall, a chill overtook me, and a cheer resounded from outside my window. "We did it!"

First of all your muscles can only pull and can't push. This is why we have opposing muscles (e.g. your bicep pulls [contracts] to pull your forearm in and your tricep pulls [contracts] to pull your forearm out). Your nerves conduct electricity. That is how your brain communicates with your muscles to tell them to contract or relax. To detect if your muscle is contracted or relaxed there is bundle of nerves called the muscle spindle located in the muscle. When the patellar ligament is struck it causes the thigh muscle spindle to stretch which causes electricity to travel through your nerves. This electricity is indicating that your muscle is stretched out (i.e. relaxed and not contracted). Obviously you can consciously bend and straighten your knee, but to be able to balance and walk there is also some subconscious behaviour that is occurring without you realizing it. When the thigh muscle spindle registers that the thigh muscle is relaxed it triggers an automatic tightening of it to ensure you don't fall over if you are standing. This is being artificially triggered by the reflex hammer.

Four of those on board, three soldiers and an airman, were stationed at RAF Odiham in Hampshire. The fifth, an Army reservist, was based in London. The Ministry of Defence said the crash near Kandahar air base appeared to have been a "tragic accident." It represents the third single biggest loss of life of British troops in Afghanistan since the conflict began. The families of all five servicemen have been told. Three of the soldiers on board the helicopter were from the Army Air Corps, based at RAF Odiham in Hampshire, the MoD said late on Saturday. A fourth member of the crew was serving with the Royal Air Force and was also based at Odiham, while the fifth man was an Army reservist from 3 Military Intelligence Battalion, in London. Maj Gen Richard Felton, Commander Joint Helicopter Command, said: "It is with great sadness that we must confirm that five UK service personnel have been killed in this incident which, at this early stage, would appear to have been a tragic accident. "Events like this, whilst mercifully rare, remind us of the risks our personnel face in their work in Afghanistan as we approach the conclusion of the combat mission later this year. "Our thoughts are with the families and loved ones of those who have lost their lives." Prime Minister David Cameron said his "heart goes out to the families and friends of those killed in this terrible tragedy." Labour leader Ed Miliband said it was "tragic and poignant reminder of the sacrifices made by our armed forces in serving our country with bravery and distinction." It is the first fatal accident involving a UK military helicopter in Afghanistan since the conflict began in 2001. BBC defence correspondent Caroline Wyatt said sources had suggested the cause of the crash may have been "technical problems" on board the helicopter, despite claims by the Taliban that its fighters had shot it down. She said the location of the crash - close to the border with Pakistan - has also led to speculation that the helicopter could have been taking part in a special forces mission. It is understood the helicopter was a Westland Lynx Mk 9. A Ministry of Defence spokesman said: "We can confirm that a UK helicopter crashed in southern Afghanistan today. "The incident is under investigation and it would be inappropriate to comment further until families have been notified." The crash is understood to have happened around 30 miles from the Pakistan border, near Kandahar air base in the Takhta Pul district. The deaths bring the number of British forces killed in the conflict in Afghanistan to 453. The fatal crash comes after a Nimrod surveillance aircraft exploded in mid-air while supporting Nato ground operations near Kandahar, killing all 14 servicemen on board, in September 2006. This incident remains the biggest single loss of UK life at one time in Afghanistan. In 2012, six British soldiers were killed when a Warrior armoured fighting vehicle in Kandahar province was hit by an explosion. The International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) coalition of international forces said it was still in the process of reviewing the circumstances of Saturday's helicopter crash. "Our thoughts and prayers go out to the family and friends affected by this tragic event," it said in a statement. Defence analyst Paul Beaver said all the indications are that the crash involved a Lynx helicopter, which he said has an "exceptional record." He said the light utility helicopter is likely to have been operating in "fairly mountainous areas," or in "challenging" terrain. "The key now will be looking at the weather," Mr Beaver told the BBC. "If enemy action is not suspected, which is what the MoD is saying, then you have to look at whether this might well be weather-related." The crash brings the total number of international troops killed in Afghanistan in April to seven. It comes after the last major helicopter crash took place in December last year, when seven Americans and four Afghans died. In August 2011, the Taliban shot down an American Chinook near Kabul, killing 30 Americans and eight Afghans in the deadliest single incident for US troops since the war began. Herbivores can occasionally eliminate their food source, though it’s rare. Certain animals, such as zooplankton feeding on single-celled algae, consume their prey entirely. However, many grazers only take small portions of plants, and livestock typically remove only surface vegetation, enabling regrowth. Kelp forests regularly experience grazing, yet the blades continually regenerate from their bases to withstand this pressure. Similarly, animals themselves can be consumed – for example, mosquitoes feed on hosts momentarily to acquire protein for their young, and starfish regenerate lost limbs.

Low engine revolutions cause the car to stall, and there’s a specific RPM range where the engine produces maximum power for each gallon of fuel consumed; exceeding or falling outside this range reduces performance. Gears exist because wheels rotate slowly at lower speeds and quickly at higher speeds, whereas engines require relatively constant rotation regardless of speed. They act as a bridge between the wheels and the engine. Think of a bicycle – using a heavy gear makes it incredibly difficult to gain momentum. This limitation prevents prolonged use of certain gears in a vehicle. Each gear corresponds to a particular speed range, and using the highest gear consistently would prevent starting from a standstill.

There's so few of us now. Monica likes to call it the "exodus." I prefer not to talk about it, but I think "abandoning" is a better term for what happened to our poor little planet, because that's exactly what what happened. They abandoned us. Left us to burn in the expanding corpse of our celestial anchor. The entire affair began as a trickle. The media actually made a considerable amount of noise about the first few "migrations." The prospect of heading out into the reaches of deep space was tantalizing, seducing in the way that only real danger can be. It was a long trip to Gliese 581 (at least thirty years, even with the most advanced propulsion systems humanity could muster), and the perils of interstellar travel had never been tested with ships holding ten, fifty, 100, 200, 500 people on them before. Most of us stayed on Earth, with our feet planted firmly in the ground, wondering when the new fad would die out, when people would realize that braving 22 light-years of empty space in a hibernation pod wasn't quite as heroic as it sounded. And yet, despite what seemed to us to be sheer lunacy, the trickle never ebbed. One ship every year became two, twenty-person cruisers became 200-person behemoth. And when the penny dropped and the public realized the journeys were about escaping a stellar apocalypse rather than an inflated sense of Manifest Destiny, the trickle exploded into an outpouring, every family with two pennies to rub together saving up to buy a ticket off this rock. Earth's population was decreasing daily, and no amount of coercing or pleading could stop Earth's society from slowly sucking itself dry, ejecting its workforce one by one irrecoverably into the abyss until Earth's governments gave in, and started making plans for what was named the "Migration." I've already told you what I think of that sort of name for it. January 13, 2257. 5:45 PM, GMT. The auto-post deposited a crisp, snow-white envelope into the mail slot of every house in the world that still had occupants. Assignments. Locations and times to board the myriad ant-like shuttles that would ferry the remainder of humanity to the hulking monstrosity of an interstellar craft that orbited just outside of Earth's gravity well. Like it or not, humankind was leaving the Earth for good, and it was happening by the end of the month. We'd stayed behind because we couldn't bear to leave the trees behind. It's funny, it sounds so trivial in hindsight, but we had spent the better part of the last 10 years nurturing that grove, and we'd be damned if we were going to abandon it at the drop of a hat. I suppose one might expect that environmentalists would be reluctant to leave the planet they fought so hard for in our cosmic rear-view mirrors, but it wasn't the planet we were reluctant to leave behind (because what in the hell could the seven of us do, when the rest of our species was fleeing with their tails between their legs?). No, it was the trees. We just couldn't bring ourselves to leave behind that lovely little grove we'd devoted so much to. Eventually, though, there was no more delaying. Not much else to do but run when the fist of God is bearing down on you. The big day was all about timetables. At 9:00 sharp, be out the door and en route to your launch site. Arrive no later than 10:00. Have everything you're taking with you compressed and compartmentalized, disassembled and demolecularized for transport. Liftoff is at no later than 11:00, because the starliner goes to warp at 3:00. Over and over, the importance of timeliness was stressed. Well, we arrive at the launch site, and there's a delay. Mechanical issues. Some of the microcircuitry shorted, and there's not enough thrust for all of us. They can't lift off with the scheduled fifty people, they need about ten or so to stay on the ground to be able to make it off the launchpad, but don't worry, they'll send a replacement shuttle for us as soon as they could. Cynthia was having a bit of an emotional moment, and she volunteered us to wait, she said she just wanted one last breath of fresh air before being sealed in a pod for three decades. We all got out of our seats, along with three other poor shmucks, and watched the shuttle's exhaust slowly disappear into the afternoon sky. We waited at that launchpad so diligently. After thirty minutes, we were just a little annoyed at the wait, at the lack of communication through the station's transponder. After two hours, some of us were getting a tad anxious. Not much time to get to the starliner and get settled in for warp, they were saying. And through it all, we just kept waiting, the minutes dripping agonizingly by, until the fear became a certainty, and the starliner orbiting above our heads engaged its thrusters, slowly gliding off over the horizon. To this day, I'm not sure what exactly happened. I suppose they just had to stick to their goddamn timetables. Cynthia just about drowned herself in tears and mucus, crying and apologizing for what had happened. I swear Jeff could have killed her then and there, if we hadn't stopped him. I couldn't say I blamed him, though. Ten of us, alone on the wide, empty Earth, food rotting on shelves and in the fields, and not enough power left in the grid to power a flashlight. It's been almost a year since that day, and every one of the six deaths we've had have been suicides. I spend every day wondering if I can hold out long enough to be number eight.

My disagreement with a friend who considers himself a wine connoisseur led me to investigate. Research revealed numerous articles demonstrating how easily external factors influence perceptions of wine characteristics. While further studies exist, these initial findings suggest a lack of robust evidence proving people reliably distinguish between different wines. I contend that perceived differences are likely due to minor variations that are undetectable, or perhaps influenced by preconceived notions about wine flavors. It’s also possible our sensory systems aren't precise enough to consistently identify nuanced tastes – fruity, nutty, etc. Essentially, I believe we overestimate our ability to discern subtle differences in wine. Many assume we can, but this is largely a subjective phenomenon driven by expectation, akin to the placebo effect. I apologize for my delayed response; I’m focusing on the specific issue of flavor differentiation rather than quality judgments. Ultimately, I simply don't believe our tongues and brains possess the capacity to systematically analyze and categorize wine tastes effectively.  Wines might vary subtly, yet we struggle to consciously recall and dissect their individual components.

Think of it like this: Your phone’s Wi-Fi connects directly to your home router, needing minimal effort to communicate. However, 3G relies on distant cell towers, requiring your phone to transmit signals over long distances, consuming significant battery power. Furthermore, Wi-Fi connections remain stable at home, unlike 3G, which frequently drops out and requires constant reconnection while traveling. Continuously searching for a weak signal rapidly drains the battery.  These experts have described the situation, and I’ll add that 4G significantly improves battery life compared to 3G. It seems counterintuitive; Wi-Fi drains my Samsung Galaxy S2 quickly, but 3G can operate for extended periods with minimal battery loss. A related question arises: why does my battery deplete faster on 3G than on LTE? My research indicates the main factor isn’t simply that 3G transmits louder – usually, phones are primarily receiving data rather than sending it. Both Wi-Fi and 3G networks periodically check for incoming messages, but Wi-Fi scans roughly ten times per second, while 3G checks only once or twice during “idle” periods. When a message arrives, the phone intensifies its listening, stopping only after a period of silence. Because Wi-Fi constantly monitors even when idle, brief interruptions mean quick rechecks. Conversely, with 3G, a pause in transmission may result in a delay of up to a second before resuming monitoring.

After a five-year approval process, the humble Yakka Skink - a secretive lizard known to hide under rocks and inside hollow logs - and the Ornamental Snake brought to a halt a A16bn (12bn; PS8bn) mine, rail and port project proposed for the Galilee Basin in Queensland. The two reptiles are among Australia's most threatened species. Because the federal environment minister failed to take into account what the mine could mean for their habitat, his earlier approval for the mine was overturned by the Federal Court of Australia. The mine may still go ahead but the delay is the latest chapter in a long history of Australian flora and fauna causing grief to developers. Back in 1995, one of the last known colonies of the endangered Green and Gold Bell frog delayed the construction of a multi-million dollar residential development in inner-city Sydney. A few years later, the frogs were found frolicking in an abandoned brick pit where authorities had planned to build a tennis court for the Sydney 2000 Olympic Games. The courts were built elsewhere while the frogs got a specially built habitat. Now they are in the way of a key major road project in Sydney. In the mid 2000s, a new species of flowering shrub was discovered in the Lower Hunter Valley, north of Sydney. Named Persoonia pauciflora, botanists were excited to discover it grew nowhere else in the world. Unfortunately, it was growing on the site of a proposed housing development. When word got around, someone ripped out 300 of the last 500 of these rare plants. The culprit was never found. The discovery of a threatened or new species can cause havoc for developers, delaying or even putting an end to a project. What overturned the Queensland mine's approval? A small conservation group in Mackay, Queensland, challenged the environment minister's decision to approve the mine on a number of legal bases, including: Approved Conservation Advices are scientific and legal documents that explain the conservation requirements of species to avoid their extinction. It was this last point that convinced the court to overturn the minister's approval. In the state of Victoria, the Orange-bellied Parrot was centre stage in a long-running saga about whether a wind farm could be built in South Gippsland. The federal environment minister banned the 52-turbine project in 2006, on advice that turbine blades posed a small risk to the critically endangered bird. The minister eventually reversed his own decision and the wind farm is going ahead. In the case of Indian company Adani's giant coal mine in Queensland, environmentalists and scientists are worried about more than threats to reptiles. Dredging associated with an expansion of port facilities for the mine poses a huge risk to the Great Barrier Reef; exports would further entrench the world's reliance on carbon polluting fossil fuels; and the mine could threaten artesian water. The Department of the Environment on Wednesday said reconsideration of the project did not require revisiting the entire approval process. New approval documentation could be ready within eight weeks. Adani described the court decision as simply a "technical legal error." But environmentalists say protecting endangered species is vital work. "To describe an endangered species as a technicality and groundwater as a technicality is in line with Adani's environmental record around the world, which is appalling," said Geoff Cousins, president of the Australian Conservation Foundation. "The government should simply strike this project down."

Put simply, a segmentation fault occurs when a program tries to read or write to a location in memory that it is not allowed to. When the operating system detects a program trying to do this, it kills the program. A segmentation fault almost always means there is a bug in the program's code - a well written program should never attempt an invalid memory access. The trace is supposed to help indicate what part of the program's code caused the segmentation fault, and may not mean much to anyone except the program's developers. You may want to report the error to them.

Under the early courts, when military conscription had been centrally controlled, military affairs had been taken out of the hands of the provincial aristocracy. But as the system broke down after 792, local power holders again became the primary source of military strength. The re-establishment of an efficient military system was made gradually through a process of trial-and-error. At that time the imperial court did not possess an army but rather relied on an organization of professional warriors composed mainly of oryoshi, which were appointed to an individual province and tsuibushi, which were appointed over imperial circuits or for specific tasks. This gave rise to the Japanese military class. Nonetheless final authority rested with the imperial court.

Light cascaded through the blinds of the first floor window of his parents home, waking him gently. Simon had been long awaiting this day; the day he'd learn his talent. Today was the day of his birthday, the day he'd be taken to the capital of his country, to be taught how to use his gift. He'd been born with a gift. Unlike his parents, who had been born with the talents of music and art, Simon had been born with the gift of healing. He was a useful gift, if not the most useful. The window was open, letting the warm summer air in. The heat would get unbearable later on in the day, but for now, it was a pleasant temperature. Simon pushed the covers off his body, letting his feet touch the wooden floor. He took a deep breath, as if readying himself for something big, which he was. He took a quick look at his reflection in the mirror on the wardrobe before grabbing his clothes for the day and walking into the bathroom. It was his birthday, so he got to skip breakfast. He showered and dressed in a simple black outfit, his hair in a neat ponytail. Simon grabbed a piece of bread, buttered it, and ate it as he walked down the stairs, towards the front door. His mother was standing outside, waiting. "Good morning, Simon." He nodded. "Mother." His mother was dressed in a simple black dress, with a thin jacket over the top. She looked beautiful, and Simon wished he could see her smile, but she was still grieving. "Come on, your father and brother are waiting for us." Simon followed his mother out of the house, and into a car. His father and brother were waiting for him in the back seat. His father was wearing a white shirt and blue jeans, and his brother was wearing a black jacket over a red shirt. They were both smiling, looking like they'd slept well. The car pulled away, and Simon looked out of the window, watching the houses pass by. "So, this is going to be a long ride. What shall we talk about?" His father asked. "Well, I don't know. You want to talk about the weather?" Simon joked. "Simon, you have a talent. You don't have to be so down about it." His father laughed. "I know, but it's not like I can control the weather. There are some people who can do that." "You can do something incredible! You can save people's lives!" "I'm just saying it's not the best talent." "It is if you're the one who needs to be saved." His mother chimed in. Simon didn't know what to say to that, so he turned to his brother, who was staring out of the window. "What's your talent, Lucas?" "I'm a telepath." Simon's eyebrows rose. "You're a telepath?" "Yes. I can hear thoughts, and communicate with people without saying a word." "That's pretty cool." Simon said. "It comes in handy when you're trying to tell your parents something without them knowing." Lucas joked. "So, you heard my thoughts?" Lucas shrugged. "Not unless I try." "What about you, father? There are a number of reasons why trying to save the pandas is not a waste of time, money, and resources. For one, pandas are a keystone species in their native habitat, meaning that their extinction would likely cause a ripple effect that would lead to the decline or extinction of other plant and animal species. Additionally, pandas are a major tourist attraction, which brings much needed revenue to local economies. Finally, as one of the world's most iconic and beloved animals, the extinction of the panda would be a significant loss to both the natural world and to humanity as a whole.

Sequence sets are prevalent across numerous disciplines, exemplified by protein structure prediction where a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) serves as input to deduce structural details. Current methods generally utilize MSAs indirectly, converting them into position-specific scoring matrices (PSSMs) – representations of amino acid frequency within each column. While PSSMs capture column-level patterns, they largely ignore the unique characteristics of individual sequences. A key limitation stems from the fact that an MSA is fundamentally an unordered sequence collection, unlike a matrix; swapping sequences doesn't alter the entire alignment. Images, conversely, present data as matrices because row swaps are meaningless. Consequently, conventional deep learning models for images aren’t suitable for sequence sets. To address this, we introduce Seq-SetNet, a new deep neural network architecture specifically designed for sequence set processing. It utilizes a symmetric function module to incorporate features from prior layers, making it insensitive to sequence ordering within the MSA. This allows for direct and complete exploitation of each protein component. Evaluations for secondary structure prediction using established benchmarks demonstrate that Seq-SetNet surpasses current leading techniques by 3.6% in precision, highlighting its effectiveness and potential applicability to diverse areas like natural language processing.

This time the poll was held under a new constitution, designed to prevent a repeat of that violence when more than 1,000 people died when supporters of rival candidates clashed. They have been choosing a president, members of parliament and senators, the new posts of county governors and members of county assemblies. The presidential contest is seen as a two-horse race between Prime Minister Raila Odinga against Deputy Prime Minister Uhuru Kenyatta. BBC correspondents around the country sum up how the voting went. The queues in some places stretched for more than a kilometre, as voters in Kibera stood patiently in line. The neighbourhood is one of Nairobi's largest slums. It is the constituency of Raila Odinga, one of the favourites for the presidential contest and the scene of some of the worst violence following the last election in 2007. Today, many had arrived before dawn, waiting patiently in line, sometimes for hours. Voters cast their ballots into colour-coded boxes - six each - for a variety of different representatives, local and national. The memories of five years ago are still fresh and, as the campaign drew to a close, a sense of apprehension was palpable. Police talked of conspiracies to cause chaos and warned that violence would be met in kind. But, in Kibera at least, as the sun grew hotter and the umbrellas came out, the mood was up-beat. "Peace, peace," one crowd shouted as a truck of paramilitary police trundled past. We came across a man with dreadlocks and a pot of white paint. His message, "Peace wanted alive," can be seen daubed on walls and roads around the neighbourhood. The real test of peace, though, is likely to come once all the ballots have been cast, and the results start coming in. As the sun begins to set, the heat is easing and some polling stations are still open after the official closing time of 17:00, with queues of people determined to cast their vote. Tensions have been running high in this insecure and arid region near the Somali border and there has been a heavy security presence at the polling stations - with between five and 10 armed police officers on guard. On Sunday night one people died in an explosion and another person was shot dead in what is believed to be election-related violence. Some people began queuing at 05:00 - an hour before the polls opened. But there has been frustration in the long queues, with some buying water to pour over their heads to cool themselves down and others sitting under umbrellas. The biometric voter ID systems have not worked at the polling stations in this north-eastern town so electoral officials have had to resort to the manual voters registers. The computerised fingerprint and facial identification was introduced after the last election to prevent fraud. This slowed the whole process down, as has the fact that about 60 of voters have needed assistance to cast their ballot as they are illiterate. One woman with a baby on her back told me that after waiting until she got to the front of the queue, she found her name was not on the roll, even though she had a voter registration card. Hundreds of people ended up giving up. One man who could not find his name after lining up in three queues over 12 hours told me he was going home without voting. In the centre of Mombasa many people lined up from 05:00 to ensure their place in the queue and avoid the sweltering temperatures that characterise the coast. A cluster of white gazebos went some way to protect the early voters from the sun and the six colour-coded ballot boxes that sheltered beneath. Nearly half a million voters are registered in Kenya's second city, with another half a million making up the surrounding counties. This is historically "opposition" territory but under the complex arithmetic of the presidential vote, the candidates cannot afford to ignore this part of the country. Many voters queuing patiently described it as an "historic day" - the first time Kenyans are voting under a new constitution. But further along the coast, election day was marred by technical hitches and sporadic violence in a handful of flashpoints. Faulty biometric voting kits caused delays in Mombasa West. In Changamwe, half an hour's drive from the city, four police officers were hacked to death with machetes by a gang, who the authorities claim were members of the separatist Mombasa Revolutionary Council (MRC). The group had urged voters to boycott the polls in protest at what they see as the marginalisation of Mombasa, but few seemed to heed that call. The crowds outside Changamwe's main polling station had swollen to several hundred by midafternoon: Women with their babies strapped to their backs and men with beads of sweat running down their brow, seemingly undeterred by the attack that took place shortly before polls opened. Many people in the crowd outside Changamwe Social Hall which was turned into the local polling station seemed unconvinced that the group was to blame. Kenya has had a long history of violent elections and areas deemed to be opposition strongholds like this, are used to what people describe as "powerful forces" seeking to scare people away from the polls. But this time there is a palpable determination to prove to the world that Kenya is on a new democratic path. A whistle stop tour by the new Inspector General of police to the "scene of the crime" helped to provide reassurance in what has otherwise been a peaceful poll. Too busy tweeting to vote?
