(basically your boot disk option, makes it's own small single purpose OS which isn't bound by the OSes rules of privileges and rank),In modern operating systems, such as various linux distros, and windows 7 and 8, you generally have two different kinds of user rights. You have your everyday user, which is the one you log on with. This log on restricts what you are able to change on your computer with respect to installing programs and messing around with configuration settings. You are allowed to mess things up, particularly in various linuxy OS's, but what you mess up only affects your particular user logon. Other people using the same computer are shielded from your mess ups and happily zoom along. The other kind of user has more power. In the windows world, this type of user is usually known as a "system administrator." When you are able to log on in the role of a system administrator onto a Windows machine, you pretty much are like god. You can do as you please, up to and including rendering the system inoperative as a result of doing something stupid. In the linux world, the equivalence of the system administrator is called "root." It's just a name. Like a windows system administrator, the "root" user wields unlimited power once he logs on to a machine. The twist is this: normally, when you log on to a remote linux server, you use your own - non root - user credentials to establish contact, and then when you want to do some system administration on the remote system you "become root" by issuing the "su (superuser primary shell) command. This prompts you for the password of the "root" system admin and if you know it, you are good to go. The problem here is that linux allows certain autonomous programs that run as a part of the system maintenance schedule to achieve "root" status automatically in order to accomplish things. So there is a way for programs to declare themselves to have "root" provileges and access, without the need of a human typing in the root password. In theory, this cannot happen without consent of the system administrator. In practice, your mileage may vary. Root kits on linux exploit this mechanism. They somehow gain root priviledges without the benefit of some human typing in the root password, and they take it away from there. Following in the wake, attacks that show similar behaviour on windows machines are also called "root kits,'Rootkits on Windows are slightly different to rootkits on Mac or Linux. On Mac or Linux, a rootkit is some piece of software that allows unauthorized users or software to gain root (superuser) access to the computer. This lets that user or software do lots of crazy things that could affect you in harmful ways such as delete files, change settings or run malware without your knowledge. On Windows, that sort of thing isn't called a rootkit, it's called a privilege-escalation exploit. On Windows, a rootkit is something specifically designed to hide malware files on your computer, by injecting itself into critical system processes and messing with their behavior. Specifically, they tend to inject themselves into the kernel or filesystem, so that when something requests a list of files in a given folder, it can intercept the request and give a response that hides the malware files. This way, virus scanners can never detect them. Windows rootkits do require Administrator access to install and run, but often they won't use an exploit to get that access, they'll just trick you into allowing them Install this video player for FREE satellite TV! Allow or Deny," etc.) In both cases, the best way to prevent them is simple: be careful what you run. Make sure the things you download and run come from a trustworthy source. Modern operating systems always ask you before allowing a random program to gain root or administrator privileges. Don't just blindly approve the request; make sure you know what program is making the request and make sure you trust that program. Once a rootkit is installed and running, removing it will be extremely difficult.

It costs an employer money to hire an employee. They have to spend time looking for them, and then spend time training them. They also come to rely on that person (i.e., the factory worker), which can be costlier than just keeping a search going (especially if they don't pay very well). But an engineer or computer programmer is relatively easy to find and train because you basically need two things: good programming skills and a willingness to work long hours at low wages in exchange for some financial security later in life. A new grad will only do this if their prospects are bleak enough; otherwise they would probably go somewhere else where they could get better paid. Economists call these people "monetarially rational consumers of labor services." As such, it makes sense for employers to move towards "horizontal matching" when hiring. This means finding employees who aren't too expensive as individuals but are cheap collectively, i.e. raw material instead of human capital. It works like this: if everyone decides to become a machine-shop technician rather than having an engineering firm build cars themselves, nobody loses anything except maybe slightly higher prices. The same idea applies with many other professions - we may think it doesn't make much economic difference whether lawyers help each other out by publishing articles online or simply put up websites saying what kind of cases they want handled, since neither option requires any technical expertise to begin with, but there really is no reason whatsoever why lawyers should not start doing so. Note how even legal materials have improved greatly over the past decade due to website technology! And speaking of law students... Police in Australia and Europe were aware of a paedophile site called the Love Zone hidden in the so-called dark web. It was protected by passwords, encryption and specialist software. Users were totally anonymous. The images and videos there were particularly disturbing - showing the abuse of babies and very young children. Members had to post increasingly graphic material to remain on the site. There were tens of thousands of accounts. Officers with Task Force Argos in Australia knew the creator of the site used an unusual greeting - the word "hiyas." After exhaustively trawling chatrooms and forums in the open internet, they found a Facebook page of a man who used the same greeting. Although the Facebook page was fake, they identified a picture of a vehicle and that led them to a man called Shannon McCoole - a childcare worker in Adelaide. When officers went through his door, he was actually online running the site. They took detailed photographs of McCoole's hands. This is where the freckle comes in - one on his finger matched exactly one seen in many of the images of abuse. In an unprecedented move, Task Force Argos assumed McCoole's identity and took over the running of the site. Last year he was given a 35-year prison sentence. One user who stood out was Huckle - given the number of children he had access to and his aggressive attitude. Using data gleaned from the site and information Huckle had posted on social media and other open internet sites, they identified who he was and where he lived. Realising he was coming back to the UK for the Christmas holidays in 2014, they tipped off Britain's National Crime Agency. As he landed at Gatwick airport he was met by officers from the NCA's Child Exploitation and Online Protection command. On his computer and encrypted drives they found tens of thousands of obscene images and videos.

Google will keep its 200,000 full-time and contract employees working remotely until at least July 2021. Sundar Pichai, CEO of Alphabet, made the announcement last week following a meeting with the company's executive team. Google had initially planned to reopen its offices in phases starting in June, but Pichai said the company will instead extend its remote work policy due to the ongoing pandemic. He also noted that while some employees may be able to return to the office in a limited capacity, Google is still encouraging most of its staff to work from home. The decision has received mixed reactions from Google employees and commentators. Some have argued that the extended period of remote work could lead to a decrease in productivity, while others have welcomed the announcement as it provides more flexibility for workers. Regardless, Google's move shows how deeply the pandemic has impacted workplace culture. As more companies embrace remote work, it remains to be seen if this trend will continue beyond 2021.

Galileo was a strong proponent of this theory and worked to refine it. His most important contribution to astronomy was the discovery of the four largest satellites of Jupiter. Galileo thought that the Copernican model was the right one. When the Roman Inquisition judged that the Copernican model was contrary to the Bible, Galileo was forced to renounce his belief in it. It exhibits the Northern Cities Vowel Shift. The East and Northeast typically resists merging pinpen, cotcaught, marymerrymarry. As a result they have more vowel variation. A new film is reviving the story of how the 1984-85 Miners Strike brought together two very diverse sections of society, which is getting its premiere in London's West End. The strike, which lasted a year, was a bitter conflict between the Thatcher government and the trade unions that involved hundreds of thousands of miners and their families. However, amidst the gloom and desperation, one heartwarming story emerged: the unlikely alliance formed between the miners and the gay community. The film, titled "United in Adversity," delves into the story of how a group of gay and lesbian activists came together to support miners through the strike, creating a bond that would transform perceptions of both communities. It tells of how the Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners (LGSM) group raised funds and offered spiritual and practical support to miners, in spite of initial suspicion and rejection from some of them. Over time, though, they formed friendships, solidarity and respect for each other's struggles. LGSM eventually raised more than 20,000 for the miners' cause, which became a lifesaver for struggling working-class communities, as government support dwindled. The film, directed by Tom Harper, stars Bill Nighy, Imelda Staunton and Andrew Scott. It premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and was praised for its uplifting message of the power of community bonding over difference. The West End premiere is expected to draw large crowds and bring attention to the enduring need for grass-roots activism, solidarity and mutual support, as communities still grapple with socio-economic, and cultural divides. Hopefully, this movie will inspire a new generation to come together in the face of adversity and strive for a better and more connected world.

Libya's economy witnessed increasing privatization; although rejecting the socialist policies of nationalized industry advocated in The Green Book, government figures asserted that they were forging "people's socialism" rather than capitalism. Gaddafi welcomed these reforms, calling for wide-scale privatization in a March 2003 speech. In 2003, the oil industry was largely sold to private corporations, and by 2004, there was 40 billion of direct foreign investment in Libya, a sixfold rise over 2003. Sectors of Libya's population reacted against these reforms with public demonstrations, and in March 2006, revolutionary hard-liners took control of the GPC cabinet; although scaling back the pace of the changes, they did not halt them. In 2010, plans were announced that would have seen half the Libyan economy privatized over the following decade. While there was no accompanying political liberalization, with Gaddafi retaining predominant control, in March 2010, the government devolved further powers to the municipal councils. Rising numbers of reformist technocrats attained positions in the country's governance; best known was Gaddafi's son and heir apparent Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, who was openly critical of Libya's human rights record. He led a group who proposed the drafting of the new constitution, although it was never adopted, and in October 2009 was appointed to head the PSLC. Involved in encouraging tourism, Saif founded several privately run media channels in 2008, but after criticising the government they were nationalised in 2009. In October 2010, Gaddafi apologized to African leaders on behalf of Arab nations for their involvement in the African slave trade.

This “dollar” was designed to weigh 371 grains and 4/16th of a grain, using either pure silver or 416 grains (27.0 grams) of standard silver. Similarly, the “eagle” was defined as 247 and 4/8th of a grain, equating to 270 grains (17 grams) of gold, again dependent on its purity. Alexander Hamilton determined the 371-grain figure by averaging the weights of a group of worn Spanish dollars – typical Spanish dollars weighed around 377 grains, resulting in the U.S. dollar being slightly less valuable than its predecessor.

"But thankfully we keep back-ups, so we didn't lose any information." All in all, Mr Radutskyi reckons his clinic's damage tally totalled 60,000 (PS46,000). Others have been unwilling to reveal how badly they were hit. Oschadbank - one of the country's biggest lenders - was among those that declined an interview with the BBC. Even now, almost a month after the so-called NotPetya strike, some companies inside and outside the nation are still facing disruption. Ukraine's top cyber-cop disclosed that some of the nation's largest companies were still too scared to share the full scale of the fallout with his investigators. And Sergiy Demedyuk - head of Ukraine's ministry of internal affairs' cybercrime division - added he has come to believe there are aftershocks still to come since the hackers appear to have compromised their targets for some time before they pounced, and might still be sitting on data they could yet exploit. NotPetya initially appeared to be a ransomware attack, but many now suspect its blackmail demands were a cover for something more ominous. Experts who have spoken to the BBC are seemingly sure of two things: first, Ukraine was the target, and second, it was not about money. Despite denials, suspicion has fallen on Ukraine's eastern neighbour, Russia. "Cyber-attacks are just one part of Russia's wider efforts to destabilise the country," Nato's former chief civil servant Anders Fogh Rasmussen told the BBC. "In my time as secretary general we agreed that a cyber-attack could trigger Nato's mutual defence clause. "The Alliance has been assisting Ukraine especially with monitoring and investigating security incidents. However.... more support is also needed for prevention." One cybersecurity veteran has been investigating how a local software developer's program, MeDoc, came to be hijacked to spread the malware. "It wasn't just [a case of] take over MeDoc's update server and push out NotPetya," explained Nicholas Weaver from University of California, Berkeley. "Instead, they had previously compromised MeDoc, made it into a remote-control Trojan, and then they were willing to burn this asset to launch this attack," he added, referring to the fact the servers have since been confiscated by the police. "That really is huge." MeDoc's tax filing services were used by more than 400,000 customers across Ukraine, representing about 90 of its domestic firms. Although it was not mandatory for local companies to use it, by virtue of its ubiquity, it's almost as if it were. "This was gold they had, basically a control point in almost every business that does business in Ukraine," said Mr Weaver. "And they burned this resource in order to launch this destructive attack." Mr Demedyuk said his police force had concrete evidence that MeDoc was hacked a long time ago and had been used to spy on economic activity within Ukraine. "The [developers] claimed on their website that it was certificated, that it had been examined with international audit and it's 100 safe. In fact, it wasn't true," he added. One ex-US Army cyber-expert said the hackers might have felt forced to carry out their attack through fear that MeDoc's computer servers were about to slip out of their control. "If you read [security firm] ESET's report, you see that they gained and lost access repeatedly as legitimate MeDocs updates were pushed," Jon Nichols said. "It is possible that the actors just wanted to cause as much damage as they could before they lost control again." This theory is backed up by another US expert. "It's not unheard of if you think you'll lose your position to launch prematurely," said Beau Woods deputy director of the Atlantic Council's Cyber Statecraft Initiative. He added that if the perpetrators had, indeed, gathered financial data about most of Ukraine's companies, they might still find ways to cause further damage. Mr Demedyuk said that although only four police officers had been assigned to his NotPetya investigation full-time, he had about 300 people across Ukraine supporting the inquiry. Furthermore, he has met with Interpol to discuss ways to share information with other international authorities. While they try to unravel how the attack was carried out, others are preparing for follow-up cyber-assaults. In particular, the chief executive of Ukraine's state-owned energy giant Ukrenergo is concerned it will be a target. "All our life as an independent country in the last 25 years, we've been connected to the Russian power grid and they've balanced us," Vsevolod Kovalchuk told the BBC. However, he explained, an agreement his firm has struck with European electricity transmission operators to modernise Ukraine's power grid might have put the firm in Moscow's cross-hairs. It might sound like paranoia, but Ukrenergo had already been hit by two cyber-attacks prior to NotPetya. One occurred just before Christmas. "That virus worked in our local network for over one year," Mr Kovalchuk said. "It collected information and after collecting the information, the hackers put another malware specific for our northern substation and switched it off for 15 minutes. It was only a test but they tried and it was successful." Before that Ukrenergo was caught up in the infamous Black Energy attack, in December 2015. It took down half a city's power for three hours in the dead of winter. The two incidents meant the firm was already battle-hardened when it was infected by NotPetya. "A dispatcher called me and said they couldn't do anything because all of their screens had turned black and were asking for money," recalled Mr Kovalchuk. "That was at 11:02 EET [Eastern European Time], and then several minutes later, other computers were in the same situation so I called to my chief IT officer and asked what is this, is this WannaCry or something similar?" he said referring to a ransomware attack that disrupted the NHS and others in May. "We disconnected our networks, switched off our computers, and then we used our protocols from the past, using paper standards, phones and continued to operate without any computers, without databases, without any systems." This time round, the electricity grid was unharmed and power flowed uninterrupted. But the company was left without secondary functions for 10 days. For Ukraine, the most important questions from here on seem to be: How bad does an attack have to be before serious international attention is paid to it? And: At what point does it become a war crime? "I think that every six months, we'll see attacks," predicted Prof Michael Schmitt, lead author of the Tallinn Manual - the definitive international legal guide to cyber-conflict. "Even though I'm not 100 sure that it's Russia, I don't understand which other country could attack Ukraine. It's the only logical answer." And Ukrainian cybersecurity experts like Alexey Yankovski believe every single business is at risk. "Ukraine is a playground for attacks, and a large part of the cyber-security community here believes that most of the companies have already been infected," he told the BBC. "Every company here should be prepared for the fact that it will be hacked sooner or later." This week BBC News is taking a close look at all aspects of cyber-security. Les robots trouvent de nouvelles applications dans notre vie de tous les jours et interagissent de plus en plus etroitement avec leurs utilisateurs humains. Cependant, malgre une longue tradition de recherche, la maniere dont les robots doivent s'adapter a leurs environnements et aux interactions avec les humains est encore un domaine de recherche active. Dans cet article, nous presentons une approche generique pour apprendre, de facon autonome, des strategies d'adaptation a l'environnement et aux interactions humaines. L'apprentissage se fait a partir d'observations du robot et des utilisateurs dans son environnement. Les strategies apprises peuvent ensuite etre utilisees par le robot pour adapter son comportement aux situations rencontrees. L'approche repose sur l'identification de modeles de taches et de situations d'execution de taches, ceci grce a un module de perception situatif. Un module de raisonnement permet ensuite d'ordonnanceur ces modeles en plans d'actions adaptes a la situation. Enfin, un module d'apprentissage automatique apprend, sans intervention humaine, de nouvelles strategies d'adaptation au fur et a mesure qu'il interagit avec les utilisateurs. Nous avons teste notre approche sur un robot humanoide NAO, qui fut capable d'apprendre, de facon autonome, a executer plusieurs taches simples face a plusieurs utilisateurs. Robots are increasingly playing an important role in our lives and are required to interact more and more closely with people. However, despite a long research tradition, how to make robots adapt to their environment and the interaction with humans is still an active research area. In this paper we present a generic approach to learn, autonomously, adaptation strategies to the environment and to human interaction. The learning is based on observations of the robot and its users in its environment. The learnt strategies can then be used by the robot to adapt its behaviour to the encountered situations. The approach is based on task and task execution models identification, using a situational perception module. A reasoning module is then used to schedule these models into action plans adapted to the situation. Finally, a learning module automatically learns new adaptation strategies as it interacts with users, without any human intervention. We tested our approach on a humanoid robot NAO, which was able to autonomously learn to execute several simple tasks in front of multiple users. Many predicted structured objects (e.g., sequences, matchings, trees) are evaluated using the F-score, alignment error rate (AER), or other multivariate performance measures. Since inductively optimizing these measures using training data is challenging, previous methods used generative models trained on held-out validation data to compute confidence scores, or used weighted accuracy. The former is expensive and the latter only has access to examples and not the target value. We show that the perplexity of a probabilistic model trained on held-out validation data can be used to create a confidence score for a held-out example. Using a language model on a held-out set of words, we show that our approach improves F-score, AER, and perplexity for POS tagging and named entity recognition.

Not a medical professional so anyone with more knowledge please correct it: Wounds have exposed nerves. Nerves send signals through ions such as sodium and potassium; chlorine exists in the blood plasma to maintain a balance in the body. When wounds are exposed to air, ions are drawn to the wounds, which can cause tingling, throbbing, and sensitivity to touch. This causes the wound to become more sensitive. In addition, nerves are sensitive to many substances. Thus, the ions can cause nerve exposure when a new substance is introduced into the wound (soap, blood, etc.). When nerves are exposed, they release endorphins and enkephalins. These chemicals cause feelings of pleasure, and thus, the tingling feeling that comes with numbness. Lastly, a substance called bradykinin is produced in the nerves and blood plasma when nerve endings are exposed. Bradykinin is a potent vasodilator, meaning it dilates blood vessels. This can cause blood to spill out of the blood vessels and fill the tissues around the wound. This can cause swelling. When the wound is still open, it is possible to introduce bacteria. This can result in an infection. Infections also cause inflammation which, similar to swelling, can cause pain. In the final analysis, many factors contribute to the feeling of tingling. Many of these factors occur while the wound is still open. This is why it is important to clean, cover, and monitor a wound.

Typically, bombs are discovered through observations similar to those made by EOD specialists – a strange object noticed, a report from a patrol, or evidence of recent digging. Because explosives are often placed strategically along frequently used routes or near troop movements, personnel attempting to avoid IEDs will carefully examine anything unusual, like animals, debris, or disturbed earth. In regions like parts of the Middle East, many bombs aren’t timed devices; instead, they’re often outdated Soviet mines with various triggering mechanisms—pressure plates, metallic detection, or even remote activation via a cell phone. These are surprisingly prevalent and necessitate surveillance until detonation. If a patrol observes someone scrutinizing an area without justification, it strongly suggests a potential threat. Consequently, operations usually involve withdrawing forces, alerting civilians, and establishing a perimeter for safety. Sending trained experts to disable the device is rarely necessary, as a safer method—using robots to remotely detonate the bomb—is almost always employed.

Understanding the origins of life requires carefully tracking relationships between organisms – knowing who’s related to whom is crucial. While classifications can seem arbitrary and are now less significant due to improved DNA sequencing, they remain valuable for tracing evolutionary history, such as our own species’ lineage. Historically, scientists observed shared characteristics across various animals and determined they were evolutionarily linked, which DNA analysis later supported. A single trait, like hair, isn’t definitive; it became associated with mammals through observation and research. For example, discovering hair on whale fins allows us to infer mammalian characteristics even in creatures vastly different from monkeys or dogs. Losing hair, as humans are doing, doesn’t change an animal’s classification because the underlying evolutionary connections are paramount. Essentially, hair represents a key developmental feature in mammal ancestors, making it a reliable indicator of mammalian ancestry.

We prove the following results regarding the linear solvability of networks over various alphabets. For any network, the following are equivalent: (i) vector linear solvability over some finite field, (ii) scalar linear solvability over some ring, (iii) linear solvability over some module. Analogously, the following are equivalent: (a) scalar linear solvability over some finite field, (b) scalar linear solvability over some commutative ring, (c) linear solvability over some module whose ring is commutative. Whenever any network is linearly solvable over a module, a smallest such module arises in a vector linear solution for that network over a field. If a network is linearly solvable over some non-commutative ring but not over any commutative ring, then such a non-commutative ring must have size at least 16 , and for some networks, this bound is achieved. An infinite family of networks is demonstrated, each of which is scalar linearly solvable over some non-commutative ring but not over any commutative ring. A filibuster in the Senate is a delaying tactic employed by a minority senator who uses their right to extended debate—often lengthy speeches—to stall proceedings without offering substantive arguments. Historically, the ability to force a vote through a “previous question” motion was eliminated due to its infrequent use. Consequently, senators gained the power to engage in unlimited speech on any matter. While “cloture,” a procedure limiting debate to 30 hours with individual senators receiving only one hour each, was established in Senate Rule 22, it still demands 60 votes to invoke. Achieving cloture can be challenging, potentially prolonging the process by several days. A simple majority of 51 senators is needed to pass most bills, but cloture necessitates 60. Therefore, a group of 41 dissenting voices can effectively block a vote indefinitely. Though a majority of 49 would lose a vote, this demonstrates the influence of the minority. Filibusters thus provide a counterbalance against overwhelming majority decisions. However, the frequency of filibusters has dramatically increased over the past four decades, often utilized as a method to inflate the threshold for passing legislation.

During the late Empire, Christian and non-Christian burial customs increasingly converged. Families often shared tombs, and elements of the traditional *novemdialis* festival aligned with Christian liturgical practices like the *Constitutio Apostolica*. The longstanding tradition of offering food and drink to the deceased persisted, though St. Augustine, influenced by St. Ambrose, worried about it resembling the ancient Parentalia rituals, yet supported funeral feasts as a way for Christians to provide charity to the needy. Consequently, Christian participation in Parentalia, along with its related observances of Feralia and Caristia, prompted the Council of Tours to ban them in 567 AD. Distinctly separate from these were traditional Roman funerary customs, which viewed the body as polluting and focused on recording dates of birth and lifespan through epitaphs. Conversely, the Christian church emphasized honoring holy relics, marking death as a passage towards “new life” on memorial inscriptions.

Discussions are already taking place with other providers, particularly the ambulance trusts, to see who could take over from NHS Direct. NHS Direct announced in June that it was pulling out of two areas - Cornwall and North Essex - even before the services were launched. NHS Direct used to be paid more than PS20 per call when it ran the old 0845 number. The payment is between PS7 and PS9 per call for the new 111 service. Projections reported earlier this month showed NHS Direct had lost PS2.8m since April and was "heading for a deficit of PS26m if we continue to run the same volume of 111 services until the end of this financial year." The organisation is now seeking a "managed transfer" of its 111 contracts, which have between two and five years left to run, to another provider. NHS Direct has already pulled out of contracts for 111 services in Cornwall and North Essex Nick Chapman, the chief executive of NHS Direct, said: "We will continue to provide a safe and reliable NHS 111 service to our patients until alternative arrangements can be made by commissioners. Dame Barbara Hakin, the deputy chief executive of NHS England, told the BBC: "We've been in discussions with other providers, particularly the ambulance trusts who, with their experience, will be able to, in a properly managed fashion, take over this service from NHS Direct. The Dispatches programme, which will air on Monday night, reports one call centre manager saying the service was "unsafe" at weekends because there were too few staff to deal with the calls coming in. Mount Everest, the world's highest peak, has seen countless climbers attempting to scale its heights since the first ascent in 1953. As a result, generations of Everest climbers have left tons of trash - including tents, oxygen cylinders, and human waste - on the slopes, contributing to environmental degradation and threats to the local ecosystem. In response to the growing problem of waste on the mountain, the Indian army has embarked on an ambitious mission to remove at least 4,000 kilograms of garbage from the peak. The team of Indian soldiers and expert climbers, led by Major General Anindya Sengupta, has been tasked with the arduous responsibility of cleaning-up the "Roof of the World." The first-of-its-kind initiative, dubbed "Clean Everest," started last week and aims to remove waste from not only the 8,848-meter peak but also the trekking route leading up to it. Part of the garbage is expected to be airlifted from the higher altitudes, while the remaining waste will be cleared manually by the team members. "With each expedition, mountaineers generate a significant amount of trash that often remains there. It's essential that the pristine nature of this location is preserved for future generations," said Sengupta. According to a study by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), an astonishing 30 tonnes of waste has accumulated on Everest since 1950. In recent years, both the Nepalese government and tourism industry have become increasingly concerned about the environmental impact of the waste left behind by climbers. The government of Nepal even introduced a regulation in 2014, requiring all mountaineers to bring back at least 8 kilograms of their waste, failing which they can be penalized. But despite these efforts, cleaning up the slopes remains a daunting task. The Indian army's "Clean Everest" drive is expected to last for up to six weeks, with members working in staggered groups to carry out the cleanup process. They have already recovered several tents, oxygen cylinders, abandoned ropes, and large bags of trash. The mission also plans to recover the bodies of climbers who perished on their ascent, with the permission of their families. Through this initiative, the Indian army seeks not only to preserve the environment but also to pay tribute to the mountaineers who lost their lives attempting the climb. Cleaning Everest is expected to be an ongoing effort, and if the Indian army is successful, it could inspire other nations to take up similar initiatives. As the world continues to enjoy the majesty of this natural wonder, efforts like the Indian Army's "Clean Everest" mission are vital to ensuring that future generations can appreciate the mountain in all its glory.

We propose a method for training a deterministic deep model that can find and reject out of distribution data points at test time with a single forward pass. Our approach, deterministic uncertainty quantification (DUQ), builds upon ideas of RBF networks. We scale training in these with a novel loss function and centroid updating scheme. By enforcing detectability of changes in the input using a gradient penalty, we are able to reliably detect out of distribution data. Our uncertainty quantification scales well to large datasets, and using a single model, we improve upon Deep Ensembles on notable difficult dataset pairs such as FashionMNIST vs. MNIST, and CIFAR-10 vs. SVHN, while maintaining competitive accuracy.

We establish several theorems concerning the linear solvability of networks using different alphabets. We show that these conditions are interchangeable: (i) linear solvability with respect to a finite field, (ii) scalar linear solvability with respect to a ring, and (iii) linear solvability with respect to a module. Similarly, (a) scalar linear solvability over a finite field, (b) scalar linear solvability over a commutative ring, and (c) linear solvability with a module having a commutative ring are equivalent.  If a network possesses a linear solution within a module, a minimal such module will appear in the corresponding vector linear solution over a field. Networks linearly solvable over a non-commutative ring but not any commutative ring require a ring of at least size 16, with this limit sometimes attained. We present an infinite set of networks that are scalar linearly solvable over a non-commutative ring yet not over any commutative one.  Specifically, if a network is scalar linearly solvable over a ring of size *pk* where *p* is prime and 2*k* < 6, then it’s also *k*-dimensional vector linearly solvable over GF(*p*). However, this implication doesn't always hold when *k* ≥ 2 and the ring is commutative.

Catastrophic flooding poses a serious threat due to its destructive nature, and climate change seems to be causing more frequent severe floods globally. Traditional physics-based flood models are expensive and difficult to apply broadly because their results depend heavily on specific locations and human-built structures. Conversely, statistical models can handle these complexities by incorporating them within the training data itself. Utilizing remote sensing data—particularly from Earth observation satellites—could lessen the demand for detailed field measurements. Here, we create adaptable flood risk maps for various river basins using data gathered from the USGS stream gauge network. We employ machine learning techniques, trained under supervision, to forecast flood vulnerability based on features like river basin characteristics, impervious surface areas identified via satellite images, and past rainfall and water level readings. We evaluate the accuracy of several models using precision-recall analysis and benchmark them against simple, basic predictions. This research advances efforts to provide reliable flood forecasting capabilities to vulnerable communities worldwide.

Conditional text generation benefits significantly from incorporating diverse outputs. Recent advancements utilizing Conditional Variational Autoencoders (CVAEs) demonstrate potential, but frequently struggle with the KL-vanishing issue. Prior attempts addressed this through ad-hoc adjustments like modifying the encoder or decoder during optimization. These approaches lacked clear guidance, making it difficult to determine the optimal intensity of intervention. This work introduces a targeted optimization objective designed specifically to counteract KL-vanishing within the CVAE framework. This objective actively steers the encoder toward an “ideal” representation favored by the decoder, thereby boosting expressiveness. A labeling network estimates this ideal encoder, providing a continuous latent space label to strengthen the link between latent variables and desired outputs. We call this approach Self Labeling CVAE (SLCVAE). Furthermore, to expedite research into varied text generation, we present a substantial, natively one-to-many labeled dataset. Rigorous testing across two tasks reveals that SLCVAE substantially enhances output diversity without sacrificing performance relative to current leading techniques.

An emulator simulates another computer or gaming console using a host machine. Unlike native execution where a console instantly processes commands, an emulator must interpret and reconstruct these actions, adding computational overhead. This delay mirrors human thought – quickly answering a direct question versus needing time to consider a related one. Games demand immediate responses, necessitating an emulator running on a significantly faster computer than the system being simulated. While a powerful processor can handle older systems like the Super Nintendo, modern consoles share components with contemporary PCs, limiting processing power and preventing detailed emulation. Consequently, inaccuracies arise due to the inability to perfectly reproduce a console’s architecture, leading to various bugs and requiring extensive developer effort to address unique issues. Some emulators, like DICE for Pong, achieve remarkable precision by mirroring circuit designs, but this level of fidelity isn’t feasible for more complex platforms such as a PlayStation 4.

This article proposes a new Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) operation paradigm to enable a large number of relatively low-cost UAVs to fly beyond-line-of-sight without costly sensing and communication systems or substantial human intervention in individual UAV control. Under current free-flight-like paradigm, wherein a UAV can travel along any route as long as it avoids restricted airspace and altitudes. However, this requires expensive on-board sensing and communication as well as substantial human effort in order to ensure avoidance of obstacles and collisions. The increased cost serves as an impediment to the emergence and development of broader UAV applications. The main contribution of this work is to propose the use of pre-established route network for UAV traffic management, which allows: (i) pre-mapping of obstacles along the route network to reduce the onboard sensing requirements and the associated costs for avoiding such obstacles; and (ii) use of well-developed routing algorithms to select UAV schedules that avoid conflicts. Available GPS-based navigation can be used to fly the UAV along the selected route and time schedule with relatively low added cost, which therefore, reduces the barrier to entry into new UAV-applications market. Finally, this article proposes a new decoupling scheme for conflict-free transitions between edges of the route network at each node of the route network to reduce potential conflicts between UAVs and ensuing delays. A simulation example is used to illustrate the proposed uNet approach.

Ceredigion Council intends to auction the former Ysgol Dyffryn Teifi school in Llandysul, which closed at the end of the previous academic year, for redevelopment.  A decision on the planned sale, scheduled for September 30th, will be discussed by the council’s cabinet next Tuesday. However, a local initiative, Plant y Dyffryn, is requesting additional time to prepare an offer to purchase the property. The site is valued between £250,000 and £300,000, and the money raised will support the construction of the new Ysgol Bro Teifi school, serving students aged three to nineteen, which recently opened. Leah Williams, a founder of Plant y Dyffryn, expressed concerns that a private developer might negatively impact the community, stating that Llandysul's size and strong Welsh identity makes it vulnerable. The site offers eight acres of valuable land with significant development possibilities.  Plant y Dyffryn is researching how the Cardigan community project, 4CG, successfully acquired and managed the Pwllhai site in 2010 – transforming it into a car park and leasing space to local businesses – as a model for raising funds and operating the land themselves. A researcher from the Swiss research institute EMPA has developed an invisible lock system that uses conductive ink on a transparent polymer film to create invisible buttons. The result is that the lock system can be thought of as a device for preventing thieves from opening and closing it and letting them know they have been robbed. The researchers used electrons collected in their cameras, which measure distances between the electrodes, to derive its characteristics. They then first tried to design a light emitting diode (LED) based on the same technology (the fluorescence emission channel), which was more sensitive than other layers of glass, and much less sensitive than the copper-based EL cells. These defects were discovered by scanning electron microscopy (SEM). When the candidates were chosen, the researchers showed that "once the light emitted from the electrode the two layers of glass had a high spatial similarity." This allowed the project's team to determine "how we could find out that the position of each edge of the optical layer is too close to those of the material being scanned," according to the report. The researchers measured whether the light emitted from the electrodes was traced back to the electrodes. Their results also demonstrated that even if the laser energy was lost in the electrodes, the light reflected off the surface of each electrode would remain visible. The paper recently appeared online in Nature Communications.

I’m not exceptionally intelligent, nor would I claim to be a good person; I mostly believe it’s simply been luck that has guided me. I enlisted in the military during tenth grade—the pay was decent, and much of our time was spent drinking and socializing. The drill sergeants constantly yelled and threatened, though rarely anything serious occurred. This continued for what seemed like an eternity, likely around four or five years. A few guys from Washington accompanied me to study explosives, although I’m unsure why I was selected. I didn’t question it, just complied. On the first day, there was a quick assessment to gauge knowledge. Being completely lost, I was called upon first. I received wire cutters and quipped, “Just like the movies,” earning laughter from those present, and I laughed along with them, proceeding with considerable perspiration. The bomb resembled four bars of butter encased in aluminum foil, tightly bound with a watch set to twelve o’clock, connected by three colored wires. I assumed the wire cutters were for precisely this purpose. Cutting the topmost wire – yellow – I anticipated severing all of them, but the instructor applauded enthusiastically, shaking my hand and proclaiming a new time-speed record. Bewildered, I accepted it without further inquiry. Years later, here I am, burdened by numerous medals weighing nearly four pounds, receiving accolades from subordinates claiming they owe their lives to me. I hold the record for disposing of the most bombs; my mother encourages me to be proud, which I suppose I am. Now, however, I mostly feel guilt. I still lack understanding of what I’m doing, yet I continue to smile and go through the motions. It wasn’t until recently that I began to wonder, what if my luck eventually changes?

We study online boosting, the task of converting any weak online learner into a strong online learner. Based on a novel and natural definition of weak online learnability, we develop two online boosting algorithms. The first algorithm is an online version of boost-by-majority. By proving a matching lower bound, we show that this algorithm is essentially optimal in terms of the number of weak learners and the sample complexity needed to achieve a specified accuracy. This optimal algorithm is not adaptive, however. Using tools from online loss minimization, we derive an adaptive online boosting algorithm that is also parameter-free, but not optimal. Both algorithms work with base learners that can handle example importance weights directly, as well as by rejection sampling examples with probability defined by the booster. Results are complemented with an experimental study.

The Naseby Battlefield Project (NBP) is planning to construct a visitor center on the historic site where the pivotal battle of the English Civil War occurred in Northamptonshire. With £9,900 from the Heritage Lottery Fund (HLF), the group will conduct a feasibility study and engage with local communities before applying for a larger grant to fund construction. This battle, fought on June 14, 1645, saw Parliament’s forces defeat King Charles I’s army in fields near Naseby. The NBP’s trustees and patrons envision the Naseby Battlefield Visitor Centre as a valuable resource offering insights into the battle, the wider Civil War period, its political and social context, the region’s landscape in the 17th century, and daily life during that time. According to Chairman Lord Arthur Hazelrigg, “We are delighted by the Heritage Lottery Fund’s backing to elevate the Battle of Naseby’s profile nationally.” Trustee Mike Ingram added that the center would serve as a central location for displaying artifacts related to the event.

The success of its football team made Notre Dame a household name. The success of Note Dame reflected rising status of Irish Americans and Catholics in the 1920s. Catholics rallied up around the team and listen to the games on the radio, especially when it knocked off the schools that symbolized the Protestant establishment in America - Harvard, Yale, Princeton, and Army. Yet this role as high-profile flagship institution of Catholicism made it an easy target of anti-Catholicism. The most remarkable episode of violence was the clash between Notre Dame students and the Ku Klux Klan in 1924. Nativism and anti-Catholicism, especially when directed towards immigrants, were cornerstones of the KKK's rhetoric, and Notre Dame was seen as a symbol of the threat posed by the Catholic Church. The Klan decided to have a week-long Klavern in South Bend. Clashes with the student body started on March 17, when students, aware of the anti-Catholic animosity, blocked the Klansmen from descending from their trains in the South Bend station and ripped the KKK clothes and regalia. On May 19 thousands of students massed downtown protesting the Klavern, and only the arrival of college president Fr. Matthew Walsh prevented any further clashes. The next day, football coach Knute Rockne spoke at a campus rally and implored the students to obey the college president and refrain from further violence. A few days later the Klavern broke up, but the hostility shown by the students was an omen and a contribution to the downfall of the KKK in Indiana.

Everyone at school used to call me stupid. I was not stupid, I just grew faster than anyone else and looked like I had been kept back a few years. Adults were not much better. They saw a 20 something that acted 16. I WAS 16. It hurt me more than I realised at the time. My grades started to suffer, which seem to prove everybody right, and I started lashing out. Not at people, at inanimate objects. The bullies soon worked out that I was an easy target. They would call me names, steal my stuff and knock my food out of my hands. I would just walk away broken, find an alleyway and beat the heck out of a dumpster, or worse, put my fist through a window. "I" was the problem kid. Vandalism, poor academic achievement, even branded "special" by my chemistry teacher. The worst of the bullies was Scissors. He did not look much, but he had a tongue on him. Whoever he targeted, he knew exactly what to say to cut them. He had some hard-ass cronies to back him up, so he never got what was coming to him. If anyone tried, they would get a pasting. He especially liked to pick on the arty kids. Having no talent of his own, I guess he was jealous. That, or they were as easy targets as me. Every time he saw Paper, he would say something to make her eyes well up, but she always looked him in the eyes in defiance. He would push past her, knocking her books to the floor. I hated that guy. Paper was always kind to me. One sunny day I was crossing the yard, and I could see Paper winding her way back to class. Even though she must have been struggling to carry her large portfolio, she looked a peace, sunlight streaking flames across her deep red hair. My trance was broken when Scissors showed up. Deliberately blocking her path, winged by his henchmen, he just stood there. I could not hear what he was saying, only by the look on Paper's face I could tell that she was unimpressed and having none of it. Perhaps through instinct, I can not remember, but I was a great deal closer than I was before. When Scissors slapped the portfolio to the ground, I could clearly hear Paper cry "No!." I was a damn-sight closer when Scissors raised his foot to trample what looked like a watercolour of a woman's face. Close enough to hear Paper scream. Close enough to punch Scissors in the mouth, knocking him on his ass. His cronies just ran. I did say I was big. Apparently, I also looked like I could murder Scissors. Maybe I would have killed him. Years of frustration was in that punch. One broken jaw; three missing teeth. Before anyone could know what would happen next, Paper threw her arms around me. As light as a feather, with all the power of a lightning strike, her kiss on my cheek took my breath away. Her deep green eyes imprinted on my soul as she whispered "Thank you, Rock." With her arms around me then, and 20 years on they still are, I was and always will be at peace.

Your mucus acts like a watery gel, drawn to moisture. When you’re ill, have allergies, or encounter irritants, moving this mucus quickly is beneficial. The men from the 1st Battalion the Yorkshire Regiment sat on the floor when ordered to stand to attention. The protest by 16 soldiers was sparked by grievances with their commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Richard Aldworth-Chapman, and Sergeant Major John Perry. Image caption Lieutenant General Mark Carleton-Smith said his "heart went out" to them Lt Gen Carleton Smith has offered a formal apology for what happened at Castlemartin in June 1809 during the Napoleonic Wars. He described it as an appalling situation which should never have occurred or been allowed to continue. A total of six companies were based around two camps at the time - one near St Martin's Mount and another near Arbegnoch beach - about 25 miles (40km) west of Cork city. They spent most of their days behind camp walls but would venture into the surrounding countryside if tasked with building fortifications or other work. As well as being short-handed due to government recruitment restrictions at home following the end of the Peninsular War, there had also been poor harvests, meaning food supplies were low. This prompted Lt Col Chapman to issue orders calling on those able bodied - including labourers not attached full time to the regiments - to help relieve some of the burden. It is estimated that between 100 and 300 civilians were employed across all three battalions over this period. However, historian Simon Cobain says many did not play any meaningful role in guarding the troops. One soldier who recently returned from a tour recalled seeing civilian workers carrying muskets while others looked after horses and carriages. Mr Cobain argues these temporary civilian employees got little more than a pat on the back before they left each day and that the majority played no part in protecting the regiment's barracks or guns. He believes officers knew what this meant today: "They essentially turned their back on our history." According to Mr Cobain, this attitude extended beyond the ranks of the regular army, leading even senior generals such as Sir Arthur Wellesley to question how effective the British Army could be in war without its "own people." In a letter to Lord Castlereagh outlining a need for reform of the militia system, he criticised "the practice of employing strangers...to supply their place," describing it as "a disgraceful exhibition of want of confidence in ourselves...and not attending strictly enough upon our own business [but] rather keeping out of the way of any danger until occasion shall compel us to run..." Another witness to the events, Captain George Macdonnell, soon joined the campaign against Napoleon Bonaparte. A veteran of the Peninsular War, he wrote of witnessing many "sad sights" behind enemy lines, including "many wretches broken down by want fatigue having fought 20 years...[who] lie every night shivering." His sadness deepened in August 1810 when hearing several South Irish residents near Youghal had suffered hunger and starvation because they helped bring in supplies. Their families subsequently died as a result. By this point, relations between the guardsmen and the officer corps had deteriorated significantly. While British commanders blamed the Irish themselves for contributing to their plight, men felt anger towards the higher command. Not only did they feel neglected but they believed their pay had failed to keep pace with inflation, leaving wives unable to buy adequate clothing or feed children properly. Their simmering frustration boiled over when they saw posters advertising 15 per month (1,560 today), supposedly paid to keep watch outside women and children sleeping rough. Some soldiers demanded equal treatment courtesy of improved wages and better recruiting policies. Those who protested further claimed they faced excessive discipline. Officers refused requests to provide medical care to wounded comrades unless they consented to amputation. Others complained of inadequate rations of bread, beef and ale. One account even alleged mass graves under a nearby hill where dead animals lay rotting within sight of the barracks. But frustrations ran deeper; at least four records show instances of mutiny. In May 1811, many infantry companies staged protests against their captain, William Wharton, demanding action be taken against him. When they tried to march to Dublin, however, they found they were blocked by rearguard units loyal to him. Despite defections among officers supporting Wharton, he eventually fled Dublin with hundreds of followers. By November that year, most Infantry Battalions reported their captains were seriously disliked. So much so that many decided to desert altogether. Then came the Battle of Waterloo. However, it wasn’t until 1988 that South Africa conceded to cease its control over Namibia, following a United Nations resolution concerning the broader region. Forces possess both strength and direction, leading them to be categorized as “vector quantities.” Unlike scalar quantities—those lacking directional information—forces adhere to distinct mathematical principles. Calculating the effect of multiple forces requires understanding their magnitude *and* direction; otherwise, the outcome is uncertain. Consider a scenario where two individuals pull on a rope with specified forces, yet their directions are unknown – it’s impossible to predict the rope's acceleration. They might pull opposite ways (like in a tug-of-war) or in the same way. Using vector notation eliminates ambiguity by explicitly representing force direction alongside its size.

Tension I hadn't realised I had accumulated left my body noticeably. "Do you have another task for me, Sir?" I asked him to which he only waved lazily. I was free to go. Upon closing the door I sighed again, this time for real and started to make my way towards the break room. I realised I still had the second mug in my hand and took a sip myself - it was real coffee for me though. At my destination I was pleasantly surprised to see Seri - a humanoid with brilliant yellow feathers covering her slim, agile body. She turned around as I entered the room and her small beak moved in a fashion I had come to recognize as a smile. I blushed a little out of habit because I had had a mild crush on her for the last few months until I had decided to move on. "Heya Charlie. How's it going?" she chirped, literally. Some of the avians, especially the songbird kind, had that really melodic way of speaking. It was fascinating and distracting at the same time. And me still liking her to some degree didn't help on that front. "Hey Seri. Not much really. Mr. Iguano is terrifying as always and I don't have much to do apart from getting copies or some kind of brew for some kind of min..." I stopped. I had meant to say minx which was slang for the new-age races but kind of..... racist? "Sorry. " , I said. She hadn't stopped "smiling." I guess she'd had to deal with worse. And now that I thought about it I couldn't help but wonder which generation of her ancestors went sentient. It was different for every species. "Don't worry Charlie, you've got my permission to use that word. After all you're my little minx!" "Urgh, please no I beg you." Too late, she was already getting a kick out of it. "Oh but you're me wittle human and I..." Luckily she was forced to stop there, as her superior entered the room. Or forced himself into it more like as he had to duck through the door, which already was more like a gate than a door. His ill fitting suit stretched dangerously thin over the huge muscles covered in thick black fur. As with most sentients his species had gotten bigger when they evolved. Only that gorillas had been considerably big to begin with. "Ms. Flavi, sorry to..." he stopped to cough violently and I had to grab and hold my mug as the table shook in rhythm. He then proceeded fumble with a small paper box trying to get one of the cigarettes out which seemed incredibly tiny compared to his huge paws. "Sorry to interrupt your break but you're needed in the SA-Department. Some new hawk type and nobody understands him and I think..." He coughed again, less violent now that he somehow had managed to light his cig. "I think they classified him a PSC 3 so be careful." Seri just nodded, gave me an apologetic look and went on her way. I was left with Mr. Gorilla. Whose last name was kind of the equivalent in genericness to a Mr. Smith, but I never understood why that was an appropriate comparison. I had yet to meet someone called Mr. or Mrs. Human. Mr. Gorilla glared at me and continued chain-smoking. I was only the intern after all. The small human trainee in the A.R.E.S.E. - the Administration for recently evolved sentient entities. - The day passed slowly, as any day did in the bureau. I guess you couldn't expect any excitement to be had as the intern, but still after 3 months of being the general drudge I was at the point of throwing the towel. Oh how I yearned to at least be able to sneak a peek at Seris job. She was working in the sentient assimilation department which handled the task of working with newly sentient beings - beings who had awoken as people called it. But, contrary to what one would assume when hearing about accelerated evolution triggers, those didn't apply to an entire species at a time but happened seemingly at random. Sometimes a lot of individual animals awoke - like in the Yukon incident, where several moose gained consciousness only to be massacred by another recently awoken pack of wolves who didn't have their instincts in check yet. One of the reasons ARESE was founded. And sometimes it only happened to a single individual. Which then lead to some really depressing stories like that of the now accomplished philosopher M. Aldabra, who awoke to realize he was not only the lone conscious representative of his species but also that the latter was nearly extinct. Not that the world wasn't being swarmed with new intelligent beings every day. Official estimates assumed the number of new unique sentient life was in the dozens every week for the last two decades. And thus far only the Chordates - the major group including mammals, birds and reptiles - had had awoken cases. Overpopulation had already been a problem but know it was through the roof - quite literally because interestingly enough where skyscraper buildings were at an all time high, some of the avian species had started constructing sophisticated nest-like complexes on roofs in heavily populated areas. Furthermore there was an entire department in the ARESE whose only job was to plan and prepare for the worst case scenario: when the Invertebrates would start to awaken. Which then would include every insect-species, outnumbering the other races by the tens of thousands. It was a scary thought indeed. I tried not to dwell on it for too long, because while I wasn't exactly insectophobic I did get a bit squeamish when confronted with a larger amount of those pesky little multi pods. The sun, unseen by me in the vast corridors of the ARESE headquarters for the last hours, had progressed quite a bit and was tinting the streets of Manhattan in gold. Quite a few reptile-type guys were sitting in the last glow of our star to warm their bodies bevore it would be gone for the night. Some of them really had a hard time with regular work schedules because of the need for external warming and labor unions were pushing for regulations on that front. The unions in general really had a lot to do these days with new workplace needs arising every week and a ton of discrimination cases. But still the streets were bustling with activity and that would only increase once the nocturnals got up. I strolled in the general direction of my apartment and was planning to stop for groceries along the way. It was quite a few blocks I would have to walk but even after all the weeks I had already spent in the city there was still a spectacle to be witnessed around every corner. A big feline-type vendor was in the process of apologizing profoundly to a small amphibian customer at his stall for something I could only guess relating to the grilled frogs on a stick the cat was selling. Meanwhile a flock of teenage bird-types were playing a complicated looking game with a ball all in the air above the streets. It seemed that one bird of prey, a hawk maybe, was especially good at whatever he was doing because an owl-type girl was moon-eyeing him with the kind of expression only a teenager in love could make. Primary systems vary significantly by state. Closed primaries restrict voting to registered party members, such as limiting participation in a Democratic primary to just Democrats. Conversely, open primaries allow anyone to choose a party’s ballot, while “jungle” primaries feature all candidates – regardless of affiliation – competing initially; a runoff determines the final winner if no candidate secures over 50% of the votes. Party membership holds considerable weight within the political landscape, offering access to party conventions that influence policy decisions. Furthermore, many states utilize conventions or caucuses to select candidates, often prioritizing party members. Affiliation also grants access to candidate fundraising email lists, a benefit typically unavailable to independents. Dissatisfaction with available candidates and concerns about systemic issues frequently drive individuals to leave a political party.

Recognizing my fate, I enlisted at sixteen – though eighteen was the mandated age—seeing no point in postponing my unavoidable destiny. Yet, each “victory” revealed a deeper loss, the true graves lay above us. It was a world where up became down, left became right, a chaotic normalcy. Four months before my twenty-second birthday, news arrived via radio – the war concluded after nearly a quarter-century of conflict. For the first time in my life, I experienced peace, a peace secured by a treaty just days later. However, as a generation shaped by war, I couldn't grasp it; we’d lost too much. This translates to approximately five to six games weekly for nearly seven months, excluding the postseason, leading to several downsides. Primarily, it causes frequent injuries among position players due to overuse, forcing rest even when a team remains competitive. Furthermore, the overwhelming volume of games makes it difficult for baseball to achieve widespread popularity like basketball or football, as simply following one team consumes a large portion of a year’s viewing time. Unlike football, where fans can easily track their team alongside broader league action, this excessive schedule diminishes interest in nationally televised games. Finally, the high number of games negatively impacts both local television viewership and stadium attendance.

"My wife is so ugly, I took her to the zoo and they said she was the missing link." The humor in that joke doesn't come from the punch line. A man being hit in the face with a pie while he's giving a speech is funny because it's exaggerated. The impact of the pie is exaggerated, the humor of the impact is exaggerated, and the man being hit in the face with the pie is exaggerated. It's never just "a pie," it's a "heavy" pie, or a "smelly" pie. All of these exaggerations lead to more laughs. Humor is about irony. "The more you run over a dead cat, the flatter it gets" is funny because it's ironic. It's not just a man being hit in the face with a pie, it's a man being hit in the face with a pie that's filled with dead cats. Humor is about timing. "I'll tell you the secret of success. If you can shock people enough with what you say, they'll laugh at it just to relieve the tension. "I'll tell you the secret of success. Start with a slap in the face. Building a bridge over the Atlantic presents significant challenges. The vastness of the ocean – larger than the United States in some areas – combined with its depth, storms, and saltwater exposure makes traditional designs impractical; pilings cannot be sunk for anchoring, and pontoon bridges would likely fail due to wave action. Furthermore, the distance would create a monotonous and fuel-limited journey. A tunnel beneath the Atlantic faces equally daunting obstacles. The immense water pressure at the ocean floor, equivalent to ten thousand times the pressure experienced when diving, poses a critical risk of collapse. Constructing such a tunnel would require incredibly robust materials and constant monitoring to prevent leaks, along with substantial ventilation systems to maintain breathable air. Similarly, refueling within the tunnel would present logistical difficulties.

The reason it's not is because a queen is a lot harder to "control" (it's attacking a lot more spaces then the rook would be). Chess rules dictate that if one side has no legal moves and isn't in check then the game is a draw; alternatively if one side has no legal moves and they are in check then that is a loss for them. Given the board setup that picture shows if white promotes his pawn to a queen then black will have no legal moves and will not be in check, so the game is a draw. If white promotes his pawn to a rook then the game will be won (not from that move alone but there is a proven endgame checkmate with KingRook v. King. The universe possesses a limited amount of energy, thus establishing an inherent theoretical limit. A further constraint arises from the Planck Temperature, beyond which our current understanding of physics fails to provide adequate models. Similar to how Newtonian mechanics struggles with black holes and subatomic particles, our existing models of matter become inadequate at extremely high temperatures. This observation aligns with the idea that the maximum temperature achievable by matter corresponds to the Planck scale, specifically the Planck Temperature. As explained in a Vsauce video ([7:00]), increasing heat leads to shorter and shorter wavelengths of emitted light – reaching 1.41 x10^32 K results in emission at 1.616x10^-26 nanometers, approaching the Planck length, considered the fundamental minimum length. Adding more energy should continue shrinking the wavelength, however, this process ultimately breaks down due to contradictions within our established definitions; the object would transcend conventional “temperature.”  Matter radiates based on its temperature—a measure of its energy—and hotter objects emit higher frequencies of radiation. Theoretically, the highest possible frequency would correspond to a Planck-length wavelength, representing the fastest possible speed of light within Planck-time, the smallest meaningful timescale at the quantum level. Attempting to exceed this wavelength would introduce paradoxes, as it implies an impossible energy state. Furthermore, the concept of particles vibrating at the speed of light is incorrect, as nothing can truly attain that velocity.

Accident and emergency waiting times for patients have lagged behind other parts of the UK. Two years ago, a major hospital in Belfast, Royal Victoria, was said to be "at breaking point," as a backlog of patients built up and a major incident was declared. But, even with the latest provisional figures showing a decline in AE performance, there is a determination among clinicians and nursing staff to draw a line and build a level of service to be proud of. There is evidence of a change of mood with the opening in August of an emergency department at Royal Victoria, part of a new PS150m critical care facility. Doctors, bruised by the turmoil in the 2013-14 winter, have developed new ways of working, designed to speed the flow of patients through the system. It's early days, but there are some encouraging signs - in recent months, there has been a 10 year-on-year increase in the number of patients treated or assessed within four hours. The most recent data for November, though, shows an increase of five percentage points year-on-year. The hospital points out it has dramatically reduced the number waiting 12 hours or more. A key policy at the Royal Victoria is putting senior clinicians close to the "front door" of the emergency department. Their task is to quickly triage patients and send them through different treatment streams. Special report page: For the latest news, analysis and video Analysis: The lost beds problem Winter across the UK: A guide to how the NHS is coping Video: Why hospitals are under so much pressure Video: How a hospital can grind to a halt The idea is to avoid a build-up of people waiting in reception. Badly injured or sick patients are dispatched through the system in the normal way, but a more sophisticated approach has been developed for those who are less seriously ill. A critical-assessment unit next to the emergency department receives patients, with the aim of dealing with their medical needs within the day. This could involve an initial appraisal and then sending a patient home for the night with an appointment booked the next day. Known as a "virtual ward," the idea is to carry out treatment without patients needing overnight stays, so reducing pressure on bed occupancy. Specialist equipment is made available to this unit, allowing doctors to order scans and other procedures to accelerate the patient's progress. Royal Victoria and other emergency departments are facing deep-rooted pressures. Northern Ireland does not have a 111 or NHS Direct helpline to guide patients, where appropriate, away from AE towards other forms of treatment closer to home. And there are only a few minor injuries clinics to take the pressure off the major hospitals. The Northern Ireland Health and Social Care Board has announced measures to boost GP out-of-hours services and promote alternatives to turning up at AE. The NHS has to cope with long-standing health problems in some areas, including mental health, which can be linked to economic decline and deprivation. The integration of health and social care offers Northern Ireland the opportunity to tackle major problems common to all parts of the United Kingdom. Problems caring for the elderly at home and in their local communities have left most UK hospitals struggling to discharge patients and free up beds for new patients to occupy. Southern Health and Social Care Trust in Northern Ireland is pioneering consultant-led care of the elderly in the community, offering, in effect, hospital care in a patient's own home. The service aims to treat at home patients with a wider range of acute illnesses. In its first year, the pilot service has prevented about 440 hospital admissions. With 1.8 million people, it will always be a challenge for Northern Ireland to sustain a full range of NHS services and specialist care. There is clearly a will to rise to that challenge, but no-one is denying the task may get harder with rising attendances at hospitals, an ageing population and complex health needs.

The numbers ‘4’ and ‘a’ displayed on your screen – barring unusual fonts – represent the accurate visual forms, appearing this way in many typefaces except when imitating handwriting. The “open 4” is favored in handwriting because it’s readily distinguishable from a ‘9’, preventing confusion during rapid writing. The alternative form of ‘a’ is simply quicker and simpler to produce. Numerous variations exist for each character; observe how different fonts present them. Notably, the ‘a’ and ‘4’ frequently utilize two distinct styles in printed materials, clearly differing from one another. Similar distinctions apply to ‘1,’ ‘7,’ ‘g,’ ‘w,’ ‘l,’ and ‘z.’ Handwriting showcases significantly greater variation. The “closed 4” originates from Arabic numeral construction, where each digit mirrors its numerical value in angles, while the “open 4” likely stems from early LCD displays. Regarding height—with both “double-story” and “single-story” options—the double-story style is preferred for cursive, though the single-story design proved more efficient for printing presses.

Numerous hypotheses attempt to explain the origin of sexual reproduction. Focusing on yeast epigenetics – specifically, gene regulation through histone modifications – I’ll outline one prominent theory. Essentially, the capacity for exchanging genetic material arose accidentally, providing a survival advantage and allowing for greater reproductive success. Sexual reproduction probably began with limited genetic sharing, progressing later to complete chromosomal recombination, which generates diversity and eliminates harmful mutations within populations. Despite the added complexities, sexual reproduction usually increases overall fitness, favoring organisms capable of it. Bacterial examples demonstrate early forms of this, where cells connect using “sex pili” and exchange genetic content. Yeast presents a distinct case; they possess both asexual (budding) and sexual modes of reproduction, including a unique "class switching" mechanism. Yeast exist in haploid (single set of chromosomes) and diploid (double set) states, with the diploid form engaging in sexual reproduction. Initially, a haploid yeast might have combined with a diploid, creating the latter. These diploids persisted until a mutation triggered division into multiple haploid cells. Over time, this process refined, eventually leading to the meiotic processes observed in modern yeast.

The problem of finding maximum (or minimum) witnesses of the Boolean product of two Boolean matrices (MW for short) has a number of important applications, in particular the all-pairs lowest -common ancestor problem, the longest path problem, etc. The MW problem is formally defined as follows: given two Boolean matrices A and B, find an integer vector v in {0,1}n such that vT A vT B 1 and the sum of components of v is minimized (or maximized). The dimension n is common for both matrices. For brevity we call the MW problem with A and B as the input matrices the (A,B) -MW problem. In this paper we focus on the (A,B) -MW problem for two large Boolean matrices A and B. We consider the case when A and B have a special structure, namely, they are sums of small Boolean rank-one matrices (we call them vectors). In this case, the problem of finding a maximum witness can be reduced to the problem of finding a maximum independent set in a graph. This reduction allows us to apply well-known algorithms for solving the latter problem. As a result, we obtain a polynomial time algorithm for the (A,B) -MW problem.
