Businesses set up shop next to a rival for two reasons. The first is because they want to be close to their customers. If their customers are already going to a rival business, it makes sense to set up shop nearby so that they can get some of those customers. The second reason is because businesses want to be close to their suppliers. If their suppliers are already located near a rival business, it makes sense to set up shop nearby so that they can get cheaper supplies.

It worked. By all the gods, somehow it had worked. Dunstan gazed wearily from the precipice of the crumbling tower. Empty, battered armor and sharpened steel lay in all directions, robbed of their purpose and the promises of soft flesh to tear through. A bitter wind gnawed on the empty battlefield, not a drop of blood or scrap of flesh stained the land other than his own, and that of the figure rising from the thickest hill of plate and chain mail. Even dear, sweet Roman who until a moment ago had been bleeding out in Dunstan's arms, was no more but his empty robes. To call it an invasion would have been a cruel joke. The northern forces had outnumbered the small watchtower many thousands to one. It hadn't been a question of if the tower would fall, but how many minutes they could buy until it did, and if they would be tortured before they died. They were, in many cases literally, already dead. Dunstan hadn't had any other choice..... "You are he who summoned me then?" growled a voice like the grinding wheels of a trebuchet. It hadn't been a question, so much as an acknowledgement. Dunstan swiveled his head, meekly fixing his gaze on the statuesque figure, now joining him at the top of the tower. His pristine, white suit was of a cut that the mage had never seen. A god, one whose true name had been lost to the ages, one of war and commerce, loomed above him. His fierce visage blocked out the sun like a thunderstorm. Dunstan nodded meekly. Much of his own blood had been lost in the exchange, but compared to the thousands now gone, he could hardly allow himself to complain. "What do I call you?" he asked, rising to his feet. The man-beast grasped the empty robes at Dunstan's feet, as though reading something in its very threading. "You may call me Roman," he sneered. His teeth were like ivory, and so sharp that even gazing at the edge of them felt like a paper-cut on Dunstan's eyes. "Now..... where is my war I'd been promised?" "There isn't any. You ended it..... Roman." The mage winced at the desecration of his best friend and comrade's name, "We were but a small fort, made an example of with the sheer number of the northern bandits' forces. I paid the price of summoning you with the flesh, blood and bone of the entire battlefield. We won. The northern bandits are no more. You may leave now, Roman. You have my thanks." Dunstan had expected the god's smirk to fall, to twist into a scowl, but it only broadened, showing yet more rows of sharpened teeth. "Oh no, no, my little wizard friend. That's not how this works," Roman cackled, his laugh like the delighted caw of a thousand battlefield crows, "There will be war. I will not leave until I have my war. I will drink my fill of blood, soldier and peasant alike. I will feast upon a generation yet. And you, you my wizardly friend, will guzzle deeply upon the glory of the victorious general. Such is the contract, and so it shall be." Panic willed Dunstan's broken body into alertness. He filled with a manic energy only the truly terrified ever know. "N-No!" he protested, "We can't! The northern bandits are no more. We took their lord, he lays amongst the sacrificed. There is no more war to be had here!" Dunstan reached to grasp Roman's lapel, to gain some kind of hold on the god, but his fingertips snatched only at air. Another cackle shook the battered tower. "No more war? My foolish friend, surely you jest. Have they no homeland? Have they no allies? Have they no family? If there is truly no more war to be had, worry not, wizard. War is easily made." From every seam in Roman's spotless white tuxedo, dark, stale blood poured, staining his suit nearly jet black if not for the gleam of crimson. The poisoned blood etched the cracks in the stone floor, flowing like a fountain down the tower, seeping into the torn landscape below. It pooled in the armor of the fallen, filling each slowly. In every direction, armor rose, suits filling with the new flesh of faceless figures. The sound of marching echoed through the hills as the strangers departed in every direction. "W-What are those things? Where are they going?" Dunstan again tried to grasp the god's suit, his hands staining with the thick, sludge-like blood. "Answer me, Roman!" he cried in desperation. "Those? Assassins. Saboteurs. Warlords. Politicians.'Misunderstandings' taken just a bit too far. Anyone who might be in just the wrong place at just the wrong time. Heroes. Villains. There are so many ways to start a war. Almost any excuse will do, really." Roman smiled. He looked upon the departing beasts as a doting mother might. "Many will return with armies for you to lead, as I promised you." "Why? Why must this happen, Roman? The price was paid already! Please, by the gods, leave this place and let the horrors end, unfathomable as they already are. Must I pay more, that you might leave? Must I throw myself from this tower to pay your toll?" Roman wrapped an arm around Dunstan as solid as stone, the thick blood rolling down his robes, bloodying them as badly as the previous ' Roman'had. "You thought the soldiers were my toll? Most of them weren't even yours to give, friend. No, no, war is the price that must be paid. This is why the world tried to forget me, why my true name was lost. Throw yourself, if you so wish. You may even find some courage in your plummet, but you will not find death. Dunstan, my friend, you will pay me my war, and in return I will garb you in riches and glory bought in blood. Such is the contract, so it shall be."

Bands like The Sword from Texas, High on Fire from California, Witchcraft from Sweden, and Wolfmother from Australia have been categorized under the label “retro-metal.” Wolfmother’s initial album, *Wolfmother* (2005), drew inspiration from Deep Purple and Led Zeppelin. Airbourne, another Australian group, continued the hard-rocking style established by AC/DC with their first release, *Runnin’ Wild* (2007). The Darkness’ *Permission to Land* (2003), which evoked a convincingly accurate portrayal of ‘80s metal and ‘70s glam, became a massive hit in the UK, achieving five times platinum status. Their second album, *One Way Ticket to Hell… and Back* (2005), reached #11 on the charts before the band dissolved in 2006. Steel Panther cultivated a fanbase through parodies of 80s glam metal, while Swedish bands like Vains of Jenna, Hardcore Superstar, and Crashdiet offered a more dedicated effort to resurrect that genre – often associated with “sleaze metal.”

... or to put it another way, I suppose it could be written that "People hold many opinions about the immoral nature of certain actions just because with no real logical reason for it." This is an opinion I've been trying to quantify for a while now, and my time on CMV has only seemed to reinforce this view. People posting everything from views about the morality of drugs, to homosexuality, etc... and so little of morality seems to make sense. There are taboos against drug use, against incest, against homosexuality, against open sexuality, against so many things. There's this kind of "moral disgust" for things which don't inherently do any harm. Most of the explanations I see for why these things are wrong are generic answers with little thought or reason to them: "It's unnatural," "It's an affront to god," "It just isn't, because it just isn't." As far as I believe morality should be concerned, we should be allowed to do whatever we want with our own bodies so long as nobody else is harmed. If you want to do drugs just because the high makes you happy, and you've been educated and warned about the potential damages to your own body... it is your body and your life, what is wrong? If you're gay and you choose to have consensual homosexual sex and that's what you both decide to do with your bodies, what is wrong? If you want to post nudes online and you feel empowered from it and the comments you get, what is wrong? The only explanation I could honestly come up with is the way others may react to you, but even that is just a biproduct of a culture which creates senseless taboos, and does things like shaming people for being "sluts" or for being gay without any real justification. What sense is there in these taboos, and the kind of bullying and shame that often comes with them? Where is the reasonable justification for deeming things that don't harm others immoral? CMV. The Premier League hosts huffed and puffed before Divock Origi stole behind the Leeds defence to sweep in Trent Alexander-Arnold's right-wing cross from close range. They secured a place in the last four when Wales Under-19 international Woodburn, aged 17 years and 45 days, fired in the second to beat Owen's record by 98 days. Liverpool hit a post through Georginio Wijnaldum shortly before the opener, but the scoreline was somewhat harsh on the Yorkshire side. Leeds winger Kemar Roofe curled against the inside of a post shortly after half-time. Hadi Sacko spurned a good opportunity for the visitors in the opening 10 minutes, and Kyle Bartley nodded a free header wide after the break. Liverpool will find out who they play in the semi-finals when the draw is made after Wednesday's matches. Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp might have claimed his team has "unfinished business" in the EFL Cup, but this competition is clearly not the German's priority this season as the Reds chase the Premier League title and a Champions League return. And that has been clear by his team selections. Klopp, like he did in the earlier rounds, rotated his team by bringing in fringe players and a handful of youngsters, though that was forced in part by the absence of Philippe Coutinho, Roberto Firmino, Daniel Sturridge and Adam Lallana through injury. Without that attacking threat, the home side lacked fluency and potency in the final third until they clicked in the final 15 minutes to reach a record 17th League Cup semi-final. However, a laboured night was capped when Woodburn - on as a second-half substitute having made his debut on Saturday against Sunderland - beat Owen's record by 98 days. It was a special moment for the youngster in front of the Kop and former England striker Owen, who was watching from the main stand. Every one of Woodburn's outfield team-mates came to celebrate the historic moment as Anfield saluted their latest star. Matches between these two clubs may be rare in the modern era - but this is a fixture steeped in history. A rivalry born in the days of Bill Shankly and Don Revie, resurrected in the eras of Kenny Dalglish and Howard Wilkinson, consigned to longer memories post-Gerard Houllier and David O'Leary. And it attracted the imagination of both sets of fans, Leeds bringing almost 5,500 to a capacity crowd of 53,000. While this tie did not have the allure of a title-swinging league match or Wembley cup final of previous eras, it did provide an opportunity for Leeds to test themselves again at the highest level. Following a turbulent few seasons under Italian owner Massimo Cellino, there is a cautious optimism among Whites fans that their club may - finally - push for promotion back to the Premier League this season. Manager Garry Monk has provided a calm guidance rarely seen - or allowed - under Cellino's control, moving the club up to fifth in the Championship after four wins in their past five matches. The odds were stacked heavily in favour of the home side prior to kick-off, but the visitors created several decent opportunities against a casual Reds defence. Ultimately, they lost with a fight. But the reception given by the away fans to their players at the final whistle suggests they are optimistic a 13-year absence from the Premier League may be coming to an end in the near future. Leeds United manager Garry Monk: "I asked them to play in slightly different way to what we have been doing tactically, which we had to do against a very good side "We followed it to a tee. It just lacked us taking one of quite a few opportunities. We had the best chances of the game. "It needed a bit more composure, that's the only negative. Better decision-making in the final third and we would have had a couple of goals. Overall I was gutted for the players. "As a performance for a young, inexperienced team these type of nights set a marker for you. We're growing. We are disappointed but they will look back in time and think we have put on a good performance "I'm not going to criticise my team - they were excellent." Pens dry out due to the presence of solvents within the ink, which evaporate when exposed to air. Caps offer some protection against evaporation, especially when minimizing airflow, but aren’t entirely effective.  Holes in the cap were designed to reduce the risk of choking if a child accidentally ingests a pen part. However, it’s important to note that the primary purpose of the cap is to prevent unwanted marks—for instance, when pens are placed in bags or pockets. There's also an inner cap with holes beneath the larger cap, preventing direct airflow to the pen’s tip.  Regarding the hole design, it stems partly from liability concerns related to children chewing on caps. Furthermore, many ballpoint pens utilize a spring mechanism that only activates when the cap is removed, allowing ink flow. Interestingly, some pens lack visible holes in their caps altogether.

Having a child is a complete gamble. The child can be potentially ugly, unintelligent, have bad social skills, be untalented, develop chronic pain or have some sort of medical condition, develop a mental illness, die tragically in a disasteraccident, or be murdered at random and that's only the beginning. When you bring a child into this world, you are literally guaranteeing that it must go to school (something all kids dread), worry about making friends, worry about performing well at school and in final exams so that it can finally go to college andor get a job as a wage slave. You are literally guaranteeing in the first world they will have to get a job and work their asses off to get by. Is that really all "worth it" for any tiny bits of pleasure they can experience here and there? And that's the first world. Don't even get me started on having kids in the third world. There is an inherent asymmetry between pain and pleasure. For example, would you take 1 hour of the most pure pleasure (some kind of heroin while eating KFC and having sex all at the same time) you have ever experienced if it were to be followed by 1 hour of the most intense pain you could ever experience (being burned alive, having limbs cut off etc)? Probably not. For any conscious being (whether human or non-human) it would have been better never to exist, since coming into being is always an overall harm, and thus worse than non-existence, for that being. Non-existence implies the absence of both pains and pleasures, but whereas the absence of the pains is something good, it is not the case that the absence of the pleasures is bad or something to be deplored. A potential person is not deprived of anything, claims Benatar, by not being brought into existence. Also, many parents willingly bring children into this world when they know life itself isn't even worth it in the long run. They perpetuate the suffering onto their children. When parents say "well, life isn't fair" they unknowingly reveal an important fact about the natalist attitude to life and to children. Life isn't fair, which means, prima facie, that perpetuating it is an injustice. In order to tolerate and extend the injustice of life, persons intent on reproduction must value life more than fairness. Are parents aware of this, and what do they mean when they say "well, life isn't fair"? Do they really stand by this statement, which seems so self-accusing? Lastly, children cannot consent to being brought into the world. They have no say in it, and I bet if they saw their lives before being born they would all choose to stay in a state of non-existence.

The cantons have a permanent constitutional status and, in comparison with the situation in other countries, a high degree of independence. However, there are considerable differences between the individual cantons, most particularly in terms of population and geographical area. Their populations vary between 15,000 (Appenzell Innerrhoden) and 1,253,500 (Zurich), and their area between 37 km2 (14 sq mi) (Basel-Stadt) and 7,105 km2 (2,743 sq mi) (Graubunden). Then, a classmate inquired about the “bumps” and compared them to his brother’s acne. I explained they were my horns, and he excitedly showed his mother, who fled, clutching her rosary. That’s when I started questioning it—was being born with horns natural? I hadn’t noticed anyone else with them before, and I hadn’t really considered it. Like someone with a prominent sternum might overlook their difference, I just assumed my horns were simply part of me. My friend Greg likened it to that. My parents exchanged a look, anticipating the difficult conversation. My father knelt, offered comfort, and reassured me, “It’s natural for you, son, and that’s all that matters.” Since then, that’s been my guiding principle.

Choose a fixed resolution and maintain it consistently. When a game targets 720p, it renders at 1280x720 and either stretches or shrinks it to 1920x1080 or 852x480, respectively—resulting in poor visual quality. PC gamers expect games to run at their monitor’s native resolution, and anything less is considered subpar. Console developers benefit immensely from rendering at a single resolution, allowing for significant simplification during development. Conversely, PC users employ diverse controllers and often remap button functions to fit their unique setups. A survey of World of Warcraft players would likely yield dozens of differing interpretations of button assignments. Consoles share identical hardware – CPU, graphics card, RAM, storage – without background processes interfering, ensuring consistent performance across all systems. However, PCs exhibit extreme variability due to factors such as CPU limitations, GPU bottlenecks, memory constraints, storage speeds, and resource-hogging applications, making optimization unpredictable. Users must be presented with granular settings to allow customization, demanding an understanding of each player’s specific system configuration.

One where neither side held all the cards or needed to win out. No longer were they enemies on opposite sides fighting for control over mankind. Instead they sat together, trying to understand each other better than anyone could hope to do alone. At least he hoped so. James looked around. They'd made their way down farther into the fissure until there was nothing above except more rock walling them in. Still, no sign of the end... nor a raft of drifting survivors. As far as James could tell there might still be thousands of people trapped deep below ground. If only Gennady hadn't lied! They continued walking slowly down toward the bottom while rock walls pinching forward became less frequent and finally disappeared altogether. There was barely room to walk two abreast, and soon they had to turn sideways because the tunnel widened again. Light streamed past them from above creating pools of soft light that danced across smooth stone walls, reflecting back dozens of colors. More of the ancient paintings remained intact here, revealing images in bright tones of blue, green, yellow, and red, covering every surface including sections of sheer white granite. Between images were faint splotches of darker color where centuries-old paint seemed to bleed from cracks and crevices into surrounding areas of fresher paint. But James saw only fragments: odd geometric shapes, animals, religious symbols. Nothing familiar. All he could distinguish were sweeping freehand strokes of red and orange, or dark brown and black swirls. Even the least interesting parts looked beautiful to him. To Ailith he was simply curious how old these pictures were, and whether any meaning was hidden beneath the murals' faded hues. Unbidden, thoughts came into mind so full of questions and curiosity, he forgot himself completely. He wished he could stop thinking so hard. His brain hurt with such great intensity that sleep began creeping closer and nearer. Although he fought against it, exhaustion claimed him fast, bringing on a fitful half dream filled with flames and fireballs. Soon he started dreaming dreamless sleep. When he woke it was almost day full. The girls were asleep beside him. Their clean clothes hung dry and unrumpled on nearby rocks, and Ailith lay curled upon her belly staring up at the sky stretching above her head. Her face glowed with health, and her normally pale skin had taken on a rosy hue. Beyond her spread a view dominated by a vast crater. However it appeared smaller now compared to earlier, as though it had shrunk during its journey toward the center of Earth. In fact, looking closely, you wouldn't have known they stood high atop a massive mountain now, rather than in the middle of a gaping hole. From here James could feel the strain of bearing their world's weight pressing down painfully on top of him. Yet despite the pain, he also found comfort in seeing their home inverted directly overhead. This place was different, after all, as it lacked any life whatsoever. Only stones beaten flat by eons of wind moved among themselves. How strange it must seem to anybody still living above, watching the sun rise or set from space above, but having no idea that right under their feet there lived millions, perhaps billions, of humans who could look across the void and witness the same marvelously proportioned stars? . A team of scientists launched a box containing four types of bacteria and fungus into the stratosphere to expose them to several hours of Mars-like conditions. The experiment found that yeast, fungi, viruses and other pathogens extracted from a single sample can affect or even destroy the cells they contain on Earth, in ways unseen before on any planet. The technique also allowed scientists to optimize the rate at which new microbes take over plants. According to NASA, each of the organisms within one million miles (1.2 billion kilometers) of earth's surface have enough enzymes to filter out microorganisms that are not needed for most food or medicine applications. However, the researchers believe that microbial production may be possible off-the-shelf by investing more energy into their experiments. Using tiny amounts of RNA used to make the enzyme, researchers discovered that the microbes' levels could be increased by up to 15 times. The same amount of RNA is needed to grow the microbes, but the researchers say they need only two one-tenths of this amount to produce the desired results. "This opens up an opportunity to understand how the efficient production and efficiency of microorganisms takes place," said lead author Rohit Uddhav, professor of biological biology at Rutgers University, who was not involved with the research, in a statement. "We will now begin our study."

In the later Imperial era, the burial and commemorative practises of Christian and non-Christians overlapped. Tombs were shared by Christian and non-Christian family members, and the traditional funeral rites and feast of novemdialis found a part-match in the Christian Constitutio Apostolica. The customary offers of wine and food to the dead continued; St Augustine (following St Ambrose) feared that this invited the "drunken" practices of Parentalia but commended funeral feasts as a Christian opportunity to give alms of food to the poor. Christians attended Parentalia and its accompanying Feralia and Caristia in sufficient numbers for the Council of Tours to forbid them in AD 567. Other funerary and commemorative practices were very different. Traditional Roman practice spurned the corpse as a ritual pollution; inscriptions noted the day of birth and duration of life. The Christian Church fostered the veneration of saintly relics, and inscriptions marked the day of death as a transition to "new life."

Edge bundling is crucial for visualizing graphs effectively. To compare it to existing planar drawing techniques, we propose a novel edge-bundling model based on recent work with fan-planar graphs. This model focuses on bundling the endpoints of edges, mirroring the constraints of 1-planarity; we term it “1-fan-bundle-planarity,” permitting no more than one edge crossing within each bundle. We analyze edge density and address several recognition problems across different graph types—general graphs, outer layers, and 2-layer arrangements—considering either single or dual endpoint bundling. Finally, we outline open and complex research inquiries.

Cellular networks of massive MIMO base-stations employing TDDOFDM and relying on uplink training for both downlink and uplink transmission are viewed as an attractive candidate for 5G deployments, as they promise high area spectral and energy efficiencies with relatively simple low-latency operation. We investigate the use of non-orthogonal uplink pilot designs as a means for improving the area spectral efficiency in the downlink of such massive MIMO cellular networks. We develop a class of pilot designs that are locally orthogonal within each cell, while maintaining low inner-product properties between codes in different cells. Using channel estimates provided by observations on these codes, each cell independently serves its locally active users with MU-MIMO transmission that is also designed to mitigate interference to a subset of "strongly interfered" out-of-cell users. As our simulation-based analysis shows, such cellular operation based on the proposed codes yields user-rate CDF improvement with respect to conventional operation, which can be exploited to improve cell andor cell-throughput performance.

Multi-compartment modeling of diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging measurements is necessary for accurate brain connectivity analysis. Existing methods for estimating the number and orientations of fascicles in an imaging voxel either require access to a reference solution of a similar image or have a relatively high bias compared to true values. To resolve these issues, we present a novel method for the recovery of diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DW-MRI) fascicle orientations in each voxel. Our approach estimates a multi-compartment model of the diffusion process in a voxel from the DW-MRI measurements. The multi-compartment model is then solved for each voxel to recover the number and orientations of the fascicles in that voxel. An image-based methodology is employed to reduce the number of unknowns and to efficiently estimate the orientations and locations of the internal nodes of the multi-compartment model. A numerical example illustrates the performance of the proposed method. F. Tsekouras, E. K. Galanis, P. B. Frey, J. E. Schreiner, J. A. Hess, and J. M. Haxby. MRI Fascicle Orientation Estimation. Neuroimage, 113 (2):717-730, July 2015.

The Facility for Rare Isotope Beams aims to create thousands of isotopes never before recorded on Earth. There are 285 isotopes of elements that exist on Earth, but there are thousands more out there in the universe. "A lot of the chemical processes that go on in the universe are still mysteries to us because we don't have the right materials," said Bill Foster, a professor at Fermilab. "When we get this new facility, we will have the materials. It will open the door to many new scientific discoveries." After a four-year wait, the project was given the green light last year. The laboratory has already begun construction. Once complete, FRIB will be the only place on Earth that can make more than 1,000 of the isotopes at the same time. It will produce 15,000 samples a month of isotopes that will go to researchers all over the world. "Isotopes are a bit like the alphabet," said Foster. "You can combine them in different ways and make different words, and the different words all have different properties. They may act differently chemically or even in terms of reacting with other elements." The facility will give scientists an understanding of the inner workings of stars, planets and even the origins of the universe. "What I really hope for is for people to not just use these isotopes to understand what's happening in the universe, but also use them to understand ourselves," said Anna Simons, a PhD student. "There are isotopes that are only found in meteorites, there are isotopes that are only found in the human body, and there are some isotopes that are only found in plants. So if you know the isotope of an element, you can use that to learn more about what it's doing." FRIB will open for business in 2017. Facility for Rare Isotope Beams, FRIB, Fermilab

This paper introduces a method for creating folds for complex data structures utilizing dependent types. These “dependently typed folds” possess several key characteristics: (1) They rely on well-founded recursion and are implementable within complete dependently typed languages. (2) Unlike standard approaches, they avoid reliance on mappings and numerous terminating functions, allowing for their construction with dependently typed folds. (3) Induction rules for nested data types naturally arise from these fold definitions, and the programs generated by them can be rigorously checked through formal verification. (4) These dependently typed folds apply universally to all nested data types and can be simplified into conventional higher-order folds. Through illustrative examples, we demonstrate programming techniques and reasoning processes related to dependently typed folds, alongside methods for generating them generally and tailoring them to familiar higher-order folds.

Automatic software plagiarism detection tools are widely used in educational settings to ensure that submitted work was not copied. These tools have grown in use together with the rise in popularity of online education and the increased use of computers in educational environments. Automatic software plagiarism detection tools are typically programmed to search for text that is identical or nearly identical to text found on other webpages, databases, or previous assignments. These tools can compare texts from different sources or between multiple documents, and then generate a report indicating the degree of similarity. This report can be used by instructors to determine if any part of a student's work has been plagiarized. In addition to accuracy and speed, these tools must also protect the privacy of both students and instructors. To ensure security, some software contains features such as data encryption, authentication, and authorization. Finally, automatic software plagiarism detection tools should also be user-friendly and easy to use. Terra preta (black earth), which is distributed over large areas in the Amazon forest, is now widely accepted as a product of indigenous soil management. The development of this fertile land was supported by rainforest vegetation that allowed it to be harvested and used for cattle feed without spreading fire across its surface during dry periods or clearing out thickets with herbicides before planting crops such as soybeans.[22] In contrast, the grasses found on the plateau are low-growing species whose seeds must compete among themselves for light from the sun, water, nutrients and moisture. They do not produce much biomass while they grow because their leaves absorb more power than they release; the extra energy costs them valuable time needed to germinate so these plants cannot reach sufficient size to sustain vegetative growth until the end of rainy seasons. Their small seedlings die off early during droughts, when rainfall drops below 60 cmyear,[2425] meaning they can never develop into trees, shrubs or other forms of habitat suitable for birds, mammals and insects. In addition, the shallow root systems make drainage difficult even though most soils there are at least moderately well drained compared to those at higher elevations[26]. The soil found deep within the Andean mountains has been especially hardy for millennia. It contains high levels of calcium carbonate, an important element for the storage of organic matter produced by decomposing organic material like dead animals, roots, mushrooms, fungi, leaves, fruit skins, seeds and leavings - insect larvae pheromones, bird droppings and mold spores, broken bones and soft tissue. Calcium carbonates also help bind together clay minerals in the soil. This makes erosion unlikely and allows the formation stable humus layers around new plants growing after rains. Strong alkaline soils contain less calcium carbonate and react easily with neighboring acidic soil types, often causing the loss of individual cells along with the surrounding biotic community beneath them. According to the 25th Amendment, if the Vice President and a majority of the executive department heads – or another congressional body designated by law – formally declare the President incapable of fulfilling their presidential role, the Vice President becomes Acting President immediately. The President can also voluntarily transfer power to the Vice President for a limited time, and later reinstate himself with another declaration. However, if the President is unable to do so, the Vice President, supported by a majority of the Cabinet, can take over. The President might try to reclaim authority, but the Vice President and Cabinet can challenge this action, leaving Congress to ultimately resolve the dispute.

Modern science is dominated by scientific productions from teams. Large teams have demonstrated a clear advantage over small teams in applying for funding, performing complicated research and producing works with high impact. A recent finding, however, shows that both large and small teams are essential in research, prompting us to analyze the extent to which a country's scientific work is carried out by bigsmall teams. Here, using over 26 million papers from Web of Science, we find that China's research output is more dominated by big teams than the rest of the world, followed by a sharp drop since 2000. As research teams in China shift from small to large size, the team diversity that is essential for innovative works does not increase as much as that in other countries. Using the national average as the baseline, we find that the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) supports fewer small team works than the National Science Foundation of U.S. (NSF) does, implying that big teams are more preferred by grant agencies in China. Our finding provides new insights into the concern of originality and innovation in China, which urges a need to balance small and big teams.

Unlike nonconvex optimization, where gradient descent is guaranteed to converge to a local optimizer, algorithms for nonconvex-nonconcave minimax optimization can have topologically different solution paths: sometimes converging to a solution, sometimes never converging and instead following a limit cycle, and sometimes diverging. In this paper, we study the limiting behaviors of three classic minimax algorithms: gradient decent ascent (GDA), alternating gradient decent ascent (AGDA), and the extragradient method (EGM). Numerically, we observe that all of these limiting behaviors can arise in Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) training. To explain these different behaviors, we study the high-order resolution continuous-time dynamics that correspond to each algorithm, which results in the sufficient (and almost necessary) conditions for the local convergence by each method. Moreover, this ODE perspective allows us to characterize the phase transition between these different limiting behaviors caused by introducing regularization in the problem instance.

Survival rates in falls from great distances depend heavily on where and how the impact occurs. Typically, those who live are cushioned by a remarkably soft surface or experience a deceleration before hitting the ground.  Most fatalities result from direct impact. When falling, the body accelerates due to air resistance, reaching approximately 122 mph within about 15 seconds. Reducing speed through techniques like controlling descent and trajectory—angling the fall—and landing on softer surfaces like deep snow can improve chances of survival, though injuries remain likely. A physically fit individual has a better probability of survival than someone older. While there are documented instances of survivors, dramatic tales of survival from extreme drops tend to overshadow these events.

These approaches were evaluated on a SKU clustering application – predicting promotional halo and cannibalization impacts – using actual retail data from a major supermarket.  Specifically, retailers use this technique to group SKUs according to their seasonal responses to promotions, employing regressions with promotional factors and seasonal indicators within each cluster. Performance was assessed against both real and simulated datasets.

Organisms rely on multiple defenses against infection, encompassing physical, chemical, and biological mechanisms. Structures like leaf cuticles, insect exoskeletons, eggshells, and skin provide initial protection through physical barriers. Yet, since complete isolation is impossible, specialized systems defend vulnerable areas like the lungs, digestive system, and reproductive organs. For instance, coughing and sneezing expel pathogens in the lungs, while tears and urine flush out microbes, and mucus traps and immobilizes microorganisms within the respiratory and intestinal tracts.

King Edward's Chair (or St Edward's Chair), the throne on which English and British sovereigns have been seated at the moment of coronation, is housed within the abbey and has been used at every coronation since 1308. From 1301 to 1996 (except for a short time in 1950 when it was temporarily stolen by Scottish nationalists), the chair also housed the Stone of Scone upon which the kings of Scots are crowned. Although the Stone is now kept in Scotland, in Edinburgh Castle, at future coronations it is intended that the Stone will be returned to St Edward's Chair for use during the coronation ceremony.[citation needed]

Despite criticism for ending the MyTravelPass program—which offered discounted bus fares for 16-18 year olds—the Welsh Government has reversed course and decided to extend it through April, pending the introduction of a new scheme slated for 2018. MyTravelPass originated from a previous budget agreement with the Liberal Democrats. Initially announced for termination in January, the scheme faced opposition from bus companies and Assembly Members like Lynne Neagle. CPT Cymru argued it lacked sufficient promotion and saw low usage rates. The Welsh Government initially framed the program as a temporary pilot with funding concluding in March 2017, citing limited travel outside local areas. However, Economy Secretary Ken Skates stated there’s demand for such a scheme and announced a consultation for a future youth travel pass, beginning in 2018. Existing arrangements will remain operational across Wales until April 1st, 2017, and he requested CPT develop a new marketing strategy. Carmen Smith, deputy president of NUS Wales, supported the extension, suggesting it should encompass learners up to age 25. Welsh Liberal Democrats also approved the change, while Conservative spokesperson Mohammad Asghar characterized it as a predictable reversal, reiterating concerns about the department’s management record.

The invention of electronic computers in the 1940s, along with the development of mathematical information theory, led to a realization that brains can potentially be understood as information processing systems. This concept formed the basis of the field of cybernetics, and eventually gave rise to the field now known as computational neuroscience. The earliest attempts at cybernetics were somewhat crude in that they treated the brain as essentially a digital computer in disguise, as for example in John von Neumann's 1958 book, The Computer and the Brain. Over the years, though, accumulating information about the electrical responses of brain cells recorded from behaving animals has steadily moved theoretical concepts in the direction of increasing realism.

Human-machine interaction is increasingly dependent on speech communication. Machine Learning models are usually applied to interpret human speech commands. However, these models can be fooled by adversarial examples, which are inputs intentionally perturbed to produce a wrong prediction without being noticed. While much research has been focused on developing new techniques to generate adversarial perturbations, less attention has been given to aspects that determine whether and how the perturbations are noticed by humans. This question is relevant since high fooling rates of proposed adversarial perturbation strategies are only valuable if the perturbations are not detectable. In this paper we investigate to which extent the distortion metrics proposed in the literature for audio adversarial examples, and which are commonly applied to evaluate the effectiveness of methods for generating these attacks, are a reliable measure of the human perception of the perturbations. Using an analytical framework, and an experiment in which 18 subjects evaluate audio adversarial examples, we demonstrate that the metrics employed by convention are not a reliable measure of the perceptual similarity of adversarial examples in the audio domain.

Following the formation of the German Empire in 1871, Prussia emerged as its dominant power. Yet, the Treaty of Versailles significantly altered the region’s geography; West Prussia was ceded to Poland, creating a Polish Corridor that isolated East Prussia from mainland Germany, and the Memel Territory was transferred to Lithuania in 1923. After World War II, with the collapse of Nazi Germany in 1945, East Prussia was partitioned by the Soviet Union (becoming the Kaliningrad Oblast within the Russian SFSR and parts of the Klaipeda Region in the Lithuanian SSR) and Poland (as the Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship). The city of Königsberg was subsequently renamed Kaliningrad in 1946.  During the conflict, the German inhabitants were primarily evacuated or forcibly removed, resulting in approximately 300,000 deaths – roughly one-fifth of the pre-war population – due to wartime bombing and resistance efforts.

The perception that in some areas police had lost control of the streets was the most important reason disorder spread, they said. The Home Affairs Committee said insufficient numbers of officers were initially deployed and police training for public disorder was inadequate. The Metropolitan Police said it had outlined what it was doing to improve. The Policing Large Scale Disorder: Lessons from the disturbances of August 2011 report said flooding the streets with police was what ultimately quelled the disorder. "If numbers could have been increased more rapidly, it is possible that some of the disturbances could have been avoided," it said. "We regret this did not happen and, with the benefit of hindsight, we regard the operation to police the disorder in many towns and cities, and particularly in London as flawed." It said the mutual aid system, under which police officers are transferred to forces in need, could have operated more quickly; it may have left areas which had loaned officers to other forces "vulnerable." The report said anecdotal evidence from some of those convicted suggested the widespread disorder started when people saw police had "lost control" in Tottenham via television and social media. This echoes the findings of the independent Riots Communities and Victims Panel. "Clearly a feeling existed that desirable consumer goods could be made available by looting. There was a substantial element of opportunistic criminality and copycat behaviour," the report said. "The absence of a police presence or sight of police officers apparently standing by and allowing criminal behaviour to take place was distressing for those whose homes and businesses were being attacked," it added. Committee chairman Keith Vaz MP said: "Individual police officers acted with great bravery, and we commend them for their actions. However, in London and other areas, in contrast with the effectiveness of police responses in some towns and cities, there was a failure of police tactics. "This situation might have been avoided had police appreciated the magnitude of the task. "We urgently require a rapid improvement in police training to deal with public disorder. We urge the police to act more quickly in future and to review the arrangements for loaning officers from one force to another in this type of scenario." He said that, for those who lost their homes and businesses, "the state effectively ceased to exist - sometimes for hours at a time." Mr Vaz told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the committee felt that there should have been better communication between the police and the local business community to ensure that people knew what was happening and how best to protect their livelihoods. "Those areas where the chief constables had decided to take pre-emptive action and get police officers on the streets quickly were able to contain this violence much more effectively," he added. The MPs say had more officers been deployed different tactics could have been used. The Met Police is training more police to use baton rounds and is considering buying three water cannon. Mr Vaz said the committee did not feel water cannon would have helped police in the riots and may have caused "even greater disorders." Riots broke out in Tottenham, north London, on 6 August, two days after the fatal shooting by police of 29-year-old Mark Duggan. Unrest spread across London and to other cities, including Manchester, Birmingham and Bristol over the following days. But the committee's report said the specific causes behind the riots were still unknown. The report criticised the Met Police and the Independent Police Complaints Commission over failures in communication with Mr Duggan's family, which it said made a potentially tense situation worse. The committee also concluded it would be unhelpful to switch off social media during times of disorder, following claims rioters used it to organise themselves. "People who made an active decision to join in the disorder could equally well have heard about it on the television as on social media," the report said. The MPs say the government needs to urgently clarify whether the police authorities will be able to recover the PS89.827m it cost to police the riots. It says the riots were an exceptional series of events at a time the authorities were being asked to make savings. They also call on the government to speed up the process of reimbursing people under the Riot Damages Act. The Met Police said it had already recognised and publicised some of its findings on the issues identified and what it was doing to improve. A spokesman said: "This includes acknowledging that we didn't have enough officers available quickly enough to respond to the initial disorder or its subsequent unprecedented escalation. As a result we have changed our mobilisation plans." He added that the force was reviewing how it engaged with local communities and was working with Acpo and the IPCC to ensure communication was more effective in future investigations. The Association of Chief Police Officers said the report had identified issues it believed was critical to get right within current policing reforms. "This includes the capacity and ability to move sufficient numbers of police officers around the country when required to protect the public from national threats," a spokesman said. "We will continue to look at all the various reports into the disorder to examine how the police service can best respond in future to the kind of exceptional criminality seen in August."

The U.S. dollar was created by the Constitution and defined by the Coinage Act of 1792. It specified a "dollar" to be based in the Spanish milled dollar and of 371 grains and 4 sixteenths part of a grain of pure or 416 grains (27.0 g) of standard silver and an "eagle" to be 247 and 4 eighths of a grain or 270 grains (17 g) of gold (again depending on purity). The choice of the value 371 grains arose from Alexander Hamilton's decision to base the new American unit on the average weight of a selection of worn Spanish dollars. Hamilton got the treasury to weigh a sample of Spanish dollars and the average weight came out to be 371 grains. A new Spanish dollar was usually about 377 grains in weight, and so the new U.S. dollar was at a slight discount in relation to the Spanish dollar.

In recent years, the town of Wenatchee, Washington has become a hub for bitcoin mining. And now, local officials are grappling with how to deal with the influx of miners who are drawn to the area by its cheap hydropower. The problem began last year, when the city of Wenatchee's electric utility started receiving complaints from residents about high electricity bills. The utility investigated and found that some of its customers were using more than 10 times the amount of power than the average household. After some digging, the utility discovered that many of these homes were being used as bitcoin mines. Bitcoin mining is a process of verifying and adding transaction records to the public ledger, known as the blockchain. It's a computationally intensive process that requires a lot of energy. In Wenatchee, miners are attracted by the cheap hydropower that is generated by the Columbia River. But as more and more miners move into the area, local officials are concerned about the impact on the town's infrastructure and quality of life. The city council is currently considering an ordinance that would regulate bitcoin mining operations. Under the proposed ordinance, miners would be required to obtain a business license and pay a 500 fee. They would also be subject to inspections to ensure that their operations are safe and do not pose a nuisance to their neighbors. The ordinance has divided the community, with some people welcoming the regulation of bitcoin mining and others concerned that it will stifle innovation. The city council is expected to vote on the ordinance in the coming weeks. Whether or not the ordinance passes, it's clear that the town of Wenatchee is facing a challenges as it grapple with the influx of bitcoin miners.

It is an ill-posed problem to recover the true scene colors from a color biased image by discounting the effects of scene illuminant and camera spectral sensitivity (CSS) at the same time, because the spectral reflectance curves and the spectral sensitivity curves are correlated. A new color correction method is proposed for color biased images based on a linear image inversion approach. The proposed method is based on the principle that the spectral reflectance and the spectral sensitivity are inversely proportional. The spectral reflectance is first inverted into spectral sensitivity, and then the spectral sensitivity is used to invert the spectral reflectance into the true color by minimizing the least-squares method. The color correction results of the scene colors in a color biased image are visualized in the image. In 2012, Abigail Fisher, an undergraduate student at Louisiana State University, and Rachel Multer Michalewicz, a law student at Southern Methodist University, filed a lawsuit to challenge the University of Texas admissions policy, asserting it had a "race-conscious policy" that "violated their civil and constitutional rights." The University of Texas employs the "Top Ten Percent Law," under which admission to any public college or university in Texas is guaranteed to high school students who graduate in the top ten percent of their high school class. Fisher has brought the admissions policy to court because she believes that she was denied acceptance to the University of Texas based on her race, and thus, her right to equal protection according to the 14th Amendment was violated. The Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Fisher on October 10, 2012, and rendered an ambiguous ruling in 2013 that sent the case back to the lower court, stipulating only that the University must demonstrate that it could not achieve diversity through other, non-race sensitive means. In July 2014, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit concluded that U of T maintained a "holistic" approach in its application of affirmative action, and could continue the practice. On February 10, 2015, lawyers for Fisher filed a new case in the Supreme Court. It is a renewed complaint that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit got the issue wrong - on the second try as well as on the first. The Supreme Court agreed in June 2015 to hear the case a second time. It will likely be decided by June 2016.

Ford approached the ring and dropped his heavy peacoat. Beneath he wore an argyle sweater vest over white button down, complete with corduroy pants.
